passages.title: The Qur'an as reminder, not burden
passages.tafsir:
**In brief.** Sūrah Ṭā-Hā opens by answering a taunt with a portrait. The idolaters of Quraysh had said that this Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ only to cause him distress. Ayat 2–3 deny that outright. Ayat 4–8 answer the very same charge from a completely different angle — not by arguing back, but by telling you *Who* sent the Book down. That is what holds these eight ayat together as one passage: the Book is defended here not by debate but by identification. It comes from the One who created the earth and the high heavens, who owns everything above you, between, and beneath the soil, who hears the word you say aloud and knows the thought that has not yet formed in your mind, and to whom belong the Most Beautiful Names. A Book from such a Sender cannot be a weight laid on a servant's back. As Qatadah said of it: He made it "a mercy, a light and a guide to Paradise."

## Ṭā-Hā: the sūrah begins by drawing a line

Ibn Kathir passes over the opening letters quickly. He has already discussed the separated letters that begin several sūrahs at the start of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and sees no need to repeat that discussion here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the range of views. Ibn ʿAbbās took *Ṭā-Hā* to mean *yā rajul* — "O man." Ibn ʿUmar took it to mean *yā ḥabībī* — "O my Dear." It has also been suggested that *Ṭā-Hā* and *Yā-Sīn* are names of the Prophet ﷺ. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges the most obvious explanation to be the one given by Abū Bakr and the majority of scholars: like the other isolated letters that open several chapters of the Qur'an — *Alif-Lām-Mīm* and the rest — this word belongs to the **mutashābihāt**, the mysteries whose meaning is known only to Allah.

It is worth pausing there, because the same posture is asked of you three more times before this passage ends. At the Throne in ayah 5, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will say that *istiwāʾ* is likewise mutashābihāt, its nature known to nobody. At "beneath the soil" in ayah 6, it will say that human knowledge simply does not reach past a certain depth. And in ayah 7, it will point out that a man does not know what thoughts will come to his own mind in the days ahead. The sūrah opens by handing you two letters you cannot decode, and then keeps showing you the edge of what you were given — while telling you, in the same breath, everything you actually need.

## The taunt, and the tenderness of the reply

Ibn Kathir gives us the occasion. Juwaybir reported that aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said: when Allah sent the Qur'an down to His Messenger ﷺ, he and his Companions adhered to it — and so the idolaters of Quraysh said, *"This Qur'an was only revealed to Muhammad to cause him distress."* Therefore Allah revealed: *Ṭā-Hā. We have not sent down the Qur'an unto you to cause you distress, but only as a Reminder to those who fear (Allah).*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what those mockers were actually looking at. In the early days of Islam, when the Qur'an was first revealed, the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions used to spend whole nights in prayer and in reciting the Qur'an, until his feet would swell from standing for long hours in prayer. And during the day he would worry over how to bring light to those who rejected the message. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Ibn Kathir's narration, that while the believers spent whole nights in prayer the disbelievers mocked and taunted them, saying that the revelation of the Qur'an had brought them nothing but hardship and allowed them no rest and peace.

Read the ayah again with that in front of you and its tenderness becomes unmistakable. The taunt was aimed at the Prophet ﷺ, but the reply is addressed *to* him, not to them. Before Allah corrects the slander, He lifts something off His Messenger's shoulders.

**The word.** *Li-tashqā* is derived from **shaqāʾ**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as pain and distress. Allah is saying: *this* is not why the Book came down. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah as seeking to lessen the burden of those long hours of prayer, informing the Prophet ﷺ that the Qur'an was not revealed to inflict toil and hardship on him, and that it was not expected of him to stay awake the whole night reciting. Thereafter, it notes, he ﷺ adopted a routine: resting in the early hours of the night, and getting up later to offer the salāh of tahajjud.

Mujahid, cited by Ibn Kathir, reads the ayah alongside *"So recite as much of the Qur'an as may be easy for you"* (73:20), and mentions how far people had gone: they used to hang ropes at their chests, to hang on to when tired, in the prayer.

Qatadah's comment is the one to memorise. On *We have not sent down the Qur'an unto you to cause you distress*, he said: **"No, by Allah, He did not make it a thing of distress. Rather, He made it a mercy, a light and a guide to Paradise."**

Notice what is denied and what is not. The night prayer is not cancelled; the Prophet ﷺ went on praying tahajjud. What is denied is the *purpose*. The Qur'an did not come down in order to grind a servant down. Effort in worship is real — but exhaustion was never the point.

## What the Book is, and who receives it

Ayah 3 states the purpose positively: *but only as a Reminder to those who fear (Allah)* — rendered in another translation as *a reminder to those in awe of Allah*. Ibn Kathir explains what that means in practice: Allah revealed His Book and sent His Messenger ﷺ as a mercy for His servants, so that the person who reflects may be reminded. Thus a man will benefit from what he hears of the Book of Allah — a remembrance in which Allah revealed what He permits and what He prohibits.

So the Book is offered as mercy; but the ayah also names the one in whose hands it becomes a reminder — the one who fears Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the contrast sharply against the mockers: these people could not sense that the Qur'an, and the knowledge communicated through it, can bring only blessings and felicity — and they could not sense it because they were ignorant and misguided.

Ibn Kathir draws the same conclusion and turns it into a principle: the matter is not as the people of falsehood claim. Rather, whomever Allah gives knowledge to, it is because Allah wants him to have an abundance of good. He supports this with a hadith **confirmed in the Two Sahihs**, on the authority of Ibn Masʿūd, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Whomever Allah wants good for, then He gives him the understanding of the religion."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same teaching in a hadith related by Muʿāwiyah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "When Allah intends to reward a person, He gives him the correct perception of religion" — attributing it to the **Sahihain**.

So the Quraysh had it exactly inverted. What they pointed at as hardship inflicted on Muhammad ﷺ was in fact evidence of Allah wanting an abundance of good for him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then quotes a further hadith, which it says Ibn Kathir recorded, related by **Ṭabarānī** from Thaʿlabah ibn al-Ḥakam, and which it calls good news for the learned. The Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Judgment, when Allah will ascend His Kursī (Chair) to pronounce judgment on the actions of His servants, He will tell the learned people that He had placed His knowledge and wisdom in their hearts for the sole reason that He wished to forgive them in spite of their failings, and that these matters were of no concern to Him.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān immediately guards the door: it is evident that the "learned people" in this hadith are only those who possess the fear of Allah, which is a sure sign of Qur'anic knowledge. Which is precisely the standard ayah 3 had already set — *a Reminder to those who fear*. Knowledge that has not produced fear of Allah is not the knowledge being praised.

*(On the mention of Allah's Kursī here, and of the Throne in ayah 5, the way of the Salaf applies: we affirm what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ affirmed, without describing how, without likening it to anything in creation, and without explaining it away.)*

## The real answer to the taunt: naming the Sender

Having denied the charge, the passage does something you might not expect. It does not argue the point further. It turns and describes the One the Book came from — and the description keeps moving: reaching down and up, then out across everything owned, then inward past where you yourself can see, until it comes to rest on a Name.

It begins at the origin. *A revelation from Him Who created the earth and high heavens* (20:4). Ibn Kathir explains: this Qur'an, which has come to you, O Muhammad ﷺ, is a revelation from your Lord. He is the Lord of everything and its King, Most Able to do whatever He wills. He created the earth with its low depths and dense regions, and He created the lofty heavens with their high altitudes and their subtleties. One sentence reaches to the bottom of the earth and to the top of the heavens. To convey something of that upper reach, Ibn Kathir cites a hadith which **At-Tirmidhi** and others graded as authentic: the density of each sky of the heavens is the distance of five hundred years' travel, and the distance between it and the next heaven is also five hundred years. Now set that beside a man standing in prayer at night until his feet swell — and hear the sentence again: *this* is not what We sent it down for.

From origin the passage moves to sovereignty: *The Most Gracious Istawa the Throne* (20:5). Of all the names that could stand at the mention of the Throne, the one used here is **ar-Raḥmān**, the Most Gracious — in a passage whose whole burden is that this Book is a mercy and not a punishment. On *istawā* itself, both sources say the same thing and stop in the same place. Ibn Kathir refers back to his discussion in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf and states the rule: the safest path to take in understanding this is the way of the Salaf, the predecessors — to accept what has been reported concerning it from the Book and the Sunnah without describing it, without reinterpreting it, without resembling it to creation, without rejecting it, and without comparing it to the attributes of creatures. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds with the majority of the early scholars: the exact nature of *istiwāʾ* is not known to anybody; it is included in the mutashābihāt. A Muslim has to believe that Allah's *istiwāʾ* over the Throne is true, its nature in accordance with the high attributes of Allah — while nobody can comprehend it in this world.

From sovereignty to ownership: *To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth, and all that is between them, and all that is under the soil* (20:6). Four sweeps, and nothing is left outside them. Ibn Kathir: all of this is owned by Him and in His grasp, under His control, will, intent and judgement; He created all of this, He owns it, and He alone is the true Deity of all of it — there is no true god other than He and no Lord other than He. The final sweep is the one that catches you. **Ath-tharā**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is wet earth — the damp soil that comes out after digging to a certain depth. Human knowledge does not go beyond it; what lies below is known only to Allah. It illustrates this with the drilling attempts reported in the newspapers of its day: with the latest and most sophisticated instruments, researchers were able to penetrate only to a depth of six miles, after which they met a rock casing they could not bore through — six miles of data on a body whose diameter runs to thousands of miles. One has to admit, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, that knowledge of what is below the soil is a special attribute of Allah. Ibn Kathir records Muhammad bin Kaʿb's explanation of *all that is under the soil*: that which is beneath the seventh earth.

Then the passage turns inward, and this is where it becomes personal: *And if you speak aloud, then verily, He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden* (20:7). Ibn Kathir ties it straight back to ayah 4 — He Who revealed this Qur'an is the same One who created the high heavens and the earth, and He knows what is secret and what is even more hidden; as Allah says elsewhere, *"Say: It has been sent down by Him Who knows the secret of the heavens and the earth. Truly, He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (25:6).

Then comes the definition that makes the ayah unforgettable. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: **the secret** is what the son of Adam hides within himself, and **that which is yet more hidden** is the deeds of the son of Adam which are hidden *before he does them* — and Allah knows all of that. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same sense: *sirr* is what a man hides in his heart and no one else knows; *akhfā* is a thought which has not even formed in his mind and will take shape later on. Allah is fully aware both of what a man is concealing in his heart at this moment and of what thoughts he will entertain in the future — while the man himself does not know what will come to his mind in the days to come.

Ibn ʿAbbās adds that Allah's knowledge encompasses what has passed and what is to come, and it is one complete knowledge, so that in this regard all creatures are as one soul to Him — which is the meaning of *"The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as a single person"* (31:28).

Feel the movement the ayah has just made. It started with speech raised out loud, went inward to the secret you tell no one, and then went further in than *you* can go — to the thought that is not yet yours.

And there the passage comes to rest: *Allah! There is no god but Him! To Him belong the Best Names* (20:8). Ibn Kathir: He Who revealed this Qur'an to you, O Muhammad ﷺ, is Allah; there is no god except Him; He is the Owner of the Best Names and the most lofty attributes. Everything the passage has laid out — creation, Throne, ownership, knowledge — funnels into this one line. He alone made it, He alone owns it, He alone knows it; therefore He alone is worshipped. And the last thing said about Him is not His power but the beauty of His Names.

## Living it

**Serve the Book; do not let it crush you.** These ayat came to a man whose feet had swollen from standing in prayer, and what they told him was that the Qur'an was not revealed to inflict toil and hardship on him. If your practice has turned into a machine that grinds you down, this passage is speaking to you: recite what is easy, rest in the early part of the night and rise later for tahajjud, and do not measure your faith by your exhaustion. As Qatadah said, He made it a mercy, a light and a guide to Paradise.

**Convey; do not carry the result.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a second consolation out of ayah 2: the duty of the Prophet ﷺ was merely to convey the message of Allah, and thereafter he need not concern himself with who accepted it and who did not. Whoever calls to Allah today inherits that relief. You are answerable for the delivery, not for the outcome.

**Let knowledge produce fear of Allah, or it is not the knowledge being praised.** The hadith about Allah's mercy toward the learned is glorious — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say that it applies only to those who possess the fear of Allah, which is the sure sign of Qur'anic knowledge. That is the same condition ayah 3 set for benefiting from the Book at all.

**Take seriously that He knows what you have not thought yet.** Ayah 7 is not offered as a threat but as a description of the One you are dealing with. It should embarrass the private sin and comfort the private grief in equal measure: the intention no one saw is known, and the pain you have never managed to put into words is already fully known — by the One to whom, ayah 8 tells us, belong the Best Names.

passages.title: Moses called at the sacred valley
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These eight ayat carry Musa (peace be upon him) from being a lost traveller on a freezing night to being a prophet spoken to directly by his Lord. A man walks toward a fire hoping for a hot coal and for someone to show him the road — and what he finds is Allah, giving him the road in the deepest sense: His oneness, revelation, prayer, and the certainty of the Hour.

## Why this story, and why here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the ayat just before this spoke of the greatness of the Qur'an and the reverence due to the Prophet ﷺ. The story of Musa follows so that the Prophet ﷺ would become fully aware of the trials and tribulations that afflict prophets in discharging their missions, and of the courage and fortitude with which the earlier prophets bore them — preparation for the great mission entrusted to him. The Qur'an states this purpose plainly elsewhere: "And We narrate to you everything from the events of the messengers with which We strengthen your heart" (11:120).

The question in ayah 9 — *"And has there come to you the story of Musa?"* — is meant to steady the one being addressed. Ibn Kathir marks this as the point where Allah begins to mention the story of Musa: how revelation began to come to him, and Allah's speaking directly to him.

## A cold night, a pregnant wife, a lost road (ayah 10)

Ibn Kathir notes that this came after Musa had completed the time agreed upon between him and his father-in-law, that he would herd sheep. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the terms: at Madyan he stayed with Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) on the understanding that he would serve him for a period of eight or ten years. Then, according to *Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, after that period expired he sought Shuʿayb's permission to proceed to Egypt to see his mother and sister. He had fled Egypt earlier fearing capture or death at the hands of Pharaoh's soldiers, but that danger had now passed with the lapse of so many years. Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) willingly gave permission and sent him away with his wife — Shuʿayb's daughter. Being apprehensive of the hostility of some of the rulers in Syria, Musa took a less frequented route. It was winter, his pregnant wife was very close to confinement, the route was unfamiliar to him, and he lost his bearings.

Ibn Kathir describes the same night: he became lost on the way during a cold, wintry night, and settled down, making camp between some mountain passes and mountains covered with snow, sleet, dense clouds, darkness and fog. He began trying to make a fire with a kindling device he had with him, in order to produce light, as was customary — but it would not kindle anything, and it even stopped giving off sparks. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that, to add to the misery, his wife had begun to experience birth pangs.

Ibn Kathir notes the light appeared to him as a fire glowing from the right side of the mountain from where he was.

**The words he chooses.** Musa says *innī ānastu nāran* — "Verily, I have seen a fire." Then two hopes, and Ibn Kathir shows how each hope quietly reports his situation:

- *bi-qabas* — "some burning brand," meaning a flame from a fire. The parallel ayah calls it *jadhwah* (28:29), which Ibn Kathir explains as a coal that has a burning flame. And there Musa adds *"that you may warm yourselves"* — which, Ibn Kathir says, proves it was in fact cold weather at that time. That he asks for a *qabas* at all proves it was dark.
- *"or find some guidance at the fire"* — meaning someone who can guide him to the road. This, says Ibn Kathir, proves he had lost the road. He supports it with what Ath-Thawri reported from Abu Saʿid al-Aʿwar, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said of this phrase: "This means someone who will guide me to the road. They were cold and had lost their way. Then, when he (Musa) saw the fire he said, 'Either I will find someone who can guide us to the road, or at least I can bring you all some fire that you can kindle with.'"

Note too the word *امكثوا* — "wait here." He tells them to stay, and goes himself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, notes that the presence of his wife on the journey is well established; according to some traditions there was a servant with him who is also addressed, and others say there were some other companions who had been separated when they lost their way.

## The fire that would not burn (ayah 11)

*"And when he came to it, he was called by name: O Musa!"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, from the *Musnad* of Ahmad on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, that when Musa drew near the fire he saw a very strange scene: a fire blazing on a green tree without scorching even a leaf or a branch — the flame instead adding manifold to the beauty and freshness of the tree. He stood there quite a while watching this strange sight, waiting for a chance to pick up a piece of burning wood. At last he collected some dry grass and tried to light it, but as soon as he pushed the grass toward the fire, it retracted. It is also related that the fire advanced toward him and he drew back in consternation. And as he stood there, not knowing what to do, a voice called him. This happened in a plain called Tuwa, which was to his right side and at the foot of the mountain.

**"He was called" — in the passive.** The Arabic *nūdiya* does not name the caller. Ibn Kathir points to another ayah that supplies it: *"He was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree: O Musa! Verily, I am Allah"* (28:30). Here in Ṭā Hā, Allah says instead *"Verily, I am your Lord"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as: the One Who is talking to you and addressing you.

**How did he know it was Allah?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly, and answers it from what is related in *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: the voice appeared to come from all directions and not from any particular direction, and the manner in which it reached his perception was most extraordinary, because it was heard not only through his ears but by the entire body — indeed, says Maʿārif, this was a miracle. Alongside this, Allah had created in his heart the conviction that the voice he heard was really the voice of Allah; and there was the circumstance that the fire, instead of burning the tree, added to its beauty and lustre. What the voice said was that the light he had seen was not fire but a particular kind of divine manifestation.

Under the heading *"Musa learned the words of Allah directly,"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays a report of Wahb mentioned in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* on the authority of the *Musnad* of Ahmad: when the voice called him, "O Musa!", he replied, "I hear the voice, O Allah! But I do not know from where it comes. Where are you, O Allah?" And Allah said, "I am above you, in front of you, to your right and your left. Indeed I am all around you." Then Musa said, "O Allah, do I hear these words from You directly or through an angel sent by You?" And Allah said, "I Myself am speaking to you." Maʿārif adds that according to *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* this proves that Musa heard these spoken words directly from Allah, and that there is a group among the Sunnis who believe that such spoken words can also be heard.

## "Take off your shoes" (ayah 12)

**The sandals themselves.** Ibn Kathir reports that ʿAli bin Abi Talib, Abu Dharr, Abu Ayyub and others of the Salaf said his sandals were from the skin of a donkey that was not slaughtered. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions a related reason: that since shoes are made from the hides of dead animals, they should be removed when entering sacred places.

**Reverence for the place.** Ibn Kathir also reports that it has been said he was commanded to remove his sandals only out of respect for the blessed spot. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this reason first — the command was given because it was a sacred place and it was necessary to remove shoes to show it proper respect — and reports that ʿAli, Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Jurayj supported this first explanation, reasoning that the real purpose was that the soles of his feet should come into contact with the soil of this hallowed place and be blessed thereby. (The two tafsirs place ʿAli on different sides of this.) Others said that by this command Musa was required to show humility, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in earlier times devout and pious believers used to take off their shoes when circumambulating the Kaʿbah.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when the Prophet ﷺ once saw Bashir ibn Khasasia walking through the graves with his shoes on, he said: "When you pass by a place which needs to be respected, take off your shoes." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a useful ruling: all the jurists are unanimous that if shoes are clean they may be worn when offering prayers, and it is established by authentic reports that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions often wore clean shoes when saying prayers — but their common practice appears to have been to remove them, because that is closer to humility.

**Tuwa.** ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "It is the name of the valley." Ibn Kathir notes that others have said the same, that it is merely mentioned as something to give more explanation to the story, and that this first opinion is the most correct. It has also been said that it means "doubly sacred," Tuwa being something that has repetitious blessings. Ibn Kathir compares *"When his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa"* (79:16). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that Allah in His divine wisdom has granted special status to some selected places — the Kaʿbah, the Aqsa Mosque, the Prophet's Mosque — and Wadi Tuwa, situated at the foot of the mount of Ṭūr, is one such sacred place.

## "I have chosen you — so listen" (ayah 13)

*Wa-ana ikhtartuka.* Ibn Kathir reads this alongside *"I have chosen you above men by My Messages, and by My speaking to you"* (7:144), explaining it as meaning over all human beings of that time. He also records — introduced with "it has also been said" — that Allah said, "O Musa, do you know why I chose to speak to you directly out of all of the people?" Musa said, "No." Allah then said, "Because I have not made anyone humble himself as much as you have humbled yourself."

Then: *"So listen to that which will be revealed"* — Ibn Kathir: now listen to what I say to you and what I reveal to you.

**How to listen.** From this word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the etiquette of listening to the recitation of the Qur'an, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: one sits still; refrains from any unnecessary movement; keeps the eyes down; concentrates the mind on understanding the meaning. The person who listens to the Qur'an in this respectful manner is rewarded by Allah with a better understanding of His word.

## The whole religion in one sentence (ayah 14)

*"Verily, I am Allah! There is no god but Me, so worship Me, and perform Salah for My remembrance."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that with these words Allah bestowed upon Musa knowledge of all the basic principles of the true faith: the oneness of Allah, prophethood, and the hereafter. *"So listen to what is revealed"* refers to prophethood; *"so worship Me"* means worship Me alone and no one else, which points to the oneness of Allah; and *"the Hour has to come"* in the next ayah points to the inevitability of the hereafter.

Ibn Kathir calls the declaration *lā ilāha illā anā* the first obligation upon all responsible people of age: that they know there is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, Who has no partners. And *fa'budnī* means: single Me out alone for worship.

**Why prayer is named separately.** Although "worship Me" already encompasses the injunction for prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that prayer has been mentioned separately to stress its special merit relative to the other forms of worship: it is the pillar of the faith, and its neglect is the mark of the infidels.

**"For My remembrance."** Ibn Kathir gives two readings, both held:

1. *"Pray in order to remember Me."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this: the essence of prayer is the remembrance of Allah, and the prayer from beginning to end is nothing but remembering Allah — with the tongue, the heart, and the other organs of the body.
2. *"And establish the prayer whenever you remember Me."* Ibn Kathir cites as supporting evidence for this second statement a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whenever one of you sleeps past the prayer, or he forgets to pray, then let him pray when he remembers it. For verily, Allah said, (And perform Salah for My remembrance.)" And in the Two Sahihs it is reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever slept past the prayer, or forgot it, then his expiation is that he prays it when he remembers it. There is no expiation for it other than that."

That second reading is quietly merciful. A missed prayer is not a closed door; the moment of remembering is when it is to be prayed.

## "The Hour is coming" (ayah 15)

*Inna al-sāʿata ātiyah* — Ibn Kathir: this means that it is established and there is no avoiding it.

**"I am almost hiding it."** The phrase *akādu ukhfīhā* drew careful comment. Ad-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to recite it as, "I almost kept it hidden — from myself," and Ibn ʿAbbas would then say: because nothing is ever hidden from Allah's Self. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means: no one knows its appointed time except Allah. Ibn Kathir joins this to *"Heavy is its burden through the heavens and the earth. It shall not come upon you except all of a sudden"* (7:187) — meaning that its knowledge weighs heavily upon the dwellers of the heavens and the earth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of *akādu*, "I would": Allah says that He wishes to keep the circumstances relating to the Day of Judgement hidden from all created things, including prophets and angels — and the word gives a subtle hint that it is only to induce people to good deeds that the coming of that Day has been disclosed at all; otherwise even this fact would have been concealed.

**"So that every soul may be given a return for the effort it makes."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*) gives two ways of connecting this clause:

- Linked with *"has to come"*: this world is not a place of requital. Here a person does not receive recompense according to his merits, and even if he receives some reward in this world it is just a token, not the full recompense of his deeds. It is therefore essential that there should be a time when everybody receives his due reward.
- Linked with *"I would keep it secret"*: the wisdom in not revealing the time of death and of the Day of Judgement is that people should continue in their endeavours and not cease to strive in the belief that their own death, or that Day, is still far away in the future.

Ibn Kathir summarises: I will certainly reward every person who does something, according to what he did — as in *"So whosoever does good equal to the weight of an atom shall see it. And whosoever does evil equal to the weight of an atom shall see it"* (99:7–8), and *"You are only being requited for what you used to do"* (52:16).

## "Do not let them turn you away" (ayah 16)

*"Therefore, let not the one who believes not therein, but follows his own lusts, divert you therefrom, lest you perish."*

Ibn Kathir says the address here is directed towards all individuals who are responsible and capable of taking heed of this message: do not follow the way of the person who does not believe in the Hour and only pursues his desires in this worldly life, disobeying his Lord. Whoever behaves like these people has indeed failed and lost. *Fa-tardā* means: you will be destroyed and ruined — which Ibn Kathir sets beside *"And what will his wealth avail him when he goes down in destruction?"* (92:11).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: Musa is here cautioned lest he allow himself to be led away by the disbelievers and become negligent about the Day of Judgement, since that would be the cause of his ruination — yet it is clear that a Prophet and Messenger who is impeccable cannot commit such a lapse. The answer given is that the warning, though addressed to him, is meant to warn his followers and mankind at large to be cautious in the matter.

## Living it

The passage begins with a man who has nothing but a flint that will not spark, a freezing family and a lost road, and it ends with the architecture of the whole religion:

- **Listen the way Musa was told to listen.** Still body, lowered eyes, mind concentrated on the meaning — that is what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, draws from *"So listen to what is revealed"* for anyone under recitation.
- **Pray, and pray as remembrance.** The prayer from beginning to end is remembrance of Allah; and when a prayer is genuinely slept through or forgotten, pray it when you remember it.
- **Let the hidden hour make you work, not relax.** On the second reading given in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, the timing of death and of that Day is concealed precisely so that people keep striving and do not slacken on the assumption that both are still far off.

passages.title: The staff, the hand, and the mission
passages.tafsir:
Allah has just spoken to Musa (peace be upon him) in the night. Now, instead of issuing the commission straight away, Allah asks him a question about the stick in his hand — and out of that ordinary shepherd's stick, and out of Musa's own hand, come the two signs that will carry him into Pharaoh's court. What holds ayat 17–24 together is a single movement: from a gentle question (17), through Musa's answer (18), the casting down and the terror and the reassurance (19–21), the second sign in his own body (22), the naming of these as "Our greater signs" (23), and finally the command that everything has been preparing him for — *Go to Fir'awn* (24). Allah does not send him until He has first calmed him and armed him.

## Why Allah asks a question He already knows the answer to

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 17 as the beginning of a special favour. Musa had just seen unusual sights and heard the Divine Word; a man in that state is overwhelmed, and Allah's purpose here was to dispel that fear. So the address turns friendly and conversational — *And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?* — a question that steadies a shaken heart the way a kind voice steadies anyone.

There is also a purpose beneath the kindness. Ibn Kathir gives two explanations: some of the scholars of tafsir said Allah asked this simply to draw Musa's attention to the staff; and it has also been said that it was to *affirm* for him what was in his hand — in other words, "that which is in your right hand is a stick that you are familiar with. You will see what We are about to do to it now." Ibn Kathir describes the wording itself as **an interrogative phrase for the purpose of affirmation** — a question asked not to gain information, but to have the listener confirm what he already knows.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical wisdom in that: the subtle purpose of the question was to make Musa aware that what he held was a staff made of wood and nothing more. And when he had satisfied himself again that it was indeed a wooden staff, only then was the miracle of its turning into a serpent revealed — precluding any doubt in his mind that in the darkness of the night he might have picked up a serpent instead of his staff. The miracle is sealed shut against explanation before it happens.

## Musa's answer — more than the question asked

*It is my staff! I lean on it, and with it I beat down leaves for my sheep, and I have other uses for it* (ayah 18).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers here, and it is the most human moment in the passage. The simple question "What is in your hand?" called for an equally brief answer — "It is a staff." But Musa volunteered additional information outside the scope of what he was asked: first, that the staff belonged to him; second, that it served him in named ways, reclining on it and beating down leaves from trees for his goats; third, that he put it to many other uses. Citing Rūḥ and Mazharī, Maʿārif describes this long and detailed reply as a perfect combination of two things at once: extreme love and adoration on the one hand, and profound reverence on the other. It is a natural human instinct, Maʿārif says, that when a person finds the object of his adoration to be kind and attentive, he wishes to prolong the conversation. Yet the dictates of extreme respect require that it not become too lengthy. So Musa stretched his answer — and then ended it with the brief *and I have other uses for it*, without giving the detail of a single one of them.

That is the etiquette of a servant who is both in love and in awe: say enough to stay in the conversation, not so much that you forget Whose presence you are in.

From this ayah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, **Qurtubi** deduced in his Tafsir that when there is need, it is permissible while answering a question to include matters which are not specifically covered in the question.

**The word *ahushshu***. Ibn Kathir explains *wa ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī* as: "I use it to shake the branches of trees so that the leaves will fall for my sheep to eat them." ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin al-Qāsim reported from **Imam Malik** a beautifully precise definition: it is when a man places his staff into a branch and shakes it so that its leaves and fruit will fall *without breaking the stick* — "It is not the same as striking or beating." Maymūn bin Mahrān said the same. Even the verb is gentle: a shepherd coaxing food down for his animals, not thrashing a tree.

**"And I have other uses for it"** — Ibn Kathir glosses *maʾārib ukhrā* as other benefits, services and needs besides these. He then adds a quiet corrective: some of the scholars took upon themselves the burden of mentioning many of these obscure uses. Musa deliberately left them unnamed; there is little profit in trying to name them for him.

**A prophetic habit.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a rule from this ayah: carrying a staff is a practice followed by the prophets, and the Prophet ﷺ also used to carry a staff in his hand — a practice with numerous religious as well as worldly advantages.

## The staff becomes a serpent

*Throw it down, O Musa!* (19) — Ibn Kathir: "Throw down this stick that is in your right hand, O Musa."

*So he did, then — behold! — it became a serpent, slithering* (20). Ibn Kathir describes what Musa saw: the stick changed into a huge snake, like a long python, and it moved with rapid movements — it moved as if it were the fastest type of small snake, yet it was in the form of the largest snake, while still having the fastest of movements. *Tasʿā*, he says, means moving restlessly. One moment wood; the next, a living thing racing on the ground.

Ibn Kathir states plainly what this was: a proof from Allah for Musa and a great miracle. It was something that broke through the boundaries of what is considered normal, and so it was brilliant evidence that none but Allah could do such a thing — and a proof that no one from mankind could come with the likes of it except a Prophet sent by Allah. That is the logic of a miracle in Islam: not a spectacle for its own sake, but a credential that cannot be forged.

**Why three different words for the snake?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Mazharī) notices that the Qur'an describes this same creature with three terms in three places. Here it is *ḥayyah* — the generic name used for snakes of all sizes and thickness. In 28:31 it is *ka-annahā jānn* — and *jānn* means a small, slim snake. In 26:32 it is *thuʿbān* — a long, thick snake. Two ways of reconciling them are offered: either the serpent was slim and small in the beginning and grew later on in size and thickness; or it was originally long and thick and was called *jānn* by reason of its fast speed, since as a general rule big and thick snakes are slow moving. Mazharī notes that the word *ka-annahā*, "as if", points to the second reading: it signals a *comparison* to a *jānn* on account of its swift movements, not that it literally was one.

## "Take it, and have no fear"

Ayah 21 is where the tenderness of ayah 17 returns. Allah does not leave Musa staring at the thing; He tells him to take hold of it, and pairs the command with the reassurance: *have no fear*. And He gives him the outcome in advance — *We will return it to its former state*, which Ibn Kathir explains as the form that it was in, as you recognized it before.

Look at the order of that sentence. The command to grasp comes first; the promise that it will be safe comes after. Musa is asked to reach out his hand toward a racing serpent on the strength of Allah's word alone — and the word is enough. This is the training of a messenger: obey first, and find that Allah's promise held.

## The second sign: his own hand

*And put your hand under your armpit; it will come out shining, unblemished* (22).

Ibn Kathir calls this the second sign of Musa: Allah commanded him to place his hand into the opening of his garment, as is clearly stated in another ayah, while here it is mentioned merely as a passing reference. He brings 28:32 alongside it — *And draw your hand close to your side to be free from fear. These are two signs (burhānān) from your Lord to Fir'awn and his chiefs* — which does two things at once: it names the pair of miracles as a single package aimed at Pharaoh, and it links the gesture itself to being free from fear. Ibn Kathir then cites **Mujahid** on that same phrase: "This means put your palm under your upper arm."

**The word *janāḥ***. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *janāḥ* means the fore-limb of an animal or the wing of a bird; here Musa was commanded to press his hand under his armpit so that when he brings it out it will shine as brilliantly as the sun — the second miracle granted to him. This, Maʿārif notes, is the meaning given to the words by Ibn ʿAbbas (via Mazharī).

**"Without any disease."** The qualifier *min ghayri sūʾ* is not decoration. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, as-Suddī and others that it means without any leprosy, ailment or disfigurement. A hand that suddenly turns white could be read by onlookers as a diseased hand; the Qur'an forecloses that. This whiteness is light, not sickness. Ibn Kathir says that when Musa put his hand into the opening of his garment and brought it out, it came out shining as if it were a half moon. **Al-Hasan al-Basri** said: "He brought it out, and by Allah, it was as if it were a lamp. From this Musa knew that he had surely met his Lord, the Mighty and Sublime."

That last line is worth pausing over. The sign was not only for Pharaoh. By it, as al-Hasan puts it, Musa himself knew — his own heart was settled about the encounter he had just had.

## "Some of Our greater signs"

Ayah 23 gives the purpose: *so that We may show you some of Our greatest signs*. Ibn Kathir attaches this directly to the shining hand — *this is why Allah says, "That We may show you some of Our greater signs."*

Read the words closely. **"Some of"** — even these two overwhelming miracles are only a portion of what Allah has. And **"show you"** — before Musa shows anything to anyone, Allah shows it to *him*. The messenger is the first witness of his own message. Certainty is built in him before he is asked to carry it to others.

## "Go to Fir'awn — he has transgressed"

Now, and only now, comes the assignment (ayah 24). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames it exactly this way: having suitably armed him with two great miracles, Allah commanded Musa to proceed to Egypt and invite Pharaoh to accept the true faith, because he had exceeded all bounds in his tyranny and misdeeds.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the command: "Go to Fir'awn, the king of Egypt, whom you left Egypt fleeing from, and invite him to the worship of Allah alone, Who has no partners. Command him to treat the Children of Israel well and to not torment them. For verily, he has transgressed, oppressed, preferred the worldly life and forgotten the Most High Lord."

Three things stand out in that sentence. **The destination**: Ibn Kathir does not let us forget where Musa is being sent — back to the very land he had fled, and to its king. **The content of the mission** is twofold, and in this order: pure *tawḥīd* — worship Allah alone, Who has no partners — and then justice for the oppressed, that the Children of Israel be treated well and not tormented. The call to Allah and the defence of the weak are not separate errands. **The verdict**: *innahu ṭaghā*, "he has transgressed", is Allah's own assessment of Pharaoh, given to Musa before he sets out — that he transgressed, oppressed, preferred the worldly life and forgot the Most High Lord. Musa is not being asked to work out who is in the wrong. The diagnosis is settled; his task is delivery.

## Living it

**Allah prepares before He assigns.** The order of these ayat is the lesson. Musa is calmed with a gentle question, invited into conversation, shown a sign, told not to fear, given a second sign in his own body — and only then told where to go. When a hard duty lands on you, look for what Allah has already put in your hand before you look at the size of the task.

**What is in your right hand?** Musa's answer to Allah's question was: a plain stick I lean on and feed my sheep with. In Allah's hands it split the ordinary world open. Allah does not ask us for equipment we do not have; He asks us to throw down what we do have.

**Obey while the fear is still there.** Ayah 21 does not say "once you are no longer afraid, pick it up." It says *take it, and have no fear.* The reassurance comes with the command, not before it.

**Speak to Allah as Musa did.** Ayah 18 is a servant who does not want the conversation to end — warm, unhurried, saying more than strictly required — and who still knows when to stop. That is a model for du'a and for standing in prayer.

**Call to Allah and stand with the oppressed.** The mission given in ayah 24 joins the two: worship of Allah alone, and "treat the Children of Israel well and to not torment them."

passages.title: Moses' prayer for help and its answer
passages.tafsir:
In ayah 24 Allah had just given the command: *"Go to Fir'awn — verily, he has transgressed."* Everything from ayah 25 to ayah 35 is Musa's reply to that order. He does not argue and he does not decline; he asks. And ayah 36 closes the passage with Allah's answer: *"You have been granted your request, O Musa."* Held together, these ayat are a complete picture of how a servant receives an assignment far bigger than himself — by turning at once from his own capacity to his Lord's, and asking for exactly what the work requires and not a word more.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point that once Musa had been honoured with conversing with Allah and granted the mission of prophethood, he did not rely "on his own self and on his own ability"; he turned to Allah for help, without which it would have been impossible to endure and persevere through the trials built into such a mission. It counts five requests in this prayer.

## Why the request was so urgent

Ibn Kathir slows down here to let us feel what Musa had just been handed, and it is the single most illuminating thing in the passage. Musa was being sent to *the mightiest king on the face of the earth at that time* — the most arrogant and severe of people in his disbelief, with the largest army and the most powerful kingdom, the most tyrannical and obstinate of rulers. This was a man who claimed not to know Allah at all, and who told his subjects he knew of no god for them other than himself.

And Musa's relationship to that man was not neutral. As Ibn Kathir sets it out: Musa had lived in Fir'awn's own home as a child, stayed in his room and slept on his bed. Then he had killed one of Fir'awn's people, feared they would kill him in return, and fled — remaining a fugitive that entire time. *Then, after all of this*, his Lord was sending him back to them as a warner, calling them to worship Allah alone.

Ibn Kathir also spells out what the mission actually was: go to the king of Egypt whom you fled, invite him to the worship of Allah alone with no partners, and command him to treat the Children of Israel well and stop tormenting them — for he has transgressed, oppressed, preferred the worldly life and forgotten the Most High Lord.

So when Musa says *"My Lord, open my chest for me and make my task easy for me,"* Ibn Kathir reads it as one sentence: **"I cannot perform this task if You do not help me, aid me and support me."** That is the key to the whole passage.

## Ayah 25 — "Open my chest for me"

The Arabic *ishraḥ lī ṣadrī* is a request for the chest to be opened out, widened, made spacious. Ibn Kathir explains it as asking Allah to expand his chest *for his mission*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the two things that expansion had to carry: the capacity to **receive all the knowledge and wisdom of prophethood**, and the capacity to **bear with equanimity the slander of the people who would oppose him**.

Notice where he begins. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the first three of these requests concern Musa's own person, and only the fourth turns to assembling the means the mission would need. Before he asks for a single external thing, he asks for the heart that will have to hold both the knowledge and the insults.

## Ayah 26 — "And make my task easy for me"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what prophethood had taught him: it is not human ability and skill, nor the other apparent causes of things, that make affairs easy or difficult. In reality things become easy or hard **as Allah wills**. That conviction is why the second request exists at all — a man who thought ease came from competence would have asked for competence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a supplication in which believers are taught to seek Allah's help in their affairs with these words: *"O Allah, be kind to us and make our difficult tasks easy, because it is easy for You to make every difficult thing easy."* (The source presents this as guidance found in hadith without naming a collection.)

## Ayat 27–28 — the knot in the tongue

*"And untie a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech."*

The Qur'an's own word for the impediment is *ʿuqda* — a **knot**. Both commentaries relate what tied it.

Ibn Kathir gives the short version: this was a lisp, the result of an incident in which Musa was presented with a date and a hot coal stone and placed the coal on his tongue instead of the date. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī and Qurṭubī, tells the story in full. As an infant Musa lived with his own mother, who nursed him and was paid for her services by Pharaoh. When he was weaned, Pharaoh and his wife Āsiya adopted him and took him away from his mother. One day the child seized Pharaoh's beard and slapped him on the face — another version has him playing with a stick and striking Pharaoh on the head with it. Pharaoh was enraged and resolved to have him put to death. Āsiya tried to calm him: *"O King, why do you take this matter so seriously? After all he is merely a child who does not understand things. Test him if you like, and you will find he cannot distinguish between good things and bad things."*

Two trays were brought, one filled with live coal and one with jewellery. The expectation was that the child would be drawn to the brightness of the burning coal and reach for it, since children are not normally drawn towards jewellery, which is not as bright — and that would settle the matter. But Musa was no ordinary child; Allah had chosen him to be a prophet whose instincts were unusual from the very moment of his birth. He put out his hand for the jewellery. Jibrīl turned his hand away and placed it in the tray containing the coal; he picked up a piece of burning coal and put it in his mouth, and it burned his tongue. Pharaoh was then fully satisfied that the earlier act had been a child's inability to tell good from bad, not mischief. The impediment that resulted is the "knot" of ayah 27.

**Read what he asks for, and what he does not.** Ibn Kathir notes the restraint precisely: Musa did **not** ask for the affliction to be removed altogether. He asked for the removal of his stammering so that people would understand what he intended in his speech — *he was only asking for what was necessary to deliver his message.* Ibn Kathir adds that had he asked for the removal of the affliction in its entirety, it would have been cured for him; but **the Prophets do not ask for any more than what is required.** Ayah 28 states the purpose in exactly those terms: *yafqahū qawlī* — "that they may understand my speech." Not that they admire it. Understanding is the whole of what the mission needs.

**Did the knot come undone?** The scholars discuss this, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out both sides. A later ayah informs Musa that all his prayers had been granted, which would suggest he was cured of the disability. Yet in another place Musa says of his brother, *"He is more fluent in his tongue than me"* (28:34), which would indicate the impediment was not fully cured and that the stammer persisted, though in a milder form; and Fir'awn later counted among Musa's defects that he *"cannot express himself clearly"* (43:52) — which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning he was not eloquent in speech. Ibn Kathir's own conclusion is that Musa **was left with the remnants of that accident**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the resolution some have offered: he had prayed for the knot to be loosened only to the extent that others could understand his words; to that extent the stammer was cured, while a trace of it remained — which is not inconsistent with his prayer being granted, because the trace was never what he asked to have removed.

There is something quietly enormous in that. The man with the damaged tongue is sent to the mightiest king on earth, and is given exactly the clarity the message requires and no more — the trace left in place, and Fir'awn, in the end, counting the way he speaks among the defects he could name against him.

## Ayat 29–30 — "and appoint for me a wazīr from my family: Harun, my brother"

With the fourth request the prayer turns outward. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the first three concerned Musa's own person, while this one relates to assembling the means that would facilitate the mission — and the most important of those was the appointment of a deputy or helper.

**The word itself.** *Wazīr* literally means **"one who carries a burden."** A minister of state is called a *wazīr* because he carries the burden of the responsibilities entrusted to him by the ruler. Musa is not asking for company; he is asking for someone to take part of the load.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this extreme foresight and prudence, because the success of any movement or enterprise depends on the selection of competent and dedicated supporters. With good and loyal workers it is easy to surmount all obstacles; with irresponsible and indifferent ones the best preparations and arrangements become futile. It adds a pointed observation: examine the causes of the decline of some modern states and the evils they suffer from, and they can all be attributed to the irresponsible conduct, mismanagement and incompetence of ministers and advisers.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from the Prophet ﷺ that when Allah appoints someone to govern a country and wishes that the country should be well administered, He provides the ruler with a good *wazīr* to assist him in whatever he does — one who, if the ruler forgets to attend to some important task, is quick to remind him and to help him in what he intends to do. (Nisāʼī, from Qāsim ibn Muhammad.)

**Why from his own family?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons: the behaviour and conduct of a family member is already well known, and there is mutual affection and understanding within a family that greatly helps towards accomplishing the mission. But it immediately guards the principle: the person selected must genuinely be competent and possess the merit necessary for the duties, so that the selection cannot be attributed to nepotism and favouritism. Where people of integrity and dedication are scarce, a ruler who appoints his own close relatives renders himself liable to public criticism; where standards of probity and integrity are high, such appointments are considered normal and are in fact conducive to sensitive assignments being performed well. It notes that all four of the Rightly Guided Caliphs who succeeded the Prophet ﷺ were in some way related to him.

Note the sequence in the prayer itself, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out: Musa first asked that the helper be from his own family, and only then asked specifically for his brother — *"Harun, my brother."* The principle first, the person second.

**Harun's side of it.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas — through Ath-Thawrī, from Abu Sa'īd, from 'Ikrimah — that **Harun was made a Prophet at the same moment that Musa was made a Prophet.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Harun was three or four years senior to Musa and died three years before him; that at the time of this petition he was in Egypt, where an angel brought him word of his elevation to prophethood and his appointment as Musa's assistant, along with instructions to receive Musa outside Egypt when he arrived — which he did.

Ibn Kathir preserves a striking scene recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim. 'A'ishah, going out intending to perform 'Umrah, stopped to camp among some bedouins and heard a man ask, "Which brother in this life was the most beneficial to his brother?" The people said, "We do not know." He said, "By Allah, I know" — and 'A'ishah says she said to herself about his swearing that he should not swear such an oath, singling himself out as knowing. Then the man said: **"It is Musa, when he asked for prophethood to be bestowed upon his brother."** 'A'ishah said, "By Allah, he has spoken truthfully."

That is the measure of the request. Ibn Kathir points out that this was a request from Musa concerning something that did not pertain to himself — and cites Allah's commendation of him elsewhere: *"and he was honourable before Allah"* (33:69).

## Ayat 31–32 — "strengthen my back through him, and let him share my task"

Mujahid glossed *ishdud bihi azrī* as **"make my back strong."** The image is of a man bracing to lift something: strengthen the part of me that bears weight, and do it *through him*.

*"And let him share my task"* — Ibn Kathir: **make him my consultant in this matter.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fine point that explains why this had to be a prayer at all. Musa had the power to appoint Harun as his *wazīr* on his own; he petitioned Allah anyway, to seek His grace in the appointment. But beyond that, he wanted Harun to share in the **prophethood** and the mission — and that power does not rest in any Prophet. So he asked the only One who could.

## Ayat 33–34 — what all of it was for

*"So that we may glorify You much, and remember You much."*

The particle *kay* means "so that" — this is the reason clause for everything he has just asked. Not so that he would succeed, be vindicated, or be safe: so that Allah would be glorified and remembered, and by *we*, not *I*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: a man by himself can pray as often as he desires, so where was the need for a companion? The answer it gives is that **good companions and a conducive environment definitely contribute towards the better performance of worship and dhikr** (remembrance of Allah). A person whose friends are negligent about Allah cannot devote himself to His worship with the same quality and quantity as someone fortunate enough to have the company of pious men and righteous friends devoted to Allah's worship and remembrance. That is the case, in one line, for choosing who you spend your life beside.

And the standard for "much" is high. Mujahid said: **a servant of Allah is not considered of those who remember Allah much until he remembers Allah while standing, sitting and lying down.**

## Ayah 35 — "Truly You have ever been Seeing of us"

Musa ends not with a plea but with a statement about his Lord: *innaka kunta binā baṣīran* — "verily, You are ever seeing us."

Ibn Kathir's reading is beautiful. The seeing Musa has in mind is not surveillance but care: it means **"in Your choosing us, giving us the prophethood, and sending us to Your enemy Fir'awn."** *So unto You is all praise for this.* The prayer ends in praise for what has already been decided, before a single request is answered.

## Ayah 36 — "You have been granted your request, O Musa"

Allah's response comes immediately and completely. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān simply notes that Musa's petition ended here and he was rewarded with the good news that Allah had granted all his requests.

Ibn Kathir points out that the answer does not stop at "yes." What follows contains a reminder of Allah's previous favours upon Musa — the inspiration given to his mother when she was breastfeeding him and feared Fir'awn and his chiefs would kill him, in a year when they were killing all the male children; the case in which she placed him and cast into the river; the river carrying him to the very home of Fir'awn. Ibn Kathir draws the lesson: they were killing the male children of the Israelites for fear of Musa's arrival, and Allah — having the great authority and the most perfect power — determined that Musa would not be raised except upon Fir'awn's own bed, sustained by Fir'awn's food and drink, receiving the love of Fir'awn and his wife. On *"and I endued you with love from Me"* Ibn Kathir says: **"I made your enemy love you."** Salamah bin Kuhayl said it means, "I made My creatures love you." And on *"in order that you may be brought up under My Eye,"* Abu 'Imran Al-Jawni said: "You will be raised under Allah's Eye." Then the sister who said, "Shall I show you one who will nurse him?" — the nursing arranged so that his mother's eyes might be cooled and she should not grieve; then the Copt killed, the distress, the flight, and safety at the water of the people of Madyan, where the righteous man said to him, *"Fear you not. You have escaped from the people who are wrongdoers."*

Which is the point. Musa had just said, *"You are ever seeing us"* — and Allah's reply is essentially: *look at your own life and see how long that has been true.*

## Living it

- **Take the order, then ask for the means.** Musa's first move under an impossible command was not analysis or refusal but *rabbi* — "my Lord." Ibn Kathir's summary of ayat 25–26 is worth carrying in substance: *I cannot do this unless You help me.*
- **Ask for what the work needs, not for a comfortable life.** The Prophets do not ask for more than is required. Musa asked only for the clarity the message needed — and the message was understood, trace and all.
- **Choose your helpers, and your company, deliberately.** A *wazīr* is one who carries a burden with you; and the people around you shape both the quality and the quantity of your worship.
- **Keep the purpose in view.** The whole prayer is aimed at *"so that we may glorify You much and remember You much."* When the aim of our asking is that Allah be remembered more, the asking itself becomes worship.

passages.title: Allah's earlier favours upon Moses
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Allah has just granted Musa's request, and before sending him on the hardest errand of his life He recites his own life back to him. Ayat 37–41 are one long recital of remembered grace, rising to the summit in ayah 41, "And I have chosen you for Myself." One unstated argument holds them together: the hand that carried you as an infant floating in a box is the hand sending you back to Fir'awn.

## "Once before" (37)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 37 as a pivot. Allah has just conferred the great gifts — the honour of conversation with Him, prophethood, the miracles — and now turns Musa's attention backwards, to the favours showered on him from birth up till that moment, and how He saved his life from one hazard after another. In time these favours belong to an earlier period; hence "another time."

## Revelation to a woman who was not a prophet (38)

"When We inspired your mother with that which We inspired." Maʿārif notes that the information given to Musa's mother concerned a matter that could be learnt only through divine revelation: put the baby in a box, float it down the river, and entertain no apprehension about his safety, because Allah will protect him and return him to her. The promise of Allah and the divine scheme to save the child's life are beyond human conception and can be made known through revelation alone.

Maʿārif takes the question head-on: **can revelation be sent to someone who is not a prophet?** The literal meaning of *waḥy* is a secret message understood only by the one addressed. In that sense the word is not restricted to prophets — the Qur'an uses it of the bees (16:68) and here of Musa's mother. Sayyidah Maryam also received divine messages, though the scholars unanimously hold that she was not a prophet. Waḥy of this type is made by way of *ilhām*, divine inspiration: Allah puts an idea into someone's heart and then confirms him in the belief that it is from Allah — saints and other devout people receive such inspirations. Abu Hayyan and some other scholars hold that such inspiration can sometimes come through an angel, as happened to Maryam when Jibra'il appeared to her in the form of a human being.

*Ilhām* is specific to the person who receives it; it is not meant for the public and is no basis for propagating the true faith. Prophetic *waḥy* aims at appointing someone to reform people and to call them to the true faith; he must not only believe it himself but bind others to accept his prophethood, and declare as disbelievers those who deny him. Some respected scholars have named the two *waḥy tashrīʿī* (legislative) and *waḥy ghayr tashrīʿī* (non-legislative). Maʿārif adds a warning: literal waḥy has always been there and always will be, whereas prophethood and prophetic waḥy ceased with the Prophet ﷺ — and the false prophet of Qadiyan used these very definitions, along with certain writings of Shaykh Muhiyy-ud-din Ibn ʿArabi, to prop up his claim, in a way contrary to what Ibn ʿArabi himself wrote.

**Her name.** Ruh ul-Maʿani gives it as Yuhanadh; Itqan says Lihyana daughter of Yasmad ibn Lawi; others say Barkha, and still others Bazakht. Some who dispense charms and amulets attribute strange properties to her name; according to Ruh ul-Maʿani there is no basis for such a belief.

## The chest, the river, and a command given to water (39)

*Yamm* means river; here it refers most probably to the Nile (Maʿārif). The commands come in a chain, ending — "let the river throw it by the shore."

The commentators asked how a river can be commanded when it has no sense or understanding. Some scholars answered that although the imperative mood is used, it is not really a command but a way of conveying that the river would cast the box onto its bank. Others held it a genuine command to the Nile, since everything Allah created possesses emotions and a sense of feeling — the properties by which, according to the Qur'an, even trees and rocks glorify Allah. Maʿārif marks the boundary: apart from human beings, jinn and angels, no created thing possesses feeling to a degree where the precepts of halal and haram can be made binding on it.

The safest thing the mother can do for her baby is put him in the water; obedience here looks exactly like abandonment. The long narration of Ibn ʿAbbas records that once she had done it, Shaytan tried to perplex her with the suggestion that she had made a mistake — even if the child had been put to death by Fir'awn's order she would at least have buried him with her own hands, whereas now he would probably be eaten by the river animals. The whisper worked: she forgot the promise Allah had made her, and grief so overwhelmed her that "the heart of the mother of Musa became empty" (28:10). The attack came after the obedience, not before it.

**"An enemy of Mine and an enemy of his shall take him."** Maʿārif raises the difficulty: Fir'awn was Allah's enemy because of his infidelity, but his enmity towards Musa needs explaining, since at that time he cherished no hostility towards him — he was incurring considerable expenditure on his upbringing. Two answers are offered (Ruh and Mazhari): the description may look ahead to the future enmity already in Allah's knowledge, or he was an enemy even then and had reluctantly agreed to bring the child up for the sake of his wife 'Asiya — which is why, at the slightest suspicion, he ordered Musa's immediate execution, and was prevented only through her wise role.

**"And I have cast love on you from Myself."** Ibn Kathir: this means "I made your enemy love you." Salamah bin Kuhayl said it means "I made My creatures love you." Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah, as Mazhari reports them, read "love" here in the sense of *being loved*: Allah bestowed on Musa an attribute that would make people show love towards him. When Fir'awn's wife opened the box and found a boy, she instinctively felt a sudden surge of love for him, something she had never experienced before. Maʿārif draws the principle: Allah bestows on His chosen servants a special grace that causes all men, friend or foe, to love them; the prophets enjoy it to a far greater degree, and many saints too.

**"And that you are fashioned under My eye."** Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said this means: "You will be raised under Allah's Eye." Maʿārif, citing Mazhari, explains *ṣanaʿtu* here as "good upbringing" — the Arabs have the phrase *ṣanaʿtu farasī*, "I trained my horse well" — and takes "under My eye" as "in My keeping." We affirm the Eye as Allah affirmed it of Himself, without likening it to anything in creation and without explaining it away. Ibn Kathir marvels at the arrangement: with Allah having the great authority and the most perfect power, He determined that Musa would not be raised except upon Fir'awn's own bed, sustained by Fir'awn's food and drink, while receiving the love of Fir'awn and his wife. Mazhari puts it starkly — Allah chose the Pharaoh to raise Musa in his own palace, unaware that the child was his enemy.

## The sister, the milk, and the wages (40)

Once accepted into the house of Fir'awn, he refused every woman brought to nurse him: "And We had already forbidden other foster suckling mothers for him" (28:12). Then his sister came with her line — "Shall I direct you to a household who will rear him for you, and look after him in a good manner?" (28:12). Ibn Kathir explains what she was proposing: someone who could nurse him for a fee. They went with her to his own mother; when her breast was presented to him he took it, Fir'awn's family were extremely happy, and they hired her to nurse him. Ibn Kathir adds that she achieved great happiness and comfort because of him in this life, and even more so in the Hereafter. "So We restored you to your mother, that she might cool her eyes and she should not grieve" — that is, not grieve over you.

Maʿārif reflects: had Musa accepted milk from any other wet-nurse, he would have spent his early years in the palace, nourished by a disbelieving woman, with his mother suffering great anguish at the separation. Instead an inscrutable decree of providence united him with his mother; Fir'awn and his wife felt beholden to her, showered gifts on her and gave her good remuneration for her services; and she escaped the necessity of living in the palace. Maʿārif closes with the Qur'anic exclamation *fa-tabāraka'llāhu aḥsanu'l-khāliqīn* — "So blessed is Allah, the best of creators."

Maʿārif also cites, on the authority of Ibn Kathir and without naming a collection, a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that an industrialist or businessman who, while engaged in his trade, also desires to win the good pleasure of Allah is like the mother of Musa — she nursed her own child and was paid for her services at the same time. The application: a mason concerned only with his wages for building a mosque receives his wages and nothing more; if he undertook that work intending it to benefit pious people, he receives the wages *and* the religious benefit.

"Then you killed a man, but We saved you from great distress, and We tried you with a heavy trial." Ibn Kathir: the man killed was a Coptic person, of the people of Egypt, Fir'awn's people; the distress was what Musa felt at Fir'awn's family intending to kill him, so he fled until he came to the water of the people of Madyan, where the righteous man said to him, "Fear you not. You have escaped from the people who are wrongdoers" (28:25).

Almost every item on the list is something Musa did not arrange: the inspiration to his mother, the river's compliance, the love cast on him, his refusal of the breast, his sister's words. The one item that was his own doing — the blow that killed the Egyptian — appears as a distress he had to be saved *from*. Maʿārif records his own verdict on it: "This is some of Shaitan's act," and his prayer, "O my Lord! I have wronged myself, so forgive me" — "so He forgave him" (28:15–16).

**"And We tried you with a heavy trial."** On *futūnā*, Ibn ʿAbbas said the words mean "We tried you repeatedly"; Dahhak rendered them "We subjected you to severe trials." When Saʿid ibn Jubayr asked Ibn ʿAbbas about this word, the answer was a long narration — the famous *Ḥadīth al-Futūn*, which Imam Nasa'i reported in the Book of Tafsir of his larger work al-Sunan al-Kubra. Its status is disputed: critics such as Imam Nasa'i and Ibn Kathir hold it *marfūʿ*, going back to the Prophet ﷺ; Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Shaykh Abu'l-Hajjaj al-Mizzi hold it *mawqūf* — the words of Ibn ʿAbbas, taken from the Isra'ili traditions of Kaʿb al-Ahbar whose narration is permissible, though it does contain sentences of the Prophet ﷺ in places. Maʿārif observes that even those who do not raise it to the Prophet ﷺ have never challenged its contents; its own author holds that Ibn ʿAbbas did not tell the story on his own authority, supported by an incident in which Muʿawiyah doubted one detail and Ibn ʿAbbas took him to Saʿd ibn Malik Zuhri, who confirmed having heard the Prophet ﷺ relate it. Ibn ʿAbbas broke off five times to mark a trial:

1. **Before birth.** Fir'awn's court, discussing Allah's promise to Ibrahim of prophets and kings from his progeny, resolved to put to death every male Isra'ili child; when they realised their labour force would thin out, they spared boys born in alternate years. Harun was born in a sparing year; Musa was conceived for a killing year. "His life was at risk even before he was born."
2. **The knives.** Soldiers learned of an Isra'ili boy in the palace and rushed there with knives to take him; the Pharaoh's wife pleaded with her husband, saying the child was the joy of her heart and his. Fir'awn answered, "Yes, I know that he is the joy of your heart, but as for me, I do not need him." Ibn ʿAbbas quoted the Prophet ﷺ here: had Fir'awn said of the boy what his wife said, Allah would have guided him to the true faith as He guided her.
3. **The sister seized.** In the market place the Pharaoh's servants suspected her of being the child's mother or a close relation and held her; she explained that she only meant the family would serve the child in the hope of gaining access to the palace. Satisfied, they released her.
4. **Coals and pearls.** Brought before Fir'awn, the child clutched his beard and pulled it; the courtiers cried that the promised overthrow was beginning, and Fir'awn ordered his death. His wife proposed a test — two trays, one with two live coals, one with two shining pearls — and the child picked up the coal (another tradition says he reached for the pearls and Jibra'il guided his hand to the coal). Fir'awn snatched the coal away, and he was spared.
5. **The flight.** After the Egyptian's death the next day's quarrel exposed him; Fir'awn at once sent soldiers to apprehend and execute him, and a follower got wind of the order and reached him through smaller streets to warn him. He left for Madyan having never undertaken a task involving physical exertion and unfamiliar with the roads, carrying one sentence: "I hope my Lord will guide me to the straight path" (28:22).

**"Then you stayed a number of years with the people of Madyan."** Ibn Kathir: he lived among them avoiding Fir'awn and his chiefs, working as a shepherd for his father-in-law until the appointed time ended. Ibn ʿAbbas told Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the contractual eight years were binding and could not be reduced in any circumstances, and it was Allah's will that he serve the additional optional two as well, so he served the full ten. Maʿārif draws lessons: Shuʿayb was a prophet, and entertaining a traveller without recompense was not beyond his means, yet at his daughter's suggestion he offered wages instead — by prophetic wisdom he perceived that a man of such noble character would not accept hospitality much longer and would move on to some place where he might suffer hardship. Prophethood is a pure gift from Allah that no amount of toil can earn, yet His wisdom decreed that a man whose life had been spent in comfort and luxury should undergo strenuous physical labour as preparation for leading and reforming people. Shepherding in particular trains the temperament: a straying goat can be neither ignored — it may be lost or fall prey to a wolf — nor harshly punished, so the shepherd must be patient. The prophets stand in exactly that position with straying humanity. Note the daughter's two words of recommendation, *qawiyy* and *amīn* — strong, with the ability to perform the duties entrusted to him, and trustworthy, with a past that proves his honesty. Maʿārif says these two words cover the selection of a person for any job or office better than the detailed parameters of many contemporary institutions, since honesty is what gets neglected today in favour of academic degrees.

**"Then you came here according to the fixed term which I ordained, O Musa."** Mujahid: "For a set appointment." Qatadah, as Maʿmar reported him and ʿAbd al-Razzaq recorded: "For the decree of messengership and prophethood." Ibn Kathir: Musa met the decree of Allah and His predetermined will without having any set appointment of his own; the entire situation was under Allah's control, and He compels His servants and His creatures to whatever end He wills. A man went out to fetch fire on a cold, dark night and walked into prophethood.

## "And I have chosen you for Myself" (41)

Ibn Kathir: this means, "I have chosen you and selected you to be a Messenger for Myself. This is as I wish and according to My will."

The gloss puts the stress where the ayah puts it — not on what Musa achieved, but on Allah's wish and Allah's will.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Adam and Musa met, and Musa said, "You are the one who made things difficult for mankind and you caused them to be evicted from Paradise." Adam said, "Are you the one whom Allah chose for His Message, and He selected you for Himself and He revealed the Tawrah to you?" Musa replied, "Yes." Then Adam said, "Did you find that it was preordained upon me before He created me?" Musa replied, "Yes." Therefore, Adam defeated Musa's argument. Both Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded this narration; Ibn Kathir brings it here concerning the tafsir of this very ayah.

## Living it
