**Reassurance is given as history, not as feeling.** Musa is about to be sent back to the court that had sentenced him to death; Maʿārif notes that he raised exactly that anxiety in his prayer, and that Allah answered by appointing Harun to share his prophethood. But first Allah answers fear by listing what He has already done. Steadiness is not manufactured by resolve; it is built by looking honestly at a life and counting the rescues.

**Allah's care runs ahead of you.** Every item was in place before Musa could understand it. What felt from inside like catastrophe was the mechanism of the rescue.

**Obedience can look like loss.** If you have done what Allah asked and are now being told you have ruined everything, you stand where the mother stood — and the promise held.

**Work can be worship without ceasing to be work.** She was paid to nurse her own son; the hadith cited by Maʿārif makes her the model for anyone who pursues a trade while also seeking Allah's good pleasure. And when choosing someone for a task, choose as Shuʿayb's daughter did: *qawiyy* and *amīn*.

passages.title: Go to Pharaoh — and speak to him gently
passages.tafsir:
**In brief.** These three ayat are the commissioning orders. Ibn Kathir heads his comment on them "Choosing Musa to go to Fir'awn and to be Soft and Gentle in His Invitation," and that heading says nearly everything. Musa is sent; his brother Harun is sent with him; they are given Allah's signs to carry; they are told never to slacken in remembering Allah; they are told exactly whose door to knock on — and they are told how to speak once they are standing in front of him.

What holds the passage together is the join between ayah 43 and ayah 44. Ayah 43 states the verdict on the man — *he has truly transgressed* — and ayah 44, in the next breath, commands the gentlest register available. Ibn Kathir does not let that pass quietly. He stops and says: **"This Ayah contains a great lesson."**

## "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" (42)

**"With My signs"** — *bi-āyātī*. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase in three words: "My proofs, evidences and miracles." Two men are being sent to the most powerful man in Egypt, and what they are handed to carry is evidence.

And it is two men. The command names a pair from the outset — *you and your brother* — and by ayah 43 the wording is "Go both of you." Maarif ul Qur'an describes the moment plainly: this is Allah "ordering Sayyidna Musa and Sayyidna Harun (peace be upon them) to go to Egypt and invite the Pharaoh to the path of righteousness."

## "And do not, you both, slacken and become weak in My remembrance" (42)

The verb is *taniyā*. Ibn Kathir preserves two explanations of it, both traced to Ibn 'Abbas: 'Ali bin Abi Talhah related from him, "This means do not be slow"; and Mujahid reported him saying, "This means do not be weak." Between the two reports the word is opened up nicely — it names two different ways of failing. Do not go slow, and do not go weak.

Then Ibn Kathir explains what they must not slacken in, and — this is the striking part — *where*:

> "The meaning here is that they should not slacken in the remembrance of Allah. Rather, they both should remember Allah during their meeting with Fir'awn so that the remembrance of Allah can be an aid for them against him. The remembrance of Allah would be their strength and their power that would defeat him."

*Dhikr* — the remembrance of Allah, keeping Him present in the heart and on the tongue — is not being prescribed here only as a private devotion to be performed before the hard meeting, or afterwards to recover from it. Ibn Kathir places it inside the meeting itself, and calls it their aid against Pharaoh, their strength, their power. The equipment they are issued for the palace is not courage of their own manufacture; it is the remembrance of the One who sent them.

## "Go, both of you, to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed" (43)

*Innahu ṭaghā.* Ibn Kathir explains: this "means that he has rebelled and become haughty and insolent against Allah and he has disobeyed Him."

Maarif ul Qur'an fills in who this man actually was: "The Pharaoh, who claimed to be a god, was also absolutely guilty of the massacre of thousands of Isra'ili children just to safeguard his life and his Kingdom."

So no judgement is being withheld or softened. It is Allah's own description of the man, and it is given to the two messengers as they are being sent to him — which makes what comes next in the very next ayah all the more arresting.

## "Speak to him gently" (44)

*Fa-qūlā lahu qawlan layyinan* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "speak to him mildly," and by Maarif ul Qur'an as "speak to him in soft words."

Here is the lesson as Ibn Kathir states it:

> "This Ayah contains a great lesson. Even though Fir'awn was the most insolent and arrogant of people and Musa was the friend of Allah among His creation at that time, Musa was still commanded to speak to Fir'awn with mildness and softness."

Both halves of that sentence carry weight. The gentleness is not owed to Pharaoh's rank, and it is not the deference of a weaker man to a stronger one — the one being commanded to be soft is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the friend of Allah among His creation at that time," and the one to be addressed softly is "the most insolent and arrogant of people."

What kind of softness? Ibn Kathir gives the measure precisely: "Therefore, their invitation to him was with gentle, soft and easy speech that is used by one who is a close friend." That is the register being asked for — not the tone of a prosecutor, not even the correctness of a stranger, but the tone of someone speaking to a friend.

And the reason given is not sentimentality but effect: "This is so that the message may have more effect on the souls, and so it would have deeper and more beneficial results." Ibn Kathir then sets the command alongside Allah's words, *"Invite (mankind) to the way of your Lord with wisdom and fair preaching, and argue with them in a way that is better"* (16:125) — the same instruction, stated there as a general rule for calling people to Allah.

## "Perhaps he may accept admonition or fear Allah" (44)

The ayah closes with two verbs, and Ibn Kathir separates them. Of *yatadhakkar* he says: "perhaps he will recant from that which he is in of misguidance and destruction." Of *yakhshā*: "meaning that he will become obedient due to fear of Allah." He compares Allah's words *"For such who desires to remember or desires to show his gratitude"* (25:62), and concludes: "Thus, to remember means to recant from that which is dangerous, and fear means to attain obedience."

Two movements, then, and in order. Remembrance is the turning away from what is destroying you; fear of Allah is the turning towards obedience. One clears the ground; the other builds on it.

**But why "perhaps"?** Maarif ul Qur'an raises the difficulty head-on. The guideline of gentle, persuasive speech was given "so that he might ponder and reflect on the message which they had brought to him" — and then comes the hard sentence: "This guideline was emphasized in spite of the fact that Allah knew that the Pharaoh would never give up his obduracy nor his perverse ways."

Allah, who knows every outcome, framed the mission around a hope that would not be realised in this man. Maarif ul Qur'an's explanation is short and worth sitting with: "Here the intention was to bind the prophets to a conduct which might induce people to reflect and ultimately instill the fear of Allah in their hearts." The command was binding on them as a manner of conduct — and it was pressed on them even in the one case where Allah knew the man would not relent.

## A vital principle of prophetic mission

Maarif ul Qur'an draws the general rule out of this ayah under exactly that heading — "A vital principle of Prophetic Mission":

> "Here an important principle has been enunciated that those who wish to reform people and lead them to a life of virtue should always be gentle and amiable towards their opponents however obstinate and perverse they may be. By such methods alone can they be persuaded to give heed to the message brought to them by the prophets."

Note the clause that does the most work: *however obstinate and perverse they may be.* The gentleness is not calibrated to how deserving the other party is. If it were, Pharaoh would have been the first exception, and he was not.

## Living it

**Remember Allah in the room, not only before it.** Ayah 42 hands the believer something to carry into every confrontation he dreads. Ibn Kathir's reading is that the two of them were to remember Allah *during* the meeting, and that this remembrance would be "their strength and their power." Whatever room you are dreading, the strength that gets you through it is meant to be with you inside it.

**Reserve your harshest tone for no one.** If the man who claimed divinity and killed children was to be spoken to in "gentle, soft and easy speech that is used by one who is a close friend," it is hard to see who is left who qualifies for worse. Maarif ul Qur'an applies this to religious people in particular, and the observation stings: "An unfortunate tendency is in vogue among the scholars of criticizing each other which they regard as a service to Islam. There is a need for curbing this tendency and the true teaching of Islam should be adopted."

**Certainty of refusal does not cancel the command.** You may be quite sure the person will not change — and Allah's knowledge that Pharaoh would not change was certain in a way yours never is. Yet Maarif ul Qur'an's point is that the guideline of gentle speech was emphasized precisely in spite of that knowledge, because its purpose was to bind the prophets to a conduct which might induce people to reflect. The manner was commanded; it was not made conditional on the odds.

**Let the diagnosis stay with Allah and carry the invitation yourself.** Ayah 43 tells the messengers exactly what Pharaoh is: one who "has rebelled and become haughty and insolent against Allah." Ayah 44 tells them how to speak to him. Ibn Kathir's stated reason for the softness is that "the message may have more effect on the souls" — the aim throughout is not to win an exchange but to reach a soul.

passages.title: "Fear not — I am with you both"
passages.tafsir:
In these two ayat we are allowed to overhear something private: two prophets telling their Lord, out loud, that they are afraid — and their Lord answering them. In ayah 45 Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) name exactly what frightens them about Fir'awn. In ayah 46 Allah answers them in one short sentence. That is what holds the passage together: a fear spoken honestly, and a reassurance given in reply.

## They took the fear to the One who sent them

Ibn Kathir describes ayah 45 as Musa and Harun "pleading to Allah, expressing their grievance to Him." Notice where the fear goes. It is not swallowed, and it is not turned into an excuse; it is carried straight back to Allah, and it opens with **رَبَّنَا — "Our Lord."** They are afraid, and the first word out of their mouths is the name of the relationship they are standing in.

## Two fears, two words

Maarif ul Quran points out that what they express here is a **twofold fear**, marked by two different words:

**أَن يَفْرُطَ عَلَيْنَا — "that he may hasten against us."** Ibn Kathir explains this as the fear that Fir'awn "might seize them unexpectedly with a punishment." Maarif ul Quran gives the sense of the word as *to cross all boundaries*, and unpacks the sentence as: "perhaps the Pharaoh would attack even before listening to us." That is the fear of a man who does not let you finish your sentence — a strike that lands before the message is even delivered.

**أَوْ أَن يَطْغَىٰ — "or that he may transgress."** Ibn Kathir explains this as Fir'awn transgressing "against them by tormenting them, when they actually did not deserve it," and notes that ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that *transgress* here means **"to exceed the bounds."** Maarif ul Quran draws out a second, sharper edge to this word: the worry that Fir'awn, *after* listening to their demands, "might become so refractory and perverse that he might speak about Allah in disrespectful terms."

Put the two together and you see the shape of what they dreaded. One fear is about what might happen **before** they speak — violence that pre-empts the message. The other is about what might happen **after** they speak — a tyrant so far past all limits that he answers a summons from Allah by insulting Allah. Two prophets, standing before the same errand, naming both.

## "But hadn't Allah already promised them?"

Maarif ul Quran raises the obvious objection and does not dodge it. When prophethood was bestowed on Musa, he prayed to Allah to send Harun with him to assist him in his mission, and that prayer was accepted. At the same time Allah informed him: **"We make your arm stronger through (the help of) your brother and will make for you the upper hand, so they will not reach you (with any harm)"** (28:35), and **"You have been granted your request, O Musa"** (20:36) — and among the things granted to him was **شرح صدر**, a *heart at peace*, which, as Maarif ul Quran puts it, means that he was made immune to fear. So, having received such firm assurances from Allah, how do we explain the fear he expresses in this ayah?

Maarif ul Quran offers two answers.

**First**, the promise is, in its words, "rather vague." Victory may refer to success in debate with the Pharaoh and his men. And even that presupposes that the Egyptians would actually *hear* his arguments and reasoning and *see* his miracles — while there remained the possibility that they might attack him before he had laid his arguments before them. The one gap the promise did not obviously close was precisely the gap Musa named.

**Second — and this is the heart of it —** شرح صدر **"does not mean elimination of natural fear."** A steadied heart is not an anaesthetised one.

## Fear is not a defect in faith

Maarif ul Quran states the principle plainly: *fear of fearsome things is a natural instinct, and even prophets are not free from it, in spite of their complete faith in the promises of Allah.*

The evidence offered is drawn from the lives of the prophets themselves. Musa was afraid to pick up his staff when it turned into a snake, and Allah reassured him with the word **لَا تَخَف**, "do not be afraid." Maarif also points to three other ayat expressing the same fear: Musa going out of the city **"in a state of fear, waiting (for what comes next)"** (28:21), being **"fearful"** in the city the next morning, **"waiting for what comes next"** (28:18), and **"Musa concealed some fear in his heart"** (20:67). In every case, as Maarif puts it, Allah removed their fears with good tidings.

Maarif ul Quran then carries the principle into our own Prophet's ﷺ life. It was this natural fear, it says, that persuaded the Prophet ﷺ to migrate to Madinah, and moved some of his Companions ؓ to migrate first to Abyssinia and later to Madinah. And in the Battle of Ahzab the Muslims were so overawed by the strength of their enemies that they dug a trench as a protective measure, even though Allah had promised them victory on numerous occasions. The conclusion Maarif draws is worth memorising: they did not have the least doubt about their ultimate victory; the fear they felt was *"the result of a spontaneous human impulse in the face of danger, and the prophets being human are not immune to this impulse."*

This is enormously freeing for an ordinary believer. Feeling afraid is not the same as doubting Allah. Trust is not the absence of a racing heart — and what these two did with their racing hearts was take the fear straight to Allah and say it plainly.

## The answer: "Fear not — I am with you both"

**قَالَ لَا تَخَافَا إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَىٰ**

*(He said: "Fear not, verily, I am with you both, hearing and seeing.")*

Ibn Kathir expands the reply into what it must have meant to them: *"Do not fear him, for verily, I am with you and I hear your speech and his speech as well. I see your place and I see his place as well. Nothing is hidden from Me of your affair."*

The two of them had just described a man whose reaction they could not predict — what he might do before they spoke, and what he might say after. The answer given to them is not a prediction about Fir'awn. It is a statement about Allah: nothing of this affair, on either side of it, is outside His hearing and His sight.

Then Ibn Kathir gives the sentence that dissolves the whole terror of Fir'awn: *"Know that his forehead is in My Hand, and he does not speak, breathe, or use any force, except by My leave and after My command. I am with you by My protection, My help and My support."*

The tyrant on the throne is not an independent power. His speech, his breath, his violence — by Ibn Kathir's reading, none of it happens except by Allah's leave and command. That does not mean he will not act; it means he cannot act outside the will of the One who is with the two who fear him.

## What "I am with you" means

Maarif ul Quran is careful here: **the word "with you" is used in the sense of divine help and support, which human senses cannot perceive.** This is not Allah being contained in a place alongside them. It is the *withness* of aid and support — exactly as Ibn Kathir spelled it out at the end of his comment: "I am with you by My protection, My help and My support."

And **أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَىٰ — "I hear and I see"** — is what Allah says of Himself in the ayah, and we take it as He said it. Ibn Kathir does not speculate about *how* Allah hears and sees; he simply shows what it meant for two frightened messengers: your speech and his speech both heard, your place and his place both seen, and "nothing is hidden from Me of your affair."

## Living it

**Name your fear, and name it to Allah.** Musa and Harun did not make a vague supplication. They said what specifically frightened them, in two clauses, and brought it to their Rabb — their Lord. Ibn Kathir calls this pleading to Allah and expressing their grievance to Him. That kind of precision in *duʿāʾ* — calling upon Allah — is not complaining; ayah 45 is a model of it.

**Sensible precaution is not a failure of trust.** This is the lesson Maarif ul Quran draws from the trench at Ahzab: the Muslims dug it as a protective measure even though Allah had promised them victory many times over, and they did not have the least doubt about that victory. Taking the danger seriously and trusting Allah completely are not rivals.

**And notice what the mission was.** Maarif ul Quran observes that Musa was told to call Fir'awn to the true faith *and* to deliver the Children of Israel from bondage — which shows, it says, that the prophets have the duty of guiding mankind towards their salvation as well as of liberating people from worldly and economic bondage. The care of Allah for two frightened messengers in ayah 46 is, in the end, tied to the rescue of an enslaved people.

For anyone who has ever had to walk into a room they were afraid of — to speak a truth to someone with power over their job, their family, their safety — these two ayat are the pattern in miniature: say the fear to Allah, honestly and by name, and hear Him answer, *"Fear not, verily, I am with you both, hearing and seeing."*

passages.title: The message delivered to Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
**These two ayat are the message itself** — the actual words Allah gives Musa and Harun to say when they are sent to Fir'awn. Ayah 47 is the whole speech: who they are, what they want, what proof they carry, and the greeting they close with. Ayah 48 is the last line of that same speech, the warning. Read together, they are a single address, given by Allah word for word, to be delivered to Fir'awn.

## The lead-in the commentators supply

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān both open their comment on these two ayat by quoting ayat 45–46 first, because the command in ayah 47 answers something said just before it. So a short word on that lead-in, and then to the message itself, which is what these two ayat are.

In ayah 45 the two brothers said, *"Our Lord! Verily, we fear lest he should hasten to punish us or lest he should transgress."* Ibn Kathir explains what they meant: that Fir'awn might seize them unexpectedly with a punishment, or transgress against them by tormenting them, when they actually did not deserve it. Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that "transgress" here means **"to exceed the bounds."**

The answer in ayah 46 is *"Fear not, verily, I am with you both, hearing and seeing."* Ibn Kathir unfolds it as though Allah were speaking directly into their chests:

> "Do not fear him, for verily, I am with you and I hear your speech and his speech as well. I see your place and I see his place as well. Nothing is hidden from Me of your affair. Know that his forehead is in My Hand, and he does not speak, breathe, or use any force, except by My leave and after My command. I am with you by My protection, My help and My support."

Allah hears and Allah sees — as the ayah itself says and as Ibn Kathir takes it: their speech and Fir'awn's speech, their place and his place. And on the phrase *"I am with you both,"* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that "with you" is used here in the sense of **divine help and support which human senses cannot perceive**.

Only then comes the command in ayah 47: *"So go you both to him…"* The reassurance is issued before the mission. The men are sent out already covered.

## The script: four moves in one ayah

**1. Identity.** *"Verily, we are both Messengers of your Lord."* The wording is dual — رَسُولَا رَبِّكَ, rendered "we are both Messengers" — Harun included with Musa in the sending. And look at whose Lord it is: not "our Lord," but **your** Lord. The same possessive returns a few words later, *"a sign from your Lord."* Twice in one ayah, Fir'awn is addressed as a man who has a Lord, and the two men in front of him come from that Lord.

**2. The demand.** *"…so let the Children of Israel go with us, and torment them not."* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out what this tells us about prophethood: Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) called upon Fir'awn to embrace the true faith **and** to deliver the Bani Isra'il from bondage. In Maʿārif's words, "This shows that the prophets have the duty of guiding mankind towards their salvation as well as to liberate their people from worldly and economic bondages" — and therefore, it adds, in this very ayah Musa is reminded of both duties at once.

**3. The credential.** *"Indeed, we have come with a sign from your Lord."* Ibn Kathir glosses آية here as **evidence and a miracle** from your Lord. A claim this large is not left to assertion; it arrives with proof attached. The message and its verification travel together.

**4. The greeting — and the condition inside it.** *"And peace will be upon him who follows the guidance."* This is not the ordinary salām of warm relations, and it is not a curse either. Ibn Kathir gives its force precisely: the meaning is **"peace be upon you if you follow the guidance."** The peace is real and it is offered — but it hangs on a condition Fir'awn himself must satisfy. Nothing is conceded, and no door is slammed.

## The same opening, in a letter to Heraclius

Ibn Kathir connects this conditional greeting to one instance from the life of the Prophet ﷺ. He writes that *because of this* — because of what that phrase means — when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote a letter to Heraclius, the emperor of Rome, it began:

> "In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Heraclius the emperor of Rome. Peace be upon him who follows the guidance. Thus, to proceed: Verily, I invite you with the invitation of Islam. So accept Islam and you will be safe, and Allah will give you a double reward."

Set the two side by side and the shape is the same: the sender named, the recipient named, the conditional peace, then the invitation and what follows from accepting it. Ibn Kathir brings this single letter to illuminate the phrase — *"Due to this,"* he then says, *"Musa and Harun said to Fir'awn"* those same words. One text lighting up another; he does not describe it as a fixed protocol beyond this.

## Ayah 48: the warning, weighed word by word

*"Truly, it has been revealed to us that the torment will be for him who denies, and turns away."*

Every part of this is careful.

**"It has been revealed to us."** They do not say *we think*, or *we warn you*. The source is named as revelation. Ibn Kathir: in His flawless revelation, Allah has revealed to us that torment is prepared **exclusively** for those who reject the signs of Allah and turn away from His obedience.

**"Him who denies, and turns away."** Two verbs, and Ibn Kathir gives each a distinct sense. Commenting on the same pair in another passage — *"So he neither believed nor prayed! But on the contrary, he belied and turned away"* (75:31–32) — he explains: **he denied with his heart and turned away by his actions.** Denial is the inward refusal; turning away is the outward walking off.

Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's own witnesses to this pairing:

- *"Then for him who transgressed all bounds, and preferred the life of this world, verily, his abode will be Hellfire"* (79:37–39)
- *"Therefore I have warned you of a blazing Fire. None shall enter it save the most wretched. Who denies and turns away"* (92:14–16)

Read the warning again with that word **exclusively** in mind. Ayah 48 does not announce that Fir'awn is finished. It states who the torment is *for*: the one who denies and turns away. It names a category — and, as we will see from Maʿārif ul Qurʾān below, a human being is precisely the kind of creature who has a say in whether he falls inside it. Coming from two men who a moment earlier feared he would seize them with a punishment, that restraint is remarkable — and these are the words Allah gave them to say.

## Why the threat is just: two kinds of guidance

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān pauses here on a question the passage raises: why should punishment attach to a creature at all for the way it responds to guidance?

The answer is that there are two different kinds of guidance. There is **guidance of Takwīn** — the guidance built into creation. Allah has given fire, water, earth and air, and their compounds, a special kind of feeling and perception, not of the same nature as that given to human beings and jinn, and through it He has assigned duties to all created things. The earth, the sky and every other created thing is busy performing its allotted tasks; air, water, fire and earth all fulfil the purpose for which they were created. They do not deviate from their destined course except by the command of Allah — and when He so commands, fire turns into a bed of flowers, as it did for Sayyidna Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and water acts as fire, as it did for the people of Sayyidna Nuh (71:25). Who taught a newly born baby to draw milk from its mother's breast, or to cry when hungry or in pain? It is this same divine guidance, received without any formal training.

Because that guidance is something a created thing is bound to follow — deviating from it is beyond its power — the laws of what is permissible and what is forbidden do not apply to fire and water. But the guidance given to human beings and jinn — the guidance the prophets carry, addressed to those gifted with intellect — is **not** inherent in the nature, and thus not compulsory but optional. And it is this freedom of choice, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān concludes, which renders them liable to reward for good deeds and to punishment for their sins.

That is the ground under ayah 48. The whole message in ayah 47 — the identification, the demand, the miracle, the conditional peace — is addressed to a creature who can be *asked*.

## Living it

**Fear can be brought to Allah.** Musa and Harun said outright that they feared what Fir'awn might do, and what came back was *"Fear not, verily, I am with you both, hearing and seeing"* — followed immediately by the command to go. The fear was answered; the errand still stood.

**Know what "Allah is with you" means here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is careful: it is divine help and support that human senses cannot perceive. It did not mean Fir'awn would become pleasant. It meant, as Ibn Kathir put it, that Fir'awn's forehead was in Allah's Hand and he could not so much as breathe except by Allah's leave.

**Speak the message the way ayah 47 speaks it.** Say who you are and on whose authority you speak. Ask for what is actually needed, including the worldly relief — Maʿārif ul Qurʾān will not let us make the prophetic errand a purely spiritual one. Bring evidence. Offer peace conditionally and honestly rather than either flattering or cursing. And when you warn, report the warning as it came rather than enlarging it.

**Watch both verbs in yourself.** *Denies and turns away* — the heart and the limbs, on Ibn Kathir's reading. A question worth sitting with: which of the two is quietly true of me, and in what corner of my life?

**Leave the outcome where it belongs.** Musa and Harun were told to go and to say. The peace was offered on a condition; what Fir'awn did with that condition was his own to decide — before the Lord whom ayah 47 twice reminded him was *his*.

passages.title: Pharaoh's questions and the Lord of all creation
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Ibn Kathir heads this section "The Conversation between Musa and Fir'awn." Fir'awn asks two questions (ayat 49 and 51), Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) gives two answers (50 and 52) — and then, instead of stopping, he keeps speaking, turning the visible world itself into evidence (53–55). What binds the passage together is his method: he never argues about Allah in the abstract. Asked "who is your Lord?", he answers by pointing at the ground underfoot, the roads across it, the rain, the crops, the cattle — and finally at the earth that receives every body and will give it back.

## "Who then is the Lord of you two?" (ayah 49)

Ibn Kathir reads Fir'awn's question as outright rejection. Allah is informing us of what Fir'awn said to Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) "in his rejection of the existence of a Supreme Maker and Creator, Who is the Deity of everything and his own Lord and Owner." The sense of the question is: *Who is the one who called you forth and sent you? I do not know him, and I have not given you any god other than myself.*

That last clause exposes the man. Fir'awn is not a curious sceptic. He is a ruler who thinks divinity is his to distribute — a god is something he *gives* his subjects.

Notice also the form of the address: *rabbukumā*, "the Lord of **you two**." Musa (عليه السلام) is named, but the question is put to two. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting here, recalls Allah's words earlier in the sūrah — *innanī maʿakumā asmaʿu wa arā*, "I am surely with you both. I hear and I see" (20:46) — explaining that "with you" there carries the sense of divine help and support of a kind human senses cannot perceive. So Fir'awn demands to know about a Lord he claims never to have heard of, while those standing before him have been assured that this Lord is with them, hearing and seeing.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws attention to what Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) had been sent to do: to call Fir'awn to the true faith, and to deliver the Bani Isra'il from bondage. This shows, it says, that prophets carry both duties — guiding people towards their salvation, and liberating them from worldly and economic bondage.

## The answer: He gave, then He guided (ayah 50)

*"Our Lord is He Who gave to each thing its form and nature, then guided it aright."*

The reply names two acts: giving (*aʿṭā*) and guiding (*hadā*). The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites open the first half in complementary ways:

- Ibn ʿAbbas, as related by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah: "He created a mate for everything."
- Ibn ʿAbbas, as related by ad-Dahhak: "He made the man a man, and the donkey a donkey and the sheep a sheep."
- Mujahid, reported by Layth bin Abi Sulaym: "He gave everything its form"; and reported by Ibn Abi Najih: "He fashioned the creation of every moving creature."

Saʿid bin Jubayr draws it out fully: He gave each of His creatures what is suitable for its creation. He did not give man the form of a wild beast, nor the wild beasts the form of the dog, nor is the dog's form like the sheep's. He gave each creature a suitable spouse and influenced it towards that mate. No species of creation is exactly like another — they differ in their actions, their forms, their sustenance and their mating.

Ibn Kathir reports that some of the scholars of tafsir read this alongside *walladhī qaddara fa-hadā*, "And Who has measured; and then guided" (87:3): Allah measured out an ordained amount — the deeds, the appointed times of death, the provisions — wrote it down, and then guided His creatures to it, and they are not able to avoid it nor able to abandon it. On that reading, Musa (عليه السلام) is saying that our Lord is the One Who created the creation, measured out its ordainment, and compelled the creatures to that which He wanted.

**Which guidance is meant?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the decisive distinction. The guidance in ayah 50 is *hidāyat takwīnī* — "creational" guidance, from *takwīn*, the bringing of a thing into existence. It is built into the making of the thing itself. Alongside it stands the other guidance, the special kind entrusted to prophets as a duty, which is addressed only to human beings and jinn, who are gifted with intellect.

Creational guidance runs through everything. Allah has given fire, water, earth and air, and their compounds, a special kind of feeling and perception — not of the same nature as that given to human beings and jinn — and through it He has assigned duties to all created things. This is precisely why the laws of the permissible and the forbidden do not apply to them. In obedience to this command of *takwīn*, the earth, the sky and every other created thing is busy performing its allotted task, and they do not deviate from their destined course *except by the command of Allah*. And when He so commands, fire turns into a bed of flowers, as it did for Sayyidna Ibrahim (عليه السلام), and water acts as fire, as it did for the people of Sayyidna Nuh (عليه السلام) (71:25). Or take something closer to home, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does: who taught a newborn baby to draw milk from its mother's breast, or to cry when hungry or in pain? Every created thing receives this same divine guidance without any formal training.

Then comes the weight of the contrast. Creational guidance is compulsory: a created thing is bound to follow it, and deviating from it is beyond its power. The guidance given to human beings and to jinn is *not* inherent in their nature and so is not compulsory but optional. It is this freedom of choice, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, which renders them liable to reward for good deeds and to punishment for their sins.

**Why the answer lands.** As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) reminded Fir'awn, in the first place, of those acts of Allah which are obviously done by Him alone and about which no one else could claim that he had performed them. Fir'awn could hand out titles; he could not give the sheep its shape or teach an infant to nurse. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that Fir'awn was totally unable to refute this argument.

## The second question is a trap, not an enquiry (ayah 51)

Beaten on the argument, Fir'awn changes ground: *"And what about previous peoples?"*

Ibn Kathir says the most correct opinion is this: once Musa (عليه السلام) had informed him that his Lord is the One Who creates, sustains, ordains and guides, Fir'awn began to argue, using the previous generations as a proof — referring to those people of old who did not worship Allah. In other words: *If the matter is as you say, then what happened to those people? They did not worship your Lord; instead they worshipped other gods besides Him.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes the sharper edge. In his confusion, Fir'awn asked a question designed to entangle Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) into giving a reply that would greatly offend the Egyptians: how did the people of bygone ages stand, who all worshipped idols, and what was their fate? Fir'awn's purpose was that if the reply came back that they were all misguided and deserving of Hell, he could then instigate his people against him — he would have his opening to scorn that it was not only him whom Musa (عليه السلام) was blaming, but all their ancestors as well, and such a situation would naturally have created doubts in people's minds. It is an old tactic and an effective one: shift the ground from truth to tribe.

## The answer: that knowledge belongs to Allah (ayah 52)

*"That knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."*

Musa (عليه السلام) neither denies, nor flatters, nor takes the bait. Ibn Kathir explains the reply: if those people did not worship Allah, then Allah knows precisely what happened to them and He will give them just recompense for their deeds, as is written in Allah's Book of decrees — al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet, which is the Book of Deeds. The verdict is real; it is simply filed where it belongs, with Allah, and not on a prophet's tongue in a public confrontation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how completely this frustrated the design: the reply Sayyidna Musa (عليه السلام) gave was so wise and discreet that Fir'awn's evil design was completely frustrated, giving him no chance to mislead the people.

**"My Lord neither errs nor forgets."** Ibn Kathir: nothing eludes Him and He does not miss anything, whether small or great; He does not forget anything, and His most exalted knowledge is described as encompassing everything — blessed be He, the Exalted, the Most Holy and free of any imperfections. He then names the two deficiencies in the knowledge creatures have: the first, that it does not completely encompass anything; the second, that the creature is prone to forget after knowing. Allah has declared Himself above such deficiencies. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further sense of *lā yaḍillu*: it is inconceivable that Allah should will one thing and something different should happen.

**Living it.** This reply is a model for anyone dragged into an argument built to trap them. It answers what actually matters, refuses the frame it was handed, gives no one an excuse to be offended on a third party's behalf, and returns what has not been disclosed to the One who knows it. "That knowledge is with my Lord" is a complete and honourable answer.

## The earth itself as evidence (ayat 53–54)

Ibn Kathir notes something easy to miss. Ayat 53–55 are from the completion of Musa's speech describing his Lord — and Fir'awn attempted to present some argumentative rebuttal *during* that reply. Yet Musa (عليه السلام) simply continued.

**"Who has laid out the earth for you."** Ibn Kathir records two recitations of the word, *mihādan* and *mahdan*, meaning "a place of rest that you settle down upon"; it may also mean that which you stand upon, sleep upon, or travel upon its back. The image is bedding, or a cradle — the planet furnished in advance for a guest.

**"And opened ways for you therein."** That is, He made roads for you to walk upon their shoulders — as Allah says elsewhere, "And placed therein broad highways for them to pass through, that they may be guided" (21:31).

**"And sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth with it pairs of various plants."** Ibn Kathir: this refers to the various species of plants, such as vegetation and fruits — some sour, some sweet, some bitter, and other kinds as well. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *azwāj* ("pairs") is used here in the sense of "kinds" or "species", different and diverse: Allah has created so many kinds of plant that they are beyond human reckoning, each containing special properties which make it invaluable to man for his wellbeing. It is impossible for man to comprehend completely all their properties and uses; scientists have worked for centuries and revealed a great deal, yet it is impossible to claim that whatever we know at present is the last word.

**"So eat, and graze your cattle."** Ibn Kathir: something that is food for you and a palatable fruit for you, and something that is for your cattle as fodder, both green and dry. One rainfall, two tables.

**"Surely in this are signs for people of understanding" (ayah 54).** *Āyāt* here, says Ibn Kathir, means proofs, signs and evidences; and *ulū n-nuhā* means those who possess correct and upright intelligence, realising that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah and no true Lord other than Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *nuhā* is the plural of *nuhyah*, used in the same sense as *ʿaql* (intelligence), so named because it enables wise and intelligent persons to avoid harmful acts. Intelligence, in this Qur'anic sense, is not sharpness in debate. A question designed to entangle an opponent is clever; it is not *nuhā*. *Nuhā* is the mind that holds its owner back.

## From it, into it, out of it again (ayah 55)

*"From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once again."*

Ibn Kathir: the earth is your beginning, for your father Sayyidna Adam (عليه السلام) was created with dirt from the surface of the earth. You also will be returned to the earth — meaning that you will become dirt when you die and decay. And "from it We shall bring you out once again" points to the resurrection, as in "On the Day when He will call you, and you will answer with His praise and obedience, and you will think that you have stayed but a little while" (17:52); and it is similar to Allah's statement, "Therein you shall live, and therein you shall die, and from it you shall be brought out" (7:25).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the obvious question. This verse is addressed to all mankind, although it is known that man is created from seed and not from earth — except Sayyidna Adam (عليه السلام), who was created directly from earth. One possible explanation is that since Sayyidna Adam (عليه السلام) is the father of all mankind and was himself created from earth, all his descendants have been similarly described. Others have said that the seed itself is made of earth, so anything created from the seed is in fact created from the earth. According to Imam al-Qurtubi, the text of the Qur'an clearly indicates that man is created from the earth.

See where the exchange has arrived. It opened with Fir'awn asking about a Lord he claimed not to know, and it closes with a description of the one place every listener is going. The earth that is a bed in ayah 53 is the earth we are returned into in ayah 55 — and then the earth we are brought out of once again.

## What this passage asks of us

- **Look down, not only up.** The proof offered here is not exotic. It is soil, road, rain, plant, animal, body. The ordinary *is* the argument — which means the evidence is available to a shepherd and a king alike.
- **Let eating be a reminder.** "Eat, and graze your cattle" sits inside a description of the Lordship of Allah. The same rain lays your table and your animals'.
- **Measure your intelligence by what it stops you doing.** *Ulū n-nuhā* are those whose minds enable them to avoid harmful acts — a very different thing from being quick in an argument.
- **Say "the knowledge of that is with Allah" and mean it.** Where knowledge has not been given to you, this is the honest and dignified answer, and it is a complete one.
- **Your freedom is the reason any of it counts.** Fire, water, earth and air cannot deviate from the course written into them. You can. That is precisely why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this optional guidance renders us liable to reward for good deeds and to punishment for sins — the burden and the dignity are the same thing.

passages.title: Pharaoh rejects the signs and sets a contest
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Musa (peace be upon him) has just finished answering Fir'awn's question about who his Lord is, and Allah now delivers the verdict on how that answer was received: every sign was shown, and Fir'awn still said no. What follows is not a new episode but the same refusal in motion — the miracles relabelled as "magic," the relabelling turned into a public challenge, and the challenge accepted by Musa on the biggest day and in the brightest hour Egypt had.

Read the four ayat as one movement: **evidence presented, evidence refused, and the refusal dressed up as a fair fight.**

## Where the conversation had reached

Ibn Kathir reads ayat 53–55 as the completion of Musa's reply to Fir'awn about his Lord. Musa had said that his Lord is *the One Who gave to each thing its form and nature, then guided it aright* — and, Ibn Kathir notes, Fir'awn tried to break in with some argumentative rebuttal in the middle of that answer. Musa simply carried on:

- **"He Who made the earth for you as a bed."** Some recited the word as *mihādan*, others as *mahdan* — a place of rest you settle down upon; it can also mean that which you stand upon, sleep upon, or travel upon its back.
- **"And opened ways for you therein"** — He made roads for you to walk upon their shoulders, as Allah says elsewhere, *And placed therein broad highways for them to pass through, that they may be guided* (21:31).
- **"And sent down water from the sky"**, bringing out pairs of diverse plants — species upon species, some sour, some sweet, some bitter.
- **"Eat and pasture your cattle"** — food and palatable fruit for you, fodder for your animals, green and dry.

These, Ibn Kathir says, are *proofs, signs and evidences* — and they are for *ulī al-nuhā*, "men of understanding": those who possess correct and upright intelligence, who realise from all this that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, and no true Lord other than Him. That phrase quietly frames everything that follows. Fir'awn is about to see far more than roads and rain, and still not understand.

On ayah 55, *"From it We created you,"* Ibn Kathir explains: the earth is your beginning — your father Ādam was created with dirt from the surface of the earth; you will be returned to it, becoming dirt when you die and decay; and *"from it We shall bring you out once again"* points to the Day when He will call you and you will answer with His praise (17:52), as He also said, *"Therein you shall live, and therein you shall die, and from it you shall be brought out"* (7:25).

**A note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** on the same words: the address is to all mankind, though we know a human being is formed from a drop of seed and not directly from earth — only Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him) was created directly from the earth. One explanation offered is that since Ādam is the father of all mankind and was himself made from earth, his descendants are described the same way. Others said the seed itself is made of earth, so whatever comes from the seed is in truth from the earth. Maʿārif reports that according to Imām al-Qurṭubī the wording of the Qur'an clearly indicates that man is created from the earth — and Maʿārif adds the striking point that every human being's composition contains, along with the seed, the earth of the very place where he will one day be buried.

## The verdict: all the signs, and still a no

*"And indeed We showed him all Our signs, but he denied and refused."*

Notice the completeness: **all** Our signs — nothing withheld, no argument left unmade. Ibn Kathir's gloss is unsparing: the proofs, signs and evidences were established against Fir'awn and *he saw them with his own eyes*, but he still denied and rejected them due to, in Ibn Kathir's words, "his disbelief, abstinence and transgression."

And Allah's verdict is doubled — *he denied* **and** *he refused*. Ibn Kathir seals the point with a verse from another sūrah describing exactly this posture: *And they belied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though they themselves were convinced thereof* (27:14). Inner certainty and outward denial, living in the same chest at the same time.

This is one of the most sobering lessons in the Qur'an about how belief actually works. Faith is not merely a conclusion the mind is forced into by sufficient data. Fir'awn is the proof: he was given the maximum, and it changed nothing, because what stood in the way was not a missing argument but a refusal. Everything in the next three ayat is that refusal looking for a respectable shape to take.

## The first shape it takes: "this is magic"

*"He said: Have you come to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Musa?"*

Ibn Kathir tells us what had just been placed in front of Fir'awn — "the great proof": Musa cast down his staff and it became a huge snake, and he pulled his hand out from under his arm while it was glowing white, without any illness. Two signs. And Fir'awn's answer, as Ibn Kathir renders it, works on two levels at once.

**First, he renames it.** "This is magic that you have brought to us." He does not say *this did not happen* — he cannot; he saw it with his own eyes. He gives it a label that lets him keep his position without examining it. This is the oldest move against a truth you do not want: you do not refute it, you categorise it.

**Second, he politicises it.** Ibn Kathir spells out the calculation inside Fir'awn's words: this magic is meant "to bewitch us and conquer the people, so that they will follow you. Then you will outnumber us." A question of truth becomes a question of numbers and territory — *"to drive us out of our land."*

And note the possessive — *our* land. The man who had just been told that the earth is a bed spread out by Allah, that from it we were made, into it we return, and from it we will be brought out again, still says "our land."

## The second shape: a contest, on terms he chooses

*"Then verily, we can produce magic the like thereof; so appoint a meeting between us and you, which neither we nor you shall fail to keep, in an open place where both shall have a just and equal chance."*

Having called a miracle magic, Fir'awn is committed to producing its equal — *bi-siḥrin mithlihi*, "magic the like of it." Ibn Kathir gives us his bluster: "Your plan will not work. We have magic just like yours, so do not let yourself be deceived by that what you are doing." Those words tell us plainly how sure he was of his own side.

Then comes the **mawʿid** — an appointment. Ibn Kathir explains it as "a day that we can come together to present some of our magic to confront yours," at a specified place and time. The Qur'an's phrasing binds both sides: a meeting *which neither we nor you shall fail to keep*. No excuses afterwards, no claim of an unfair setup.

The condition **makānan suwā** — "an even place," "a place where both shall have a just and equal chance" — receives two complementary explanations:

- ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said it was a flat place where all the people were on the same level, having an equal view of the event, with nothing there that would obstruct the view so that some people could see what others did not.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the proposal as a place that should, as far as possible, be within easy access of the Egyptians, of Sayyidnā Musa (peace be upon him), and of the Banī Isrāʼīl.

So the man who refused the evidence now asks for perfect visibility — and here the movement turns against him. Maʿārif notes that Musa *readily accepted* the proposal, and went on to fix the day and the time himself.

## Musa answers with the biggest day and the brightest hour

*"Your appointed meeting is the day of the festival, and let the people assemble when the sun has risen."*

Given the choice of a stage, Musa picks the largest one in the country.

**The day.** Ibn Kathir describes *yawm al-zīnah* as the day of the Egyptians' celebration and their New Year's festivity — a holiday, when they took vacation from their work and came together for a large gathering. The classical authorities describe it a little differently:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "The day of their festivity was the day of ʿĀshūrāʼ."
- **As-Suddī, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd**: "It was the day of their great celebration."
- **Saʿīd ibn Jubayr** said it was the day of their great bazaar.

Ibn Kathir's judgement is that these statements are not contradictory — a national holiday, a religious festival and a great market day are easily the same day. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a similar spread of opinion: some say it was a special festival when the Egyptians, in beautiful dress, gathered outside the towns; some say it was a Saturday; and according to some others it was the tenth day of Muḥarram. Where the scholars differ like this, the honest position is to hold the views side by side rather than force one; the point of the ayah does not depend on which is right.

Ibn Kathir then adds a remark of his own worth pausing over: he says that Allah destroyed Fir'awn and his armies on a day similar to this, "just as is confirmed in the Sahih." The day Fir'awn chose to display his power became, in the end, the anniversary of his ruin.

**Why that day?** Ibn Kathir: it was selected so that *all* the people could witness the power of Allah to do whatever He wills — they would see the miracles of the prophets and the futility of magic to contest them. Hence Musa's added condition, *"and let the people assemble"* — meaning all of them. Maʿārif calls it a wise move: on the festival day every Egyptian, high and low, was expected to assemble at an appointed place.

**The hour.** *Ḍuḥā* — Ibn Kathir explains it as the morning, just before noon, and gives the reason for the choice: in this way the contest would be most visible, well lit, apparent and obvious, in plain view. Maʿārif adds further reasons: it is the time when people, having finished their daily chores, are free to engage in other things; and daylight and visibility are at their best then, so that people dispersing after witnessing a momentous event spread the news far and wide — which is why, when Allah gave Musa a crushing victory over the Egyptian magicians, the story became known that same day to people living in far-flung places.

## "This is the way of the Prophets"

From Musa's choice of hour Ibn Kathir draws a principle that deserves to be quoted plainly: **the work of the Prophets is always clear and apparent. It is never something hidden, or something for sale.** That, he says, is precisely why Musa did not propose that the meeting be at night, but during the bright part of the day.

Two negations, and both are tests we can still apply: not hidden, and not for sale. A sign from Allah has nothing to lose by being looked at closely, and nothing to gain by being charged for. Fir'awn asked for level ground thinking his men would win on it; Musa answered with a full crowd and the clearest hour of the day.

For a full treatment of magic — its truth, its forms and the rules governing it — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to its discussion of Hārūt and Mārūt in Sūrah al-Baqarah.

## Living it

**Watch for the label that ends the thinking.** Fir'awn's word "magic" did all the work an argument should have done. We have our own versions of it — a word or a category we can drop on an uncomfortable truth so we never have to weigh it. The honest question is always: am I answering this, or am I just naming it?

**Ask whether it is really evidence you are waiting for.** Ayah 56 says Fir'awn was shown *all* the signs, and Ibn Kathir says he saw them with his own eyes. If more proof were the missing ingredient, he would have believed. When we stall on something we already know Allah has commanded, the shortfall is usually not in the proof but in the refusal.

**Do your work in the daylight.** Whatever is truly for Allah can stand being seen: your dealings, your money, your private hours. Musa chose the festival morning; the believer's instinct should run the same way — not hidden, and not for sale.

**Notice who chose the terms — and Who decided the outcome.** Fir'awn set the challenge, Fir'awn's men were the professionals, Fir'awn named the kind of ground he wanted. Musa walked into all of it and picked the busiest day on the calendar, because what the people were gathered to witness — as Ibn Kathir says — was the power of Allah to do whatever He wills. When you know the outcome belongs to Allah, you stop needing the conditions to be in your favour.

passages.title: Pharaoh gathers his magicians for the day
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the hours before the contest — the calm, busy, sinister preparation. Musa (peace be upon him) and Pharaoh have agreed, as Ibn Kathir puts it, on an appointed meeting at a specified place and time, and now the Qur'an turns its attention almost entirely to the other side: how a kingdom mobilises against a prophet. Ayah 60 builds the machine; ayat 61–64 show it shudder under a few sentences of truth, argue with itself in secret, and then lock itself into a single rank. No miracle happens in this passage. This is the portrait of falsehood in the moment before it is exposed.

## Ayah 60: Pharaoh withdraws, gathers, and returns

*"So Fir'awn withdrew, devised his plot and then came back."*

Three verbs, and an empire moves: **he withdrew, he gathered his scheme, then he returned.**

The middle verb is the striking one — *fa-jamaʿa kaydahu*, literally "he gathered his *kayd*," his plot. You do not normally "gather" a plot; you gather people and equipment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it exactly that way: these words indicate that Pharaoh assembled his magicians and their tools. The plot *was* the men and their apparatus.

Ibn Kathir fills in the scale. Pharaoh began gathering magicians from the cities of his kingdom — every person who had any affiliation with magic at that time was summoned, and magic in that era was very widespread and in demand. Ibn Kathir points to Pharaoh's own order elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"Bring me every well-versed sorcerer"* (10:79). Every one of them.

On numbers, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a wide range and does not settle it: according to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) there were seventy-two magicians, while others have put the figure anywhere from four hundred to nine hundred thousand. Their leader, it mentions, was a blind man named Shamʿūn. Such details are transmitted reports, not part of the ayah's own claim — the Qur'an's point is simply that Pharaoh brought *everything*.

**The staging.** Ibn Kathir describes the day itself, and it is worth picturing. The day came — the day when all the people gathered, which was well known, being the day of the festival. Pharaoh sat upon his throne, surrounded by the elite officials of his kingdom, the subjects all standing on his right and his left. The magicians stood before him in rows while he prodded them, incited them, and encouraged them to do their best that day. They wanted to please him; he was promising them and inspiring them. Ibn Kathir quotes the bargain they struck: *"Will there surely be a reward for us if we are the winners?" He said: "Yes, and you shall then verily be of those brought near to myself"* (26:41–42). Wages, plus access to the throne.

And then, into that arena, **Musa (peace be upon him) came forward leaning upon his stick, accompanied by his brother Harun (peace be upon him).** Ibn Kathir gives the detail almost in passing, but it carries the whole picture: a state, a throne, a crowd, an army of specialists on one side; on the other, two brothers, one of them leaning on a stick.

## Ayah 61: Musa speaks — not to Pharaoh, but to the hired hands

*"Musa said to them: 'Woe unto you! Invent not a lie against Allah, lest He should destroy you completely by a torment. And surely, he who invents a lie will fail miserably.'"*

Notice whom he addresses. Not the tyrant on the throne — the professionals Pharaoh has bought. These men have been assembled to defeat him, and the first concern of Musa (peace be upon him) is that they are about to ruin themselves.

**What is the "lie against Allah" here?** Ibn Kathir is precise, and this is the key to the ayah. It means: *"Do not make an illusion before the people of something that is not real, making it appear as if it were a creature, when it is not really a creature. If you do this, then you would be lying on Allah."*

He leaves it there, and it is worth leaving it there too. Notice only how much weight the warning carries in his reading: what the crowd would experience as a performance, Musa (peace be upon him) names as a lie told *against Allah* — and the very next clause attaches destruction to it.

**"Lest He should destroy you completely by a torment"** — *fa-yusḥitakum bi-ʿadhāb*. Ibn Kathir: He will destroy you with a destructive punishment that will not spare anything, or anyone. A total scouring, not a rebuke.

**"And surely, he who invents a lie will fail miserably"** — *wa qad khāba man iftarā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same clause: *"And loser is he who fabricates a lie."* Hold onto that verdict. It is about to be answered by the magicians' own slogan three ayat later.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames this whole address beautifully. Before the start of the contest, it says, Musa (peace be upon him) addressed some words of friendly advice to the magicians, to warn them of divine punishment if they persisted in denying Allah's miracles and other manifestations of His power. And it adds a realistic observation: it was hardly to be expected that magicians who had entered the field with all the might of Pharaoh behind them would pay any heed. However — and this is the point — the prophets and their followers possess a hidden power, so that their plain and simple words penetrate the most unruly and perverse minds. His address, it says, caused discord and dissension among the magicians: some of them thought these could not be the words of a magician but of a higher being, and were therefore against the contest; but others were adamant.

Those few sentences did not win the argument on the spot. They did something else: they got inside.

**Living it.** There is a whole manner of daʿwah in this ayah. Musa (peace be upon him) does not open with a taunt or a boast about what is coming. He warns his opponents, sincerely, of a fate he does not want for them — while they stand in rows to defeat him. And he speaks plainly. No performance, no cleverness: a warning, a consequence, a principle. That, the sources say, is what broke through.

## Ayah 62: the crack in the ranks

*"Then they debated one with another what they must do, and they kept their talk secret."*

Two verbs, and the united front is no longer united. Ibn Kathir says of the first, *fa-tanāzaʿū*, that it has been said to mean they argued among themselves. He preserves the actual exchange: one of them said, **"This is not the speech of a magician, but it is the speech of a Prophet."** Another said, **"No, he is only a magician."** Ibn Kathir notes that there are other opinions mentioned about what they discussed, and closes with the scholar's honesty: *and Allah knows best*.

That first voice matters enormously. These were men summoned precisely because of their affiliation with magic — and one of them, hearing Musa (peace be upon him), said: this is not our craft; this is prophetic speech. The dissent came from inside the ranks, before the contest.

*Wa asarrū al-najwā*, "and they kept their talk secret," means, Ibn Kathir says, that they held secret counsel among themselves about this matter. The disagreement stayed inside the huddle. It was raised, and it was never made public.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the outcome of that private counsel: ultimately their unanimous decision was to proceed with the contest, because in their opinion Musa (peace be upon him) and Harun (peace be upon him) were both magicians who wished to drive Pharaoh and his men out of Egypt by their magic and to eradicate their ideal way of life. Unanimous — but only after dissent had been argued down. The doubt was settled by decision, not by answer.

## Ayah 63: what they told each other they were defending

*"They said: 'Verily, these are two magicians. Their object is to drive you out from your land with magic, and to take you away from your exemplary way.'"*

**A note on the Arabic.** The reading *in hādhāni la-sāḥirāni* is, Ibn Kathir explains, a way of speaking with some of the Arabs, and this ayah has been recited according to the grammar of their dialect. Others recite it *inna hādhayni la-sāḥirāni*, which carries the same meaning — "verily, these are two magicians" — and is the popular style of language in Arabic grammar. Ibn Kathir observes that the grammarians have extensive discussions in reply to the first recitation and its grammatical explanation, then declines to enter them — "this is not the place for such a discussion" — and steers straight back to the meaning. That restraint is itself instructive, and this commentary will follow it: the point of the ayah is not the dual ending.

**The argument they used on each other.** Ibn Kathir renders the sense of what the magicians said among themselves: "You all know that this man and his brother are two knowledgeable magicians who are quite aware of the skill of magic. They want to defeat you and your people today and conquer the people, causing the masses to follow them. They want to fight against Fir'awn and his armies, and they are seeking victory over him. And their ultimate goal is to expel you from your land."

Read that carefully. They said he was a fraud, and in the same breath that he was about to overcome Pharaoh and his armies. Fear was doing the reasoning.

**"Your exemplary way"** — *ṭarīqatikum al-muthlā*. The commentators open this phrase in several directions, and each adds something:

- **Ibn Kathir**: it means, *"they want to expose this way of yours openly, which is magic."* The magicians were considered great because of their magic; they had wealth and sustenance because of it. His paraphrase of their fear is unsparing: "If these two are victorious, they will destroy you and expel you from your land. In doing so, they will be the first individuals to do so, and they will be given great power of leadership without you."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: it means *"their kingdom, which they were in, and their livelihood."*
- **ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd**: "This superior way means that which they were upon" — their whole standing order.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**: *muthlā* is the feminine of a word meaning "most excellent." The Egyptians believed that their religion — the religion that regarded Pharaoh as god — was the best there was, and that Musa (peace be upon him) and Harun (peace be upon him) wanted to destroy it and supplant their own religion in its place. It adds that *ṭarīqa* is also used to describe the chiefs and leading citizens of a people, and that according to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās and Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them) the word is used in that sense here: these two men wished to finish off all their leaders and important citizens — and it was therefore, in their view, the duty of the Egyptian magicians to unite and use their best endeavours to defeat the enemy.

Put the readings side by side and a single picture emerges. What the magicians called "our exemplary way" was a package: a state religion, a ruling class, a professional craft, and the wealth and sustenance it generated. Truth threatened all of it at once. Ibn Kathir's reading is the sharpest of them — *they want to expose this way of yours openly* — because it locates their deepest fear not in defeat but in exposure.

And notice the phrase *"your land."* It is Egypt they are defending, in the name of a religion that regarded Pharaoh as god. Whenever a way of life is defended as *ours* rather than as *true*, this ayah is describing the argument.

## Ayah 64: one rank, one throw

*"So devise your plot, and then assemble in line. And whoever overcomes this day will be indeed successful."*

**"Devise your plot"** — *fa-ajmiʿū kaydakum*. The Qur'an hands the magicians the same two words it used for Pharaoh in ayah 60, *fa-jamaʿa kaydahu*. The passage opens and closes on gathered *kayd*: the master gathers his plot, and his instruments gather theirs. That is the architecture of these five ayat.

**"Then assemble in line."** Ibn Kathir explains the instruction concretely: "All of you come together in one row, and throw that which is in your hands at one time in order to dazzle the eyes of the people and defeat this man and his brother." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the military logic: formation of troops in ranks in battle has an unsettling effect on the enemy, so the Egyptian magicians arranged themselves in ranks for the contest. Every element of this is aimed at the audience's eyes and the opponent's nerve — falsehood arriving as choreography.

**"And whoever overcomes this day will be indeed successful."** Ibn Kathir unpacks their meaning: *"Between you and us. As for us, we have been promised to be given an abundance of power and sovereignty. And in reference to him, he will gain great leadership."* That is their definition of success, and it is worth stating baldly, because it is the same definition people live by now: whoever comes out on top, today, has won.

Set that beside the word of Musa (peace be upon him) in ayah 61. The magicians say *aflaḥa*, "will be indeed successful," and attach it to *al-yawm*, "this day," and to overcoming. Musa (peace be upon him) says *khāba*, "will fail miserably" — "loser is he who fabricates a lie" — and attaches it to inventing falsehood, with no day attached at all. Everything that follows decides between those two sentences.

## What this passage leaves us holding

It ends before the outcome — deliberately. What we are given is falsehood at its most impressive: state backing, summons sent through the cities, a festival crowd, skilled professionals, disciplined ranks, synchronised spectacle. And we are shown, from the inside, that it was already fractured — arguing in secret, overruling the one voice among them that recognised prophetic speech, defending its wealth and its livelihood while calling it a way of life.

And on the other side: two brothers, one leaning on a stick, offering sincere warning to the very men assembled to defeat them, in words plain enough to reach past every guard. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the prophets and their followers possess a hidden power, so that their plain and simple words penetrate the most unruly and perverse minds. It looked like nothing that day. It had already begun to work.

passages.title: The contest and the magicians' prostration
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single, unbroken scene: the public contest between Musa (peace be upon him) and the magicians of Egypt, and the astonishing way it ends. A challenge issued (65), an illusion unleashed (66), a prophet's hidden fear (67), Allah's reassurance (68), the command that settles everything (69), and the ending (70) — the professionals themselves face down on the ground.

## The word that runs through the whole scene

Almost every ayah here turns on one Arabic verb: **alqā**, "to throw, to cast down." The magicians ask whether Musa (peace be upon him) will *cast* (تُلۡقِيَ) or whether they should be the first to *cast* (أَلۡقَىٰ) in ayah 65. He answers, "Rather, you cast" (أَلۡقُوا) in ayah 66. Allah commands him, "And *cast* what is in your right hand" (وَأَلۡقِ) in ayah 69. Then in ayah 70 the same verb returns, now in the passive and with the magicians as its subject: **فَأُلۡقِيَ ٱلسَّحَرَةُ سُجَّدٗا** — rendered in our sources, "So the magicians fell down prostrate." The men who began the day deciding what to throw ended the day thrown down in prostration. Follow that one word through the passage and you have the whole story in miniature.

## Why Musa (peace be upon him) let them go first

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the instruction just before this scene — *"So, make your plot firm and come forth in one row"* (20:64) — reflects battlefield practice: troops drawn up in ranks have an unsettling effect on the enemy, and so the Egyptian magicians arranged themselves in ranks for the contest. They were confident of their success, and in a mood of complacency they offered Musa (peace be upon him) the choice in ayah 65: you first, or us?

His reply in ayah 66 — *"Rather, you throw"* — was not a small courtesy. Ibn Kathir reads it as strategy in the service of clarity: let the magicians go first *"so that we can see what magic you are going to perform and so that the true state of their affair will become obvious to the people."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds three further reasons. First, the Egyptians had shown courage in inviting him to open the contest, and that called for an equally generous and chivalrous response. Second, their offer implied they had already won; by handing the opening move straight back to them, Musa (peace be upon him) conveyed that he regarded the result as a foregone conclusion in his own favour. Third, he wished to see their tricks before planning his own strategy.

There is a lesson here in how truth handles falsehood. It does not need to move first, and it is not afraid of letting falsehood put on its best performance in full public view. It only needs the last word.

## What the crowd actually saw

The wording of ayah 66 is exact and worth slowing over: **يُخَيَّلُ إِلَيۡهِ مِن سِحۡرِهِمۡ أَنَّهَا تَسۡعَىٰ** — "their ropes and their sticks, by their magic, *appeared to him* as though they moved fast." Notice that the language is the language of appearance, not of transformation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit about what that means: the Egyptian magicians had cast a hypnotic spell on the onlookers, so that it appeared to them that the staffs and the ropes had turned into snakes and were running about on the ground, *"whereas in fact no such transformation had taken place."*

That is the hinge of the whole passage. Their achievement was real *as an achievement* — Ibn Kathir cites Allah's description of it elsewhere, *"They bewitched the eyes of the people, and struck terror into them, and they displayed a great magic"* (7:116) — but what it worked on was the eyes of the people, not the ropes. Ibn Kathir also brings in what they said as they threw: *"By the might of Fir'awn, it is we who will certainly win!"* (26:44). They swore by the wrong power.

Ibn Kathir describes the scale: they were a large group, and each one of them threw a stick and a rope until the valley became full of snakes piled on top of each other. Picture the noise of it, and the crowd.

## The fear of a prophet

Ayah 67 is a remarkably intimate line: **فَأَوۡجَسَ فِي نَفۡسِهِۦ خِيفَةٗ مُّوسَىٰ** — "so Musa concealed fear within himself." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the sight of so many snakes crawling around evoked a sense of fear in him "which he did not reveal to anyone." Not a word of it reached anyone else. Allah reports it because Allah knows what is in the self, not because anyone standing in that valley could see it.

What was he afraid of? Ibn Kathir's answer is that Musa (peace be upon him) feared **for the people** — that they would be tested and deceived by the magic before he even had the chance to throw what was in his right hand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles the question with care: even if the fear had been for his own personal safety, that could be regarded as a natural human reaction to a dangerous situation and does not conflict with the mission of prophethood. But it is clear, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, that the fear he felt was not for his own life. His apprehension was that if the immense crowd, which had assembled to see the contest, sensed that the Egyptian magicians had the upper hand, then the purpose of his mission would be frustrated.

Keep both readings in view. A prophet feels what a human being feels; and what weighed on this prophet was the crowd's faith, not his own skin.

## "Fear not — it is certainly you who will prevail"

In ayah 68 Allah answers the fear that no one else even knew was there: **لَا تَخَفۡ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡأَعۡلَىٰ** — "Do not fear; it is certainly *you* who will be uppermost." Notice the timing, and notice what it teaches about Allah: the fear was hidden inside a man's chest in the middle of a valley full of snakes, and it was answered while it was still hidden. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, these doubts and fears were dispelled when Allah gave him this assurance in the very next ayah.

Then comes the command in ayah 69: **وَأَلۡقِ مَا فِي يَمِينِكَ** — "And throw what is in your right hand." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Allah commanded this by means of *waḥy*, revelation. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah revealed it to him "at the right moment."

## The staff, and the end of the contest

Ibn Kathir describes what happened when he threw it: the staff became a huge, monstrous creature with legs, a neck, a head and fangs. It went after those ropes and sticks until none of them remained, except that it was devoured and swallowed by this beast. And the crucial detail — the magicians and all of the people were watching with their own eyes, seeing this amazing event in broad daylight. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: his staff turned into a huge snake and ate up all the imaginary snakes which the Egyptian magicians had produced by their magic.

Set the two accounts side by side and the point is unmissable. Their snakes were *imaginary*; his was real, and it consumed theirs. Illusion cannot survive contact with reality. As Ibn Kathir sums it up: "the miracle was performed and the evidence was clear. The truth prevailed and the magic was proven to be falsehood."

Ayah 69 then delivers the verdict in Allah's own words: **إِنَّمَا صَنَعُوا۟ كَيۡدُ سَٰحِرٖ** — "that which they have made is only a magician's *kayd*." It is the same word used a few ayat earlier, when the magicians were told to *"make your plot (kayd) firm"* (20:64) — rendered "plot" there and "trick" here. What they were commanded to gather with all their strength is named for what it was: the trick of a conjuror.

And then the sentence that reaches far beyond that valley: **وَلَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلسَّاحِرُ حَيۡثُ أَتَىٰ** — "and the magician will never be successful, to whatever amount of skill he may attain." This is not a comment on one contest. It is a rule about a whole category of activity: no level of mastery redeems it, and no venue makes it come out right.

## The men who knew every trick

Ayah 70 is the outcome, and its power lies in *who* is prostrating. Ibn Kathir makes the argument explicitly: when these men saw the event and witnessed it with their own eyes, "while they were knowledgeable of the various tricks and methods in the sciences of magic, they knew with conviction that what Musa had done was not magic or illusionary tricks." They recognised it as the truth without any doubt. They knew that no one had any power to do this except the One Who says to a thing "Be," and it is.

The men who knew every trick in the trade were the ones who said, without doubt, that this was no trick. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: these Egyptian magicians, masters of their art, realised at once that what they had just witnessed was not magic but a miracle brought about by a Supreme Power.
