So they went down. **فَأُلۡقِيَ ٱلسَّحَرَةُ سُجَّدٗا** — the magicians fell down in prostration, declaring: *"We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa."* Note what they said and what they did not say. Their faith was in the **Lord** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as declaring openly their faith in Allah, the Lord of Musa (peace be upon him) and Harun (peace be upon him). They did not attach themselves to a man; they named the Master whom these two men served. Ibn Kathir renders their words: "We believe in the Lord of all that exists, the Lord of Musa and Harun."

Consider the turn. Moments earlier they had thrown their ropes crying "By the might of Fir'awn, it is we who will certainly win!" Now they were on the ground, declaring their faith openly.

## A day that turned

Ibn Kathir preserves several reports from the early authorities about this moment.

- **Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr** both said: *"At the beginning of the day they were magicians and at the end of the day they were outstanding witnesses of faith."* One day. No long apprenticeship in religion, no gradual softening — the evidence came, and they took it.
- **Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas**: "The magicians were seventy men who were magicians in the morning, but witnesses of faith by the time evening came."
- **Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from Al-Awza'i**: "When the magicians fell down in prostration, Paradise was raised up before them until they were looking at it."
- **Sa'id bin Jubayr**, on the words "So the magicians fell down prostrate," said: *"They saw their places in Paradise made clear before them while they were in their prostration."* Ibn Kathir notes that **'Ikrimah** and **Al-Qasim bin Abi Bizzah** both said the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions the same theme — that according to some traditions these magicians did not raise their heads until they had seen a glimpse of heaven and hell — reported from 'Ikrimah.

These are transmitted reports from the early authorities about what was disclosed to the magicians in that prostration, not statements of the Qur'anic text itself; Ibn Kathir passes them on with their sources, and they are best received in that spirit. What they convey is a stunning exchange: heads that went down in the middle of Pharaoh's own contest came up with Paradise already in view.

## Living it

**Truth does not fear the other side's best case.** Musa (peace be upon him) let them go first, in full view, at full strength — so that, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the true state of their affair would become obvious to the people. Confidence in the truth looks like patience while falsehood exhausts its repertoire.

**Fear at the decisive moment is not a failure of faith.** The Qur'an records that Musa (peace be upon him) felt it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say such a reaction does not conflict with the mission of prophethood. What matters is what you fear *for* — his apprehension was for the crowd's faith and the purpose of his mission, not for his own life — and what you do with it. He kept it inside himself and waited on his Lord.

**Allah answers what is hidden.** "Do not fear" came while the fear was still concealed from everyone else. Nothing you carry inwardly is unknown to Him, and nothing you carry inwardly is beneath His attention.

**Skill is not success.** *"The magician will never be successful, to whatever amount of skill he may attain."* Excellence at something Allah has condemned is still a road that ends nowhere. It is worth asking honestly which of our own competencies are being sharpened, and toward what.

**When the evidence is clear, act on it today.** Seventy men, in Ibn 'Abbas's report, were magicians in the morning and witnesses of faith by the time evening came — the epitaph any of us would want.

passages.title: The magicians defy Pharaoh's threats
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the moment after the contest is over. Fir'awn's own magicians have fallen in prostration, and now the humiliated tyrant turns on them with accusation and terror — and they answer him without flinching. What holds ayat 71–76 together is a single exchange: a threat (71), a refusal (72–73), and then something no one expected — the new believers stop defending themselves and start preaching to Fir'awn about the Hereafter (74–76).

## The tyrant's real complaint (ayah 71)

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Allah is showing us Fir'awn's "disbelief, obstinance, transgression and haughtiness against the truth in favour of falsehood." He had seen the magnificent miracle and the great sign, and he had seen the very men whose help he had sought accept faith in the presence of all the people; he was, in Ibn Kathir's words, "absolutely defeated." So he did what cornered power does: he began to behave arrogantly and cast accusations, and he fell back on his esteemed honour and his might against the magicians.

Listen to what he actually objects to. Not *that* they believed — but that they believed **قَبْلَ أَنْ آذَنَ لَكُمْ**, "before I give you permission." Ibn Kathir explains his meaning: "I have not commanded you to do so, by which you have rebelled against me." His grievance is not theological; it is about authority. A man who claims lordship cannot tolerate hearts moving without his clearance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human texture: disgraced before a vast multitude, he was furious, and he *stormed* at them — how dare they accept the religion brought by Musa (peace be upon him) without his prior permission.

Then comes the charge: **إِنَّهُ لَكَبِيرُكُمُ الَّذِي عَلَّمَكُمُ السِّحْرَ**, "he is your chief who taught you magic." Ibn Kathir is blunt that this was "a statement that he, the magicians and all creatures knew was a forgery and an utter lie." Its meaning: you took your magic only from Musa, and you have made an agreement with him against me and my subjects to help him be victorious. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — he suspected they were all Musa's (peace be upon him) pupils and had accepted defeat in connivance with him. Ibn Kathir points to another ayah where Allah records Fir'awn saying, *"Surely, this is a plot which you have plotted in the city to drive out its people, but you shall come to know"* (7:123). Note the tactic: rather than answer the sign, he reframes faith as a political conspiracy. It is easier to accuse than to admit.

## The threat, and the words he chose (ayah 71)

**فَلَأُقَطِّعَنَّ أَيْدِيَكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُم مِّنْ خِلَافٍ** — "I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of date palms."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains "on opposite sides": first the right hand, then the left foot — apparently the mode of inflicting punishment under the laws of Fir'awn — and then, after the cutting, crucifixion on the trunks of palm trees, where they would remain suspended until they died of starvation. Ibn Kathir gives the purpose in one line: "I will certainly make an example of you, I will kill you in a public execution." Ibn 'Abbas said that Fir'awn was thus the first person ever to do this — reported by Ibn Abi Hatim.

Then the taunt: **وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ أَيُّنَا أَشَدُّ عَذَابًا وَأَبْقَىٰ** — "you shall surely know which of us is severer in punishment and more lasting." Ibn Kathir unpacks the sarcasm: "You say that my people and I are astray and that you, Musa and his people are following correct guidance, but you will come to know who will be punished and remain punished."

Keep the two words **أَشَدُّ** (severer) and **أَبْقَىٰ** (more lasting) in mind. Fir'awn has just claimed both severity and permanence for himself. The rest of the passage takes those two claims apart.

## The answer that could not be threatened (ayah 72)

"So when he attacked with this and threatened them," says Ibn Kathir, "their souls eased them because of their belief in Allah, the Mighty and Sublime." That is a striking observation: the threat did not disturb them; their faith actually *settled* them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees — the magicians stood firm and did not waver in the face of Fir'awn's threats.

**لَن نُّؤْثِرَكَ عَلَىٰ مَا جَاءَنَا مِنَ الْبَيِّنَاتِ** — "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us." They do not say "we disagree with you"; they say *we will not rank you above what we have seen*. Ibn Kathir's gloss: "We do not choose you over the guidance and conviction that we have received." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way — they told him plainly that they would not give him, nor anything he said, preference over the clear proofs and the miracles which Allah had shown them.

**وَالَّذِي فَطَرَنَا** — "and the One who created us." Ibn Kathir mentions two possible ways of reading this:

- It may be an **oath**: "By He Who has created us!" — they swear by Allah in Fir'awn's face.
- Or it may be **joined in meaning to "the clear proofs"**: "we will not prefer you over our Originator and Creator."

On the second reading Ibn Kathir draws out the meaning: He is the One "Who produced us from a beginning that was nothing. He created us from clay (or mud). Therefore, He alone deserves worship and humility and you do not (Fir'awn)!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same movement: they confirmed their belief in the One who created the earth and the skies, and rejected Fir'awn's claim to divinity. Men who had built their lives on illusion are now pointing to the One who brings things into being out of nothing — and telling Fir'awn which side of that line he stands on.

**فَاقْضِ مَا أَنتَ قَاضٍ** — "so decree whatever you will decree." Ibn Kathir: "Do whatever you wish and whatever your hands are able to achieve." There is a quiet contempt in that phrase *whatever your hands are able*. And the limit is stated immediately: **إِنَّمَا تَقْضِي هَٰذِهِ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا** — "you can only decree in this worldly life." Ibn Kathir: "You only have power in this world and it is a world that will come to an end. Verily, we are hoping in the eternal abode." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders their reasoning almost as speech: you can punish us as long as we live, but when we die we will be out of your reach — whereas we are in the power of Allah both in this life and after death, and it is *His* punishment that is of greater concern to us.

That is the whole logic of courage: tyranny's leverage is only the span of a human life, and once a person truly fears the One whose reach extends past death, the tyrant has run out of currency.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates from Sayyidnā ʿIkrimah that when the magicians prostrated themselves before Allah, He gave them a glimpse of the eminent places and the gifts which were to be their reward in Paradise.

## "Forgive us the magic you forced on us" (ayah 73)

**إِنَّا آمَنَّا بِرَبِّنَا لِيَغْفِرَ لَنَا خَطَايَانَا** — "we have believed in our Lord so He may forgive us our faults." Notice the very first instinct of a new believer: not a demand for vindication, but a plea for forgiveness. Ibn Kathir says this covers "whatever evils that we did," and specifically what they were forced to do of magic, in order to oppose the sign of Allah and the miracle of His Prophet.

On **وَمَا أَكْرَهْتَنَا عَلَيْهِ مِنَ السِّحْرِ** ("and the magic you compelled us to"), Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas a remarkable piece of background: "Fir'awn took forty boys from the Children of Israel and commanded that they be taught magic at Al-Farama. He said, 'Teach them knowledge that no one in the land knows.'" Ibn 'Abbas then said that these were among those who believed in Musa (peace be upon him) and among those who spoke this very ayah. 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said the same. If so, the sorcery Fir'awn leaned on that day had been cultivated by his own command, in men he had taken as boys.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: the magicians came to the contest of their own free choice and had even negotiated beforehand their reward if they were victorious, so how can they say they were *compelled*? Two possible answers are offered:

1. They were, to begin with, tempted by promises of generous rewards for taking part; but they soon realised they stood no chance against miracles and wanted to withdraw from the contest — and it was *then* that Fir'awn forced them to take up the challenge.
2. Under a law passed by Fir'awn, everybody was compelled to learn magic in the first place.

Either way, the point stands: what was pressed on them by a tyrant is still something they bring to Allah asking for pardon. They do not hide behind the excuse. They name the coercion and still say *forgive us*.

Then the counter-punch: **وَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ** — "and Allah is better and more lasting." Ibn Kathir: "He is better for us than you," and more lasting in reward "than what you promised us and made us aspire to." Fir'awn had claimed to be severer in punishment and more lasting. They hand the word **أَبْقَىٰ** straight back to him. Whatever he can do ends at a grave; what Allah gives does not end at all.

## From the accused to the preachers (ayat 74–76)

Ibn Kathir states plainly that these ayat are "a completion of what the magicians admonished Fir'awn with." They warned him of the vengeance of Allah and His eternal and everlasting punishment, and they encouraged him to seek Allah's eternal and endless reward. The men on trial have become the ones delivering the summons.

**إِنَّهُ مَن يَأْتِ رَبَّهُ مُجْرِمًا** — "whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal." Ibn Kathir keeps it simple: this means whoever meets Allah on the Day of Judgment while being a criminal. Notice that they do not say "you, Fir'awn" — they state a principle, and let him place himself under it.

**لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ** — "he will neither die therein nor live." Death would be relief; life worth the name is denied. Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels: *"Neither will it have a complete killing effect on them so that they die, nor shall its torment be lightened for them. Thus do We requite every disbeliever!"* (35:36); *"But it will be avoided by the wretched, who will enter the great Fire. There he will neither die nor live"* (87:11–13); and the cry of the damned, *"O Malik! Let your Lord make an end of us,"* answered with *"Verily, you shall abide forever"* (43:77).

Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal recorded that Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The dwellers of Hellfire, who are those who deserve it, they will not die in it, nor will they be living. Rather, they will be a people who will be punished by the Fire due to their sins. It will be gradually killing them and devouring them until they become burnt coals. Then, intercession will be allowed and they will be brought (out of Hell) group by group and they will be spread on the rivers of Paradise. It will then be said, 'O people of Paradise, pour (water) over them.' Then, they will start to grow like the growing of a seed on the muddy banks of a flowing river." A man among the people said, "It is as if the Messenger of Allah lived in the desert." Ibn Kathir notes that this is how Muslim recorded the narration in his *Sahih*. So the terrible phrase "neither dies nor lives" belongs to those who are the Fire's own people — while others, by the intercession Allah permits, are brought out.

**وَمَن يَأْتِهِ مُؤْمِنًا قَدْ عَمِلَ الصَّالِحَاتِ** — "and whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous good deeds." Ibn Kathir's comment is worth memorising: whoever meets his Lord on the Day of Judgment as a believer *in his heart*, then his intentions in his heart will be affirmed to be true by his statements and his deeds. Faith in the heart and action in the limbs are not rivals; the second is the evidence of the first.

**فَأُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمُ الدَّرَجَاتُ الْعُلَىٰ** — "for them are the high ranks": Paradise, says Ibn Kathir, which has the highest levels, the most tranquil rooms and the nicest homes. He cites two narrations here:

- Imam Ahmad reported from 'Ubadah bin As-Samit that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Paradise has one hundred levels and between each level is a distance like the distance between the sky and the earth. Al-Firdaws is the name of the highest of its levels. From it springs the four rivers and the Throne is above it. Therefore, when you ask Allah, then ask Him for Al-Firdaws." At-Tirmidhi also recorded it.
- In the Two Sahihs — that is, the two collections each titled *Sahih*, the most rigorously screened of the hadith books — it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, the people of the 'Illiyyin will see those who are above them just as you see the fading star in the horizon of the sky, due to the different status of virtue between them." The people said, "O Messenger of Allah, these are the dwellings of the Prophets." He ﷺ replied, "Of course. And I swear by the One Whom my soul is in His Hand, (it is for) men who had faith in Allah and they believed the Messengers." In the Sunan collections — the hadith books arranged by chapters of Islamic law — this narration comes with the additional wording, "And verily Abu Bakr and 'Umar are of them and they will be most favoured."

Two things follow. Paradise is not one flat reward — ranks differ, so ambition in faith is legitimate. And those heights are not reserved for prophets alone: the Prophet ﷺ swore that they are also for men who had faith in Allah and believed the Messengers — which is exactly what these magicians had just done.

**جَنَّاتُ عَدْنٍ** (ayah 76) — Ibn Kathir explains *ʿAdn* as meaning established as a residence, used here in reference to the high ranks just mentioned; rivers run beneath them, and **خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا** means that they will abide in it for eternity. And **وَذَٰلِكَ جَزَاءُ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ**, "that is the reward of whoever purifies himself" — Ibn Kathir: one who purifies himself from dirt, filth and associating partners with Allah; this is the person who worships Allah alone, without ascribing partners to Him, and follows the Messengers in the good they came with. That is the definition of *tazkiyah* (purification) the passage leaves us with: not vague self-improvement, but purification from shirk plus following the Messengers.

## Magicians in the morning, witnesses of faith by evening

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to miss. These words about the Islamic beliefs and the Hereafter were spoken by men who had only recently become Muslims and who had not yet been instructed about the principles and obligations of their new faith. It was the result of their brief association with Musa (peace be upon him) that Allah, in an instant, revealed to them the mysteries of that faith — so that they gave scarce heed to Fir'awn's threats. With their adoption of the religion of Allah they attained a state that is given to others only after long and assiduous exertion. Sayyidnā Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubaid Ibn 'Umair said it was a divine marvel that the magicians who started the day as infidels became saints before it ended; as Ibn 'Abbas and others of the Salaf put it, "They woke up in that morning as magicians, but they became witnesses of faith by the evening."

Ibn Kathir adds a sobering, beautiful line. It is apparent, he says, that Fir'awn was bent upon their punishment — and that what he did to them "was a mercy from Allah for them." Their tormentor became, without knowing it, the instrument that sealed them in their best state.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records, from Qurtubi, what was happening in the palace that same hour: while the contest was in progress Fir'awn's wife kept herself informed of the minute-to-minute developments, and when she learned that Musa (peace be upon him) had emerged victorious she at once declared her adherence to the true faith. Told of it, Fir'awn ordered that a huge rock be thrown upon her; when 'Asiyah saw the rock coming she raised her eyes in supplication to Allah, who took away her soul, so that the rock fell on a body already at rest.

## Living it

- **Notice what tyranny actually demands.** Fir'awn's fury in ayah 71 was over permission, not truth. Any authority that requires your convictions to wait for its approval is asking for something that belongs to Allah alone.
- **Answer the accusation with the evidence.** In ayah 72 they never argue the conspiracy charge; they simply say: we saw the clear proofs, and we will not rank you above them.
- **Locate the limit of the threat.** "You can only decree in this worldly life" is a sentence for hard days: whatever anyone takes from you, they cannot follow you past the grave.
- **Bring your coerced sins to Allah anyway.** They had a genuine excuse and still asked for forgiveness (ayah 73). Excuses are for people; repentance is for Allah.
- **Aim high.** The Prophet ﷺ told us that when we ask Allah, we should ask Him for al-Firdaws. Do not settle your du'a for less than what he told you to request.

passages.title: The sea crossed and Pharaoh drowned
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the escape itself: the departure from Egypt by night, the sea opened as a road, the pursuing tyrant swallowed by the water he rode into. What holds them together is a single movement — a command from Allah (ayah 77), the consequence for those who chased the believers (ayah 78), and the verdict on the man who led them there (ayah 79). Notice how compressed it is. Ibn Kathīr points out that Allah expounds on this same episode at greater length in other surahs; here it is telescoped into three ayat.

## What comes just before

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: Fir'awn had already suffered a decisive defeat in the contest between right and wrong, between miracle and magic. His power was broken, and the Children of Israel stood united under the leadership of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him). It is at that point that Allah commanded Mūsā to take his people out of Egypt. Maʿārif also notes that this story has already been narrated earlier in this very surah, in the passage it refers to as *Ḥadīth ul-Futūn* (the name the commentary uses for that earlier section of the surah, not a separate prophetic report being quoted here) — so by ayah 77 the Qur'an is returning to ground the listener has already walked.

Ibn Kathīr adds the immediate reason for the command: Fir'awn had refused to release the Children of Israel and send them with Mūsā. So Allah commanded Mūsā to journey by night with them, to take them away from Fir'awn's captivity.

## Ayah 77: "Travel by night with My servants"

The command is **أَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي** — rendered by Ibn Kathīr as *"Travel by night with My servants."* The movement is made under cover of night, out of the land of an empire that held them.

Weigh the phrase **بِعِبَادِي**, "with **My** servants." They were still, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, in Fir'awn's captivity — and Allah calls them His own servants. The word choice is worth sitting with before we move on.

Ibn Kathīr describes the morning after: the people of Egypt awoke to find that not a single one of them remained in Egypt. Fir'awn became extremely furious. He sent callers into all of the cities to gather his army from all his lands and provinces, saying to them what Allah records in Surah ash-Shuʿarā': *"Verily, these indeed are but a small band. And verily, they have done what has enraged us"* (26:54–55). Then, when he had gathered his army and organised his troops, he set out after them — and Ibn Kathīr says they followed them at dawn, when the sun began to rise.

## The moment of no escape

Then the two hosts saw each other — **فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ** (26:61), which Ibn Kathīr explains plainly: each person of the two parties was looking at the other party. Not a rumour of pursuit; the two forces in plain sight of one another.

Mūsā (peace be upon him) had stopped with the Children of Israel, the sea in front of them and Fir'awn behind them. His companions said what any of us would have said: **إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ** — *"We are sure to be overtaken."* And he answered: **كَلَّا ۖ إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ** — *"Nay, verily, with me is my Lord. He will guide me"* (26:61–62).

Look closely at that answer. He does not say *I have a plan*. He does not claim to know what happens next. He says only that his Lord is with him and will guide him — certainty about Allah, not about the exit. And Ibn Kathīr places the revelation of the second half of ayah 77 *at exactly that moment*: then, at that moment, Allah revealed to Mūsā, **فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا** — "and strike a dry path for them in the sea."

So ayah 77 folds two moments into one sentence: the command to leave by night, and the command at the water's edge. The lesson sits in the gap between them. The way out was not shown when the journey began. It was shown when there was no other way.

## The road was made dry

The word **يَبَسًا** — *yabasan*, "dry" — is not decoration. Ibn Kathīr reports that Mūsā struck the sea with his stick and said, *"Split for me, by the leave of Allah."* Note the wording of a prophet with a miracle in his hand: he attributes the power to Allah's permission even as it happens through him. Thus it split, and each separate part of the water became like a huge mountain. Then Allah sent a wind to the land of the sea, and it dried the soil until it became like the ground that is on land. It is for this reason, Ibn Kathīr says, that Allah described the path as **dry**. The rescue reached down to the ground under their feet.

## Two fears, both answered

**لَّا تَخَافُ دَرَكًا وَلَا تَخْشَىٰ** — "fearing neither to be overtaken nor being afraid."

Ibn Kathīr separates the two precisely:

- **دَرَكًا** (*darakan*, being caught up with) — this means being caught by Fir'awn. The danger behind.
- **وَلَا تَخْشَىٰ** ("nor being afraid") — meaning, "Do not be afraid of the sea drowning your people." The danger ahead.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole crisis the same way: the move out of Egypt was full of danger — first the risk of pursuit by Fir'awn, and second the water, which they had no means of crossing, barring their flight — and Allah dispelled both these fears from the mind of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him). One short clause of ayah 77 disarms the threat on both sides at once. That is the shape of divine reassurance: it does not address only the fear you name loudest, it addresses every fear you actually have.

## Twelve roads through the water

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the crossing. When the time came, Mūsā (peace be upon him) struck the surface of the water with his staff, and masses of water stood asunder, revealing **twelve** dry paths — matching what Surah ash-Shuʿarā' says: **فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ** — *"And each part became like a big mountain"* (26:63). On these twelve dry passageways the twelve tribes of the Children of Israel crossed to the other side in safety.

And one exquisite detail: the walls of water dividing the passages were so formed that those going on one road could see and talk to those travelling on the other roads. Maʿārif names the purpose — it imparted to them all a sense of security. Allah did not only save them; He saw to their reassurance while He saved them.

## The numbers — and a scholar's honesty

Maʿārif reports from *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* that Mūsā (peace be upon him) embarked on the journey towards the Red Sea soon after sunset. Earlier, the Children of Israel had announced that one of their festivals was approaching, which they would celebrate outside the city — and on this excuse, and to allay the suspicions of the Egyptians, they borrowed some jewellery from the Copts, promising to return it after the festival.

As for how many left: at that time they numbered six hundred and three thousand, while another version puts their number at six hundred and seventy thousand. Fir'awn's pursuing force is described as a large army whose advance units consisted of seven hundred thousand horsemen.

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says something worth pausing on. It states openly that these figures **may be exaggerated**, that they have been taken from Isrāʼīlite traditions, and that one thing appears certain — namely, that the people were divided into twelve very populous tribes.

Maʿārif then draws out what the numbers are actually *for*: these large numbers were themselves a gift from Allah, because the first arrivals in Egypt in the days of Sayyidnā Yūsuf (peace be upon him) were just the twelve brothers. Now the twelve tribes descended from those twelve brothers left Egypt numbering well over six hundred thousand.

## Ayah 78: the water closes

**فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِ** — "Then Fir'awn pursued them with his hosts."

Maʿārif preserves the psychology of the last moments, and it is chilling. Fir'awn saw all this and was frightened by it. And then he urged his men on by declaring that the dry paths had formed because the river had stopped flowing out of the awe it felt in his presence. Saying so, he spurred his horse into the river and ordered his army to follow him. When they were all in the middle, Allah commanded the river to resume its flow, and the water covered them over.

He did not fail to see the sign. He saw it, and rewrote it so that it flattered him. That is what disbelief so often is — not blindness, but a story told over the top of the evidence.

**فَغَشِيَهُم مِّنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُم** — "there covered them from the sea *what covered them*."

Ibn Kathīr glosses **الْيَمِّ** (*al-yamm*) simply: *al-yamm* means the sea. But notice the second half of the phrase. The Qur'an does not say *the water drowned them*. It says: there covered them **what covered them** — the thing left unnamed. Ibn Kathīr explains it as being covered up with a thing that was well-familiar in such a situation, and he points to the same construction used elsewhere, of the overthrown cities: **وَالْمُؤْتَفِكَةَ أَهْوَىٰ ۝ فَغَشَّاهَا مَا غَشَّىٰ** — *"And He destroyed the overthrown cities. So there covered them that which did cover"* (53:53–54). The army exits the narrative in half a line, without even a description.

## Ayah 79: the verdict on a leader

**وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَىٰ** — "And Fir'awn led his people astray, and he did not guide them."

The second half looks redundant next to the first — if he led them astray, obviously he did not guide them. It is not redundant; it is a stripping away of his central claim. The man who presented himself as the one showing his people the right way is answered on his own terms: he misled them, and guide them he did not.

Ibn Kathīr extends the line into the hereafter. As Fir'awn pursued them into the sea, misled his people and did not lead them to the path of correct guidance, so likewise he will go ahead of his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Hellfire — "and evil indeed is the place to which they are led." The same man, the same position at the front, the same followers walking behind him into destruction.

## What to carry away

**Certainty is about Allah, not about the exit.** Mūsā (peace be upon him) said "with me is my Lord; He will guide me" while standing between a sea and an army. The path was revealed after the words were said, not before.

**Relief can arrive at the last possible moment — and that is not abandonment.** Ibn Kathīr places the command to strike the sea precisely at the point where the sea was in front of them and Fir'awn behind them.

**Allah's care extends past bare survival.** The seabed was dried so they could walk; the walls of water were formed so they could see and talk to one another across the passages, giving them a sense of security. The rescue included their peace of mind.

**Fear the habit of explaining signs away.** Fir'awn's ruin was not that he lacked evidence — a split sea stood open in front of him, and it frightened him. It was that he had a self-serving explanation ready, and he rode into the water behind it.

**Ask who is in front of you.** Ayah 79 is a warning about followership as much as leadership. Fir'awn's people followed a man into the sea. On the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathīr says, he will go ahead of them again. Choose carefully whose back you are walking behind.

passages.title: Allah's favours and warning to Israel
passages.tafsir:
The account of Musa and Fir'awn has just closed with the destruction of the tyrant. Now, in ayat 80–82, Allah addresses the people who were rescued: **O Children of Israel!** These three ayat name the favours Allah gave them (deliverance, the appointment at the Mount, manna and quail), attach a command with a warning to those favours, and then state His forgiveness.

## The rescue they watched

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah here reminds the Children of Israel of His tremendous favours upon them and His numerous blessings. The first is deliverance: He saved them from their enemy, Fir'awn, and — in Ibn Kathir's phrase — **He relieved their eyes** by drowning him and his hosts all at one time while they watched. Ibn Kathir supports this with the Qur'an's own reminder, *"And We drowned Fir'awn's people while you were looking"* (2:50). Those addressed had seen it happen.

Ibn Kathir then brings a narration in this connection. **Al-Bukhari recorded** that Ibn 'Abbas said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Al-Madinah, he found the Jews fasting the day of 'Ashura'. He asked them about it and they said, "This is the day that Allah gave Musa victory over Fir'awn." The Prophet ﷺ then said, *"We have more right to Musa (than them), so fast it."* **Muslim also recorded this narration in his Sahih.**

Notice what Ibn Kathir has placed beside the ayah. The rescue of Musa's people is not treated as somebody else's history. The Prophet ﷺ claimed Musa — *we have more right to him* — and told the believers to fast that day. So when Allah says in ayah 80 "We saved you from your enemy," the Muslim reading it is not eavesdropping on a conversation that has nothing to do with him.

## The appointment at the right side of the Mount

The second favour in ayah 80 is that Allah *made a covenant with you on the right side of the Mount* — rendered in Ma'arif ul Qur'an as *"appointed for you the right side of the mount Tur."* Both renderings are worth holding together: it was a promise, and it was a summons to a particular place.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an fills in the scene. After their deliverance from the threat of Pharaoh, once they were safe across the river, Allah made a promise to Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) and, through him, to the Bani Isra'il: that they should move to the right side of the mount of Tur, so that Musa might be given the Torah, and so that **they might witness him speak with Allah**.

Ibn Kathir notes that this covenant was made after the destruction of Fir'awn, and gathers what this one mountain witnessed:

- It is the Mountain upon which **Allah spoke to Musa**.
- It is the Mountain He told Musa's people to look at when they requested to see Allah.
- It is the Mountain upon which **Musa was given the Tawrah**.

And Ibn Kathir adds one more line to that list, in the same breath: while Musa was being given the Tawrah on that mountain, *at the same time the Children of Israel began worshipping the statue of a calf* — as Allah relates, he says, in the ayat that follow. He places the honour and the betrayal in a single sentence. Allah names the favour here in ayah 80; and in ayah 82, as we will see, He will speak of forgiveness for exactly that sin.

## Manna and quail in the years of punishment

The third favour: *"And We sent down to you manna and quail."*

Ibn Kathir describes them plainly. **Manna** was a sweet substance that descended upon them from the sky. **Salwa**, the quail, was a type of bird that would fall down to them. They would fill every pot with them as ample provisions until the following day. Ibn Kathir calls this a kindness and a mercy from Allah upon them, a manifestation of Allah's good treatment of them.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an supplies the setting. This provision came after they had crossed the river and were commanded to enter a sacred city — and **refused**. As punishment they were confined to the valley known as the valley of Tih (Sinai), where they stayed for forty years. And Ma'arif ul Qur'an makes the point explicitly: *in spite of the punishment which they were undergoing, they continued to receive gifts from Allah*, and the Mann and Salwa were among those gifts, given to them for their sustenance.

That is a sentence worth reading twice. A people under punishment, still receiving gifts. Allah's justice was in operation and His generosity was not withdrawn. A believer who is being corrected for his own sins can take something from this: being under discipline is not the same as being abandoned.

## "Eat — and do not transgress in it"

Ayah 81 attaches the command: *"Eat of the good things (Tayyibat) wherewith We have provided you, and commit no transgression or oppression therein."*

Notice first what is *not* said. The command is **eat** — and eat of the *tayyibat*, the good and wholesome things. Ibn Kathir has just called this provision a kindness and a mercy; the ayah tells them to receive it.

The limit falls on *how* it is taken. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *"Eat from this sustenance which I have provided for you, and do not transgress against My sustenance by taking it without necessity, or you will be opposing what I have commanded you."* The transgression warned against, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is taking beyond need. And the offence is defined precisely: it is *opposing what Allah has commanded*. The wrong is not done to the food. It is done to the One who sent it.

There is a standard here for our own lives. What Allah gives is given to be received, but within His command; the failure Ibn Kathir names is not enjoyment but taking without necessity. The word "necessity" in his gloss is a useful measure to hold against our own consumption.

## "Lest My anger descend on you"

The consequence is stated with weight: *"lest My anger should justly descend on you. And he on whom My anger descends, he is indeed perished"* (ayah 81).

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the first phrase is a single line: it means **"I will become angry with you."** He does not elaborate beyond that, and neither will we.

On *"he is indeed perished"* (*faqad hawa*), Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, through the narration of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah: **"This means that he will indeed be made miserable."** Ibn 'Abbas' words name what that ruin amounts to — wretchedness, misery.

## Then the door opens

Straight after that comes ayah 82: *"And verily, I am indeed forgiving to him who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, and then is guided."*

Ibn Kathir's summary of it is one line, and it is enormous: **"Whoever turns to Me in repentance, then I will accept his repentance regardless of whatever sin he did."** And he immediately gives an example from this very context — Allah, the Exalted, *even accepts the repentance of the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf*.

That is the same sin Ibn Kathir mentioned a moment earlier, committed by these very people, at the very mountain named in ayah 80, while Musa was receiving the Tawrah. If that repentance was accepted, the reader has been given something to weigh against his own despair.

## Four things, in this order

Ayah 82 does not say "forgiving to whoever repents" and stop. It names four things, and Ibn Kathir observes that **there is a specific order in which these things are presented**. He takes them one by one:

1. **He repents** (*taba*) — Ibn Kathir: to turn away from what one was involved in of disbelief, associating partners with Allah, disobedience of Allah, or hypocrisy. It is a turning *away from* what you were doing.
2. **He believes** (*amana*) — "the person's belief in his heart." The inward reality.
3. **He does righteous deeds** (*'amila salihan*) — "his action with his bodily limbs." Belief that has come out of the heart and into the hands.
4. **And then he is guided** (*thumma ihtada*) — a further stage, after the first three.

On this fourth word Ibn Kathir reports two explanations:

- From **Ibn 'Abbas** (via 'Ali bin Abi Talhah): *"This means that he then does not doubt."*
- From **Qatadah**: *"This means he adheres to Islam until he dies."*

Ibn Kathir notes that this staged pattern is like Allah's saying, *"Then he became one of those who believed and recommended one another to perseverance and patience and recommended one another to pity and compassion"* (90:17) — where again a *"then"* adds a further stage on top of what came before.

## What to carry away

- **Allah names specific mercies, not vague ones.** He recalls the rescue, the Mount, the manna and quail. Ibn Kathir calls them tremendous favours and numerous blessings.
- **Take what you need from what Allah gives, and stop there.** The transgression named in ayah 81, as Ibn Kathir reads it, is taking Allah's sustenance without necessity — and the offence is against His command.
- **Punishment is not the withdrawal of Allah's giving.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an: in spite of the punishment they were undergoing in the valley of Tih, they continued to receive gifts from Allah.
- **Do not let the size of a sin argue you out of repenting.** Ibn Kathir: repentance is accepted *regardless of whatever sin he did* — and he points to the very people who worshipped the calf.
- **Then keep going.** Repentance, faith and deeds are followed in the ayah by *thumma ihtada* — not doubting, said Ibn 'Abbas; adhering to Islam until death, said Qatadah.

Allah's last word in this passage, addressed to a people whose worst failure is about to be recounted, is not the warning. It is *"I am indeed forgiving."*

passages.title: The golden calf made in Moses' absence
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat tell one story: a prophet hurrying up a mountain out of love for his Lord, and a nation collapsing into calf-worship the moment he is out of sight. The unit runs from Allah's question in ayah 83, through the news of the trial in ayah 85, to Musa's furious return and cross-examination in ayah 86, the people's excuse in ayah 87, the making of the calf in ayah 88, and Allah's own devastating reply in ayah 89.

## Where we are in the story

Ibn Kathir sets the scene just after Fir'awn's destruction. Having crossed the water in safety, the Children of Israel passed a people devoted to idols and said, *"O Musa! Make for us a god as they have gods."* He answered, *"Verily, you are a people who know not. Verily, these people will be destroyed for that which they are engaged in, and all that they are doing is in vain"* (7:138–139). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the flavour of their request: these people have gods they can see and touch — give us one like that.

The calf did not create the craving; it answered one they had already voiced out loud.

Then Allah appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten more — forty in all — the covenant being that he fast through those days and nights (Ibn Kathir). Musa hastened to the Mountain, leaving his brother Harun in charge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that he was leading the nation toward Ṭūr to receive the Torah — a book that would be their whole code of life — but in his eagerness he pushed ahead to begin the prescribed days as soon as possible, expecting them to catch up. While the caravan moved at its leisurely pace behind him, Sāmirī worked his mischief, split them into three factions, and their journey toward the Mountain stalled.

## Ayah 83: a question that is not really a question

*"And what made you hasten from your people, O Musa?"*

Allah already knows. So why ask?

**Ibn Kathir's reading:** the question is the doorway to the news. Musa is standing there unaware, waiting for his people to arrive; the question opens the subject so that Allah may inform him of the catastrophe unfolding behind him.

**The reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī:** the question carries an implied rebuke. Musa's haste left his people without supervision and gave Sāmirī his opening; a prophet's station makes it binding on him to stay with his people and keep watch over them. That commentator draws a principle of leadership from it: when travelling with those in your charge, bring up the rear rather than racing ahead — as Allah commanded in *"and follow them at the rear"* (15:65).

Notice how the ayah is worded: not "why did you hurry to Me" but *ʿan qawmika* — "away from your people." The haste is framed by what it left behind.

## Ayah 84: the most beautiful answer a servant can give

*"They are close on my tracks."* Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that they have already arrived and settled near the Mountain — which is what Musa sincerely believed.

Then: *wa ʿajiltu ilayka rabbi li-tarḍā* — *"and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased."* Ibn Kathir's gloss: *"so You will be more pleased with me."*

Musa's whole motive is the pleasure of his Lord — not reward, not status, just *li-tarḍā*. Even if his haste carried an oversight, the engine driving it was love. Hold that beside what his people were doing at that very moment.

## Ayah 85: "We have tried your people"

*"Verily, We have tried your people in your absence, and As-Sāmirī has led them astray."*

The verb is *fatannā* — from *fitna*, a trial or testing. The *testing* is attributed to Allah, the *misguiding* to Sāmirī. The test is from Allah; the choice to fail it is theirs and their deceiver's.

Ibn Kathir also points out what Musa was receiving while this was happening: Allah was writing for him the Tablets containing the Torah — *"And We wrote for him on the Tablets the lesson to be drawn from all things and the explanation for all things: hold unto these with firmness, and enjoin your people to take the better therein. I shall show you the home of evildoers"* (7:145), which Ibn Kathir explains as, "I will show you the final outcome of what will happen to those who abandon My obedience and oppose My command." Guidance was literally being inscribed for them at the top of the mountain while they were bowing to metal at the bottom.

## Who was Sāmirī?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the reports, and they do not agree with one another:

- Some say he was an Egyptian Copt, a neighbour of Musa who accepted the true faith and joined the exodus.
- Some say he was chief of an Israelite clan called Sāmira, still known in Syria.
- Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said he was a Persian from the Kirmān province.
- Ibn ʿAbbas said he belonged to a nation of cow-worshippers who reached Egypt and pretended to join the religion of the Children of Israel, while in reality he was a hypocrite (reported via Qurṭubī).
- Another version makes him a cow-worshipper from India who embraced the faith and later returned to disbelief — or embraced it hypocritically from the start.

His name is generally said to have been Mūsā ibn Ẓafar. Ibn Jarīr relates from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was born in the year Fir'awn ordered every male Israelite child killed; his mother hid him in the hollow of a cave, and Allah appointed Jibrīl to nourish the infant. The Arabic couplet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes catches the irony with a blade: *the Musa whom Jibrīl brought up became an infidel, and the Musa whom Fir'awn raised became the Prophet of Allah.*

The couplet's own moral is that when a person is not fortunate in his birth, those who raised him are left bewildered and those who hoped in him are disillusioned. A privileged upbringing guarantees nothing, and — as Ibn ʿAbbas' report has it — a man can stand inside the community of faith with his heart somewhere else entirely.

## Ayah 86: Musa comes down — *ghaḍbāna asifā*

*"Then Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved."*

The word to feel here is *asif*. Ibn Kathir says it is used to **emphasise the severity** of his anger — not anger cooled by sadness but anger deepened by it. Mujahid glossed *ghaḍbāna asifā* as "worried." Qatādah and As-Suddī said *asif* here means "in a state of sadness because of what his people had done after him." Ibn Kathir sums up the state: extremely angry, extremely upset, and very worried *for* them. His fury is not wounded pride at being disobeyed; it is the anguish of a shepherd who came back to find the flock eating poison — and this, Ibn Kathir notes, at the very time he was receiving the Torah containing their Sharīʿah, a great honour for them.

**"Did not your Lord promise you a fair promise?"** Ibn Kathir: did He not promise you, through everything I conveyed, every good in this life and the next and a good final outcome — and have you not already witnessed how He helped you defeat Fir'awn and blessed you with other bounties besides? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the promise Musa invokes is the Book of guidance they were on their way to receive.

**"Did then the promise seem to you long in coming?"** Ibn Kathir: were you waiting on what Allah promised, and in the waiting you forgot His previous favours and the covenant He took from you? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the logic: not much time had elapsed. It is inconceivable that they had forgotten it, and equally inconceivable that a delay this short could give anyone reason to despair of its fulfilment. So neither forgetfulness nor despair works as an excuse.

**"Or did you desire that wrath should descend from your Lord upon you?"** Ibn Kathir explains that "or" (*am*) here carries the force of **"nay, but"** — it separates a previous item from a coming one: *nay, but you want to make Allah's anger fall upon you by what you have done, and so you broke your promise to me.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: since neither of the first two possibilities can be contemplated, the only remaining verdict is that they knowingly and of their own choice invited the wrath of Allah.

## Ayah 87: the excuse, and what it reveals

*"We did not break our promise to you of our own will."* Ibn Kathir: *bi-malkinā* means "by our power and our choice." They plead that they were carried along, not culpable — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: they claimed they did not do it by their own choice but merely followed the example set for them.

Then the details: *"we were made to carry loads (awzār) from the ornaments of the people, so we cast them."*

**The word *awzār*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *awzār* is the plural of *wizr*, a burden or load. Because on the Day of Judgment every person will carry his bundle of sins on his shoulders like a load, *wizr* also came to mean sin itself. Both senses are live here — these were heavy ornaments, and they were a moral weight. "The people" means the Egyptians, from whom the Children of Israel had borrowed jewellery on the pretext of wearing it on their festival day and then carried away without returning it.

**Why the jewellery was a problem.** Non-Muslims living under a Muslim state and abiding by its laws (*dhimmīs*), and those bound to Muslims by treaty, remain in full control of their property — Muslims may not deprive them of any part of it. A hostile belligerent's property may become lawful, but Imām Muḥammad's research — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls very weighty and closest to the truth — is that even then it counts as spoils of war only if acquired by the sword in the course of a proper jihād. Property obtained otherwise is *fayʼ*, usable only with the owner's consent. The borrowed Egyptian ornaments were neither: not *fayʼ*, since the owners never transferred ownership, and not spoils, since no religious war took them. So the Children of Israel could not lawfully have used them for their personal benefit. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that under the law in force before Islam spoils could not be used personally at all — they were heaped as an offering for fire from the sky to consume — while under Islamic law Muslims were later permitted to benefit from them, noting that a hadith on this issue appears in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim.)

**The standard the Prophet ﷺ set.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that when the Prophet ﷺ decided to migrate to Madinah he was holding many valuables that the idolaters of Arabia had entrusted to him for safekeeping — they had such faith in his honesty and integrity that they had given him the title *al-Amīn*, the honest. He was so solicitous about those deposits that he placed them in the hands of ʿAlī with explicit instructions to restore them to their rightful owners before leaving. This shows plainly, the commentary concludes, that it is not lawful for Muslims to appropriate for their own use the valuables of non-Muslims.

**How the casting happened.** By the *ḥadīth ul-futūn* narration, Harun warned them of their guilt and directed them to throw all the ornaments into a pit; other versions say it was Sāmirī who told them that holding on to what did not belong to them was a sin and urged them to throw it in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says both versions may well be true. It then reports that Harun had a great fire lit in the pit, the ornaments melted into one solid piece, and the decision about the metal was deferred until Musa's return — until Sāmirī came with something concealed in his fists, asked permission to throw it in, and asked Harun first to pray that a wish of his be granted. Harun, unaware of the evil planned, prayed. What Sāmirī threw was not jewellery but dust from under the hoof-marks of Jibrīl's horse, in which he had seen signs of life appear. The molten lump then assumed the form of a calf and began making bovine sounds. Other traditions place the sprinkling of the dust after the shaping.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid about all this: these accounts come through Isrāʼīlite traditions, related by Qurṭubī and others, and "cannot be wholly relied upon, yet at the same time we do not possess sufficient ground to disprove them either." Nothing in the passage's meaning depends on them.

Ibn Kathir, describing the same casting: *"This calf was an ordeal, a hindrance and test."*

**The deepest irony** is one Ibn Kathir underlines: their whole excuse was that they were merely ridding themselves of the Copts' jewelry — something detestable — and in the process they wound up doing something even worse. He compares it to a narration reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar: a man from Iraq asked him whether a garment with mosquito's blood on it was fit to pray in. Ibn ʿUmar replied, "Look at the people of 'Iraq. They killed the grandson of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Al-Husayn, and yet they're asking about the blood of the mosquito." Meticulous about specks; blind to catastrophes.

## Ayah 88: a body, and a sound

*"Then he brought out for them a calf — a body with a lowing sound."*

*ʿIjlan jasadan* — a calf, *a body*: a lump of matter with a shape. Commentators divide over the sound: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some held it a body without life whose sound came from a special contrivance, while the majority held that the calf in fact possessed signs of life. Ibn Kathir preserves the first view in its sharpest form, from Ibn ʿAbbas: *"Nay, by Allah, the moaning sound of the calf was nothing but wind that would enter into its behind and come out of its mouth, thus causing it to make a sound."* A draught through a hollow statue — and a nation prostrated to it. (Ibn Kathir also mentions, in a Hadith of Al-Fitun recorded from Al-Hasan Al-Basri, that the calf's name was Bahmut.)

*"This is your god, and the god of Musa."* Ibn Kathir reports through Muhammad bin Ishaq from Ibn ʿAbbas that they became religiously devoted to it "and they loved it with a love that they had never loved anything else with before." That is the anatomy of every idol: not stupidity so much as misplaced adoration.

*Fa-nasiya* — "and he forgot." The commentators read the pronoun two ways. **Ibn Kathir** takes it as Sāmirī: he *forgot*, meaning he abandoned what he had been following of the religion of Islam. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** takes it as part of the sales pitch Sāmirī and his friends were making to the Children of Israel: "It seems Musa has forgotten — that is why he has gone elsewhere in search of god." Read either way, the ayah exposes the swindle: either the salesman has abandoned his faith, or he is slandering a prophet to a crowd that wants to be convinced.

## Ayah 89: the one question that ends the argument

*"Did they not see that it could not return them a word, and that it had no power to harm them or to benefit them?"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the structural turn: the excuses of the Children of Israel end with the previous ayah, and in this ayah Allah Himself reminds them of their folly. And it does not argue theology — it asks them to use their eyes.

Ibn Kathir: do they not see that it does not respond to them when they ask it and when they speak to it? And "no power to harm or benefit" means, he explains, in their worldly affairs *and* in the matters of the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further: even if the calf had life and made bovine noises, would that be sufficient reason to adopt it as an object of worship? They were well aware that it could not answer their prayers, nor had it power to harm them or to benefit them.

Two tests of a god, then. **Can it speak back to you? Can it do you good or harm?** Musa's Lord had just addressed him at the Mountain and had already defeated Fir'awn for these very people. The calf could do neither. Everything a person sets up in the place of Allah — wealth, an image, a reputation, a fear, a habit — fails at exactly these two points. It never answers, and on the day you truly need help or protection it has none to give.

## Living it

- **Musa's *li-tarḍā*** is the standard: do the thing because Allah will be pleased with it, not for what it gets you.
- **Leadership means staying at the back.** The principle Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī applies to a father, a teacher, an imam: those in your charge are most your responsibility when you are moving fast and they are not.
- **"We didn't do it of our own will"** is the oldest excuse there is, and Musa did not accept it. Nobody put the calf in their hearts; they had asked for a visible god long before Sāmirī cast anything.
- **Other people's property is other people's property** — the Prophet ﷺ made sure the idolaters' deposits were returned to their owners before he left for Madinah.
- **Watch the small scruple that hides the large wrong.** Keep Ibn ʿUmar's answer about mosquito blood close whenever we find ourselves fastidious about the trivial and relaxed about the enormous.

passages.title: Aaron's warning and Moses' rebuke
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat step back in time and then forward again. Ayat 90–91 show us what happened *while* Musa (peace be upon him) was still on the mountain — his brother Harun (peace be upon him) standing in front of a people who had begun to worship a golden calf, warning them, and being refused. Ayat 92–94 show us the moment Musa returned, saw it with his own eyes, and turned on his brother in anger — and Harun's tender, wounded reply. What holds the passage together is a single question: what should a righteous man do when the community entrusted to him collapses into falsehood while he is not strong enough to stop it?

## The warning that came first

Ayah 90 opens with **وَلَقَدْ قَالَ لَهُمْ هَارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ** — "and Harun (peace be upon him) had already said to them *beforehand*." That word "beforehand" is doing important work. Before Musa (peace be upon him) ever came down, before any rebuke was uttered, Harun had already spoken. He was not a silent bystander who had to be shamed into action after the fact. Ibn Kathir frames the whole ayah this way: Allah is *informing* us of Harun's attempt to stop them worshipping the calf.

His warning has three parts, and each one is chosen with care.

**"You are only being tried by this" (إِنَّمَا فُتِنتُم بِهِ).** He names the calf for what it is. Ibn Kathir puts it directly: Harun told them that this was *only a test for them* — a trial, a *fitnah*. The calf is not a god; it is the examination. The very thing dazzling them is what they are being tested with.

**"And indeed your Lord is the Most Gracious" (وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَٰنُ).** He does not merely say "your Lord is Allah." He names Him as *ar-Rahman*, the Most Beneficent. Ibn Kathir unfolds what Harun was pressing on them: their Lord is the One Who created everything and decreed for everything its just measure; He is the Owner of the Mighty Throne; He is the One Who does whatever He wills. Set that beside a calf, and the argument makes itself. Why would people who have a Lord like that stoop to a manufactured animal?

**"So follow me and obey my order" (فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي).** Ibn Kathir explains this plainly: *follow me in what I am commanding you with, and leave what I forbid you from.* This is not Harun asserting a personal claim; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes him here precisely as the *deputy* of Musa — the man calling them back to the trust his brother left him with.

## The answer of a people already committed

Their reply is chilling in its calmness: **لَن نَّبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ** — "we will not cease to worship it." And they add the condition: **until Musa (peace be upon him) returns to us.** Ibn Kathir gives the sense: "We will not cease in our worship of this calf until we hear what Musa has to say about it."

Notice the reversal. They will not obey a prophet standing in front of them, quoting the truth to their faces, because they have decided to wait for a *different* authority. Harun (peace be upon him) was not unclear; he was simply not the man they wanted to hear it from. And Ibn Kathir records how far that went: they opposed Harun in this matter and they fought against him, nearly killing him. It is the same defence Harun would later offer — reported elsewhere in the Qur'an and brought in here by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — that the people had taken him as weak because of the small number of his supporters, and were about to kill him (7:150).

**The people were not one bloc.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Qurtubi, describes three factions. One group stayed loyal to Harun and refused to be misled by Samiri — twelve thousand of them, by Qurtubi's report. A second group took up calf-worship with a reservation: if Musa forbade it on his return, they would give it up. A third group were zealots who believed Musa would approve and even join them — and who resolved that even if he did not, they would never give up their new faith. Knowing this makes ayah 91 land differently: Harun was not facing a united mob, but a fracturing nation, with a large body of believers still standing behind him.

## Musa returns, and the news becomes a sight

Ibn Kathir describes the return: Musa (peace be upon him) saw the great matter that had taken place among his people, was filled with anger, threw down the Divine Tablets he had in his hand, and grabbed his brother Harun (peace be upon him) by his head, pulling him towards himself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that he seized him by his beard and the hair of his head.

At this point Ibn Kathir refers the reader back to his commentary on Surat al-A'raf, where he mentioned the Hadith **لَيْسَ الْخَبَرُ كَالْمُعَايَنَةِ** — *information is not the same as observation.* (He names no collection here, so we take the teaching as he transmits it.) That is a mercy to understand about ourselves: hearing that a wrong exists and standing in front of it are not the same experience, and the second can shake a person in a way the first did not.

His rebuke in ayat 92–93 is two questions and then a third that is really a verdict:

- **"What prevented you, when you saw them going astray…"** (مَا مَنَعَكَ إِذْ رَأَيْتَهُمْ ضَلُّوا)
- **"…from following me?"** (أَلَّا تَتَّبِعَنِ)
- **"Have you then disobeyed my order?"** (أَفَعَصَيْتَ أَمْرِي)

**What did "following me" mean?** The commentators read it more than one way, and the difference matters.

Ibn Kathir takes it as: *you should have informed me of this matter as soon as it happened* — Harun should have come after him with the news rather than staying.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out two readings. One: once Harun saw that Bani Isra'il had strayed from the righteous path and were beyond recall, he should have abandoned them and joined Musa at the mountain of Tur. The other, adopted by some commentators: once they had forsaken the True Faith, Harun should have fought them, as Musa would have done had he been present. Either way, the charge is the same — Musa held that his brother should either have fought them or parted company with them and joined him at Tur, and that his continuing to live among them was an unwise act.

**"Have you then disobeyed my order?"** Ibn Kathir specifies exactly which order: what Musa had entrusted to him on departing — *"Replace me among my people, act in the right way and follow not the way of the mischief-makers"* (7:142). So this is not a general accusation of insubordination. Musa is holding his brother to one specific, named instruction.

## "O son of my mother"

Harun's reply in ayah 94 is one of the most humane sentences in the Qur'an. He does not say "O Musa," and he does not say "O my brother." He says **يَا ابْنَ أُمَّ** — *O son of my mother.*

Ibn Kathir explains why: this mentioning of the mother was Harun's attempt to soften Musa's anger. He was Musa's biological brother and they had the same parents; he could have invoked either. He chose the mother, and Ibn Kathir says the mention of the mother here is *more delicate and profound* in bringing about gentleness and mildness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the same phrase as an implied plea: *do not judge me too harshly.*

Pause on what is happening. The elder brother, a prophet himself (peace be upon him), being held by his beard and hair, does not defend his rank, does not raise his voice, does not counter-accuse. He reaches for the one word most likely to reach his brother's heart — the word that recalls the mother who bore them both. He disarms the anger instead of matching it.

**"Seize me not by my beard, nor by my head."** Then he explains himself. Ibn Kathir reads what follows as Harun's excuse to Musa for being delayed from coming to him and informing him of the great mishap that had taken place:

**"Verily, I feared…"** (إِنِّي خَشِيتُ) — "I was afraid to come after you and inform you of this, because I thought you might accuse me of leaving them alone and causing division between them." That is the fear he voices: *lest you say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you have not respected my word."* Ibn Kathir glosses that last phrase — *and you did not take care of what I commanded you to do when I left you in charge of them.*

Read it slowly and the tragedy becomes clear. **Harun was caught between two ways of failing the same instruction.** Musa had told him to take his place and *set things right*. If he abandoned the calf-worshippers to chase after Musa, he would have caused division and been blamed for it. If he stayed, he would be blamed for tolerating the calf.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in his reasoning. Harun understood Musa's parting advice — *"Take my place among my people and keep things right"* (7:142) — to mean that he should maintain harmony among the people and prevent differences at all cost. He judged that fighting the calf-worshippers, or leaving with his twelve thousand men, would have caused discord and strife among them. And he had hope: that when Musa returned, Musa would be able to handle the situation satisfactorily.

And Ibn Kathir closes the passage with a single line from Ibn 'Abbas that should govern how we read the whole scene: **"Harun was respectful and obedient to Musa."** Whatever the rebuke sounded like, the man receiving it was not a rebel.

## Two prophets, two judgements, no villain

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes a section to this under the heading *Differences between two prophets when the opinions of both could be right*, and it is the most instructive part of the passage.

It describes each brother as holding a considered opinion arrived at *by way of ijtihad* — a word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself renders simply as *assessment*. Musa's assessment (peace be upon him) was that in the situation as it took shape, Harun should have totally dissociated himself from Bani Isra'il by removing himself and his followers from their company, and that by continuing to stay with them he had compromised his position. Harun's assessment (peace be upon him) was that such an action would have caused a permanent split among Bani Isra'il and divided them into factions — and since there was hope they would see the error of their way when Musa returned, he thought it wise to adopt a conciliatory attitude.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about what this does and does not mean. **The purpose of both prophets was identical**: strict adherence to the commands of Allah, and ensuring that Bani Isra'il remained steadfast in the True Faith and in belief in the Oneness of Allah. They differed only over the *manner* in which those objectives could be achieved — whether to make a complete break with the dissidents or to bear with them in the hope that things would improve ultimately. Both views have merit, and it is not possible to pass a firm and final judgement on them.

Then it draws the lesson out to us: the differences among the jurists that rest on ijtihad are of a similar nature, and those holding different opinions on such matters cannot be charged with having broken any religious laws. That is a remarkably steadying principle to carry into our own arguments about strategy in religious life — when to separate and when to stay, when to confront and when to hold a community together.

**And how did it end?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Musa did not press the matter any further with his brother; he turned instead to Samiri and asked him to explain his conduct in the whole affair. The Qur'an does not indicate whether Musa accepted Harun's excuses, or whether he regarded his brother's mistake as one of ijtihad and dropped the matter. As for the seizing of the hair and beard, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it simply as showing anger and frustration at the situation that had developed in his absence — and notes that on hearing the explanation, Musa prayed to Allah to forgive them both.

## Living it

**Say the truth even when you will be refused.** Harun (peace be upon him) spoke *beforehand*, to a crowd that answered him with violence, and Allah recorded his words in the Qur'an. The value of his warning was never dependent on it working.

**Name the trial for what it is.** Harun's first move was to tell people that the thing attracting them was a test, not a treasure. Half of resisting a trial is recognising that you are inside one.

**Refuse the excuse of "let me wait and see what someone else says."** Bani Isra'il had clear truth in front of them and postponed obedience pending a more congenial authority. We do the same when we know a ruling and go shopping for a voice that will excuse us.

**When you are the one being rebuked, reach for the softest true word.** *O son of my mother* is a whole method. Harun answered heat with tenderness and explained without accusing — and it is his obedience, not his defence, that Ibn 'Abbas remembered him for.

**When you are the one rebuking, remember that information is not the same as observation.** Musa's anger (peace be upon him) was the anger of a man who had just *seen* it. That is a reason to be slow in judging others who react strongly to what they have witnessed — and a reason to give yourself a moment before speaking when you are the one who has just seen.

**And leave room for the person who chose differently.** Two prophets, both sincere, both aiming at the same goal, reached opposite conclusions about method — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to pass a firm and final judgement between them. The passage ends not with a verdict on Harun, but with Musa praying that Allah forgive them both.

passages.title: The Samiri exposed and banished
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the account of the golden calf. Musa (peace be upon him) has finished with his people and with his brother; now he turns to the one man who engineered the whole disaster, hears his excuse, sentences him, destroys the idol, and — in the last ayah — states the truth that the whole episode had obscured. What holds the passage together is a single movement: interrogation (95), confession (96), judgement (97), and then the clean declaration of tawhid (98) that puts everything back in its right place.

## Where we are in the story

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene briefly. While Musa was at the mountain, the Bani Israʼil were smitten with the mischief of calf-worship, and Harun (peace be upon him), left as his deputy, remonstrated with them without effect. The people split three ways: one group stayed loyal to Harun and refused to be misled by the Samiri — twelve thousand of them, according to Qurtubi; a second took up calf-worship with the reservation that they would drop it if Musa forbade it on his return; a third were zealots who assumed Musa would approve and join them, and resolved that even if he did not, they would never abandon their new faith.

Musa returned, rebuked the people, and then turned on his brother, seizing him by the beard and the hair of his head and demanding why he had not followed him to the mountain once the people's disbelief was obvious. Harun's answer — "O son of my mother!" — was itself a plea not to be judged too harshly: breaking with the people, or fighting them, would have torn the community apart, and he had understood Musa's parting instruction, "Take my place among my people and keep things right" (7:142), to mean holding them together at all cost.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this long enough to draw out one lesson worth carrying into the rest of the passage. Musa's considered judgement — his ijtihād, meaning a reasoned assessment in a situation with no explicit instruction — was that Harun should have cut himself and his followers off entirely. Harun's ijtihād was that such a break would have split the nation permanently, and that patience was wiser while there was still hope. Both men wanted exactly the same thing: obedience to Allah, and the survival of the people's belief in His Oneness. They differed only over method. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that both positions have merit, that no final verdict can be passed between them, and that the disagreements of the jurists based on ijtihād are of this same kind — those holding differing views cannot be charged with having broken the religion. Musa's seizing his brother's hair shows only his anger and frustration at what had happened in his absence; having heard the explanation, he prayed to Allah to forgive them both.

Musa did not press his brother further. He turned to the Samiri.

## Ayah 95: the question with no good answer

**"What did you think you were doing, O Samiri?"** Ibn Kathir unpacks the question as: "What caused you to do what you did? What presented such an idea to you causing you to do this?" It is not a request for information — Musa already knows what happened. It is the demand that a man state his own reasoning out loud, in front of everyone, so that it can be heard for what it is.

**Who was he?** Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Samiri was a man from the people of Bajarma, a people who worshipped cows, and that he still had the love of cow-worship in his soul — though he acted as though he had accepted Islam along with the Children of Israel. His name, by this report, was Musa bin Zafar. Qatadah said he was from the village of Samarra.

That detail is the quiet key to the whole affair. The man who built the calf had never actually left the calf behind. He was there among the Children of Israel, outwardly one of them, carrying an old attachment intact underneath. When the moment came, it surfaced in the shape it had always had.

## Ayah 96: the confession

**"I saw what they did not see."** Ibn Kathir: this means, "I saw Jibril when he came to destroy Firʿawn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the traditions around this. One is that Jibril was present on his horse at the river crossing, as the Bani Israʼil reached the far bank safely and Pharaoh's army entered the water in pursuit. Another is that after Musa had crossed, Jibril came to him riding a horse to invite him to the mountain of Tur — and that at that time the Samiri alone, and no one else, saw him. The reason given, on a tradition from Ibn ʿAbbas, is that Jibril had nourished him when his mother left him in the cave, so he knew him well.

Read that carefully. The man's whole claim rests on a privilege: *I saw what you did not.* And by these reports the privilege was real — he had been nourished by an angel and could pick him out where no one else could. What he did with that privilege is the tragedy. Special access is not the same as guidance. A man can be given something no one else in the camp was given and use it to lead the camp into idolatry.

**"So I took a handful."** The Arabic is *fa-qabadtu qabdatan min athar al-rasūl* — "I took a *qabdah* from the print of the messenger." Ibn Kathir explains *the messenger* here as Jibril, and *the print* as the hoof print of his horse; he notes that this is what is well known among many of the scholars of tafsir, indeed most of them. Mujahid glossed it as "from under the hoof of Jibril's horse," and gave the word *qabdah* two senses: a palmful, and also that which is grasped by the tips of the fingers. Either way the physical image is tiny — a fistful, or a pinch, of ordinary dust from the ground.

Why he took it: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says Shaitan planted in his heart the idea that the earth under the hooves of Jibril's mount must somehow contain signs of life, so he picked up some of it. A tradition from Ibn ʿAbbas puts the thought like this — that if he sprinkled this earth on something and said, "You become such-and-such," it would change its original form and become that thing. Some exegetes add that the Samiri had observed grass sprouting unfailingly from the earth under the hooves of that horse, and deduced that it contained traces of life; Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī adopts the same explanation on the authority of the Tabiʿin and the majority of commentators.

**"And I threw it."** Ibn Kathir: "I threw it along with those who were throwing" — that is, with the crowd casting their jewellery in. Mujahid said the Samiri threw what was in his hand onto the jewellery of the Children of Israel, and it became moulded into the body of a calf, which made a light moaning sound; the wind that blew into it was the cause of its sound. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sequence as: he moulded the ornaments the Bani Israʼil had thrown into the pit into the shape of a calf, sprinkled the earth on it, and by a miracle of Allah it developed signs of life and could even make a sound.

**"Thus my inner self suggested to me"** — *wa kadhālika sawwalat lī nafsī*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise and devastating: his soul considered it something good, and it was pleasing to his self. That is the entire defence. Not evidence, not a command from Allah, not even a claim of revelation — simply that it appealed to him. He wanted it, so it looked right to him. That is how the *nafs*, the inner self, works when it is left unchecked: it does not usually argue you into sin, it makes sin look attractive and lets you supply the reasoning afterwards.

## Ayah 97: the sentence

**"Go away then!"** The punishment is announced in two parts, one for this world and one for the next.

**"Touch me not" —** *lā misāsa*.
