Ibn Kathir draws out the exact fit between crime and consequence: "Just as you took and touched what was not your right to take and touch of the messenger's foot print, such is your punishment in this life, that you will say, 'Do not touch me.'" The meaning, he says, is: "You will not touch the people and they will not touch you." The hand that reached out for what was not his is the hand no one will now take.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that everyone was to sever all contact with him and not come near him, and that he too was commanded not to touch anyone — so he was condemned to spend the rest of his life away from all social contact, like a wild animal. Whether this punishment was awarded by Musa by means of a law binding on the Samiri and the Bani Israʼil alike, or whether the Samiri was smitten by some peculiar affliction that deterred people from any physical contact with him, is not known. Some traditions have it that Musa laid a curse on him such that if anyone touched him, both parties came down with fever (Maʿālim). So he spent all his life hiding from people, and whenever he saw someone approaching he would call out *lā misāsa* — "Don't touch me."

Qatadah connects the sentence forward in time: "This is referring to a punishment for them, and their remnants today still say, 'Do not touch.'"

**A striking note on why he was not executed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, on the authority of *Al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ*, that Musa had initially intended to execute the Samiri but Allah stopped him, because the Samiri was a very generous person who helped people in distress. A man who invented an idol and dragged a nation into worshipping it was spared execution on account of his kindness to those in need. Nothing here excuses what he did, and the sentence he received was severe. But it tells you something about how carefully deeds are weighed, and that no good is thrown away.

**"And you have a promise that will not fail."** Ibn Kathir: the promise is the Day of Resurrection, and *lan tukhlafahu* means you will have no way to escape it. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Abu Nahik read it as, "You will not be absent from it." Exile could be endured, hidden from, waited out. The appointment cannot. This world's sentence has an end; the other does not.

**"Look at your god."** Ibn Kathir: look at that which you worshipped, that which you established worship of, which was the calf — and now watch it burnt and its particles scattered in the sea. Musa does not merely destroy the idol; he makes its worshippers stand and watch it destroyed. A god that can be burnt and thrown into the water in front of you needs no further refutation.

**How was a metal calf burnt?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question about *la-nuḥarriqannahu*, "we will certainly burn it": gold and silver melt under extreme heat, they are not reduced to ashes. Four possibilities are advanced. First, that once signs of life had appeared in it, the calf ceased to be a figure of gold and silver and became an animal of flesh and blood, which could be slaughtered and burnt. Second, that it was filed with a rasp into very minute particles of dust (Ad-Durr al-Manthūr). Third, that it was burnt by means of some chemical device (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī). Fourth, that it was burnt by some miracle (Bayān ul-Qurʼān). The scholars genuinely differ here, and the Qurʼan does not settle the mechanism — the point of the ayah is the fate of the idol, not the metallurgy.

## Ayah 98: the truth that ends the story

Musa turns from the idol to the people: **"Your only god is Allah, there is no god but Him. He has full knowledge of all things."**

Ibn Kathir renders Musa's meaning: this is not your god; your only object of worship is Allah, beside whom there is no true deity. Worship is not befitting to anyone except Him, for everything is in need of Him and everything is His servant. That last line is the argument in miniature. The calf was made of the people's own jewellery, shaped by a man's hands, given its sound by the wind that blew into it — a thing entirely dependent on other things. Whatever is in need cannot be worshipped; only the One whom everything needs can.

**"He has full knowledge of all things."** Ibn Kathir notes a point of grammar: the word *ʿilm* ("knowledge") stands in the accusative case for distinction — that is, the sentence says His reach extends over all things, and this word marks out the respect in which it does so. The meaning, Ibn Kathir says, is that He is the All-Knower of everything.

He then gathers the parallels across the Qurʼan: "Allah surrounds all things in His knowledge" (65:12); "And He keeps count of all things" (72:28); "Not even the weight of a speck of dust escapes His knowledge" (34:3); "Not a leaf falls but He knows it; there is not a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record" (6:59); "And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah, and He knows its dwelling place and its deposit — all is in a Clear Book" (11:6). The ayat that mention this, he says, are numerous.

Notice how exactly this closing attribute answers the passage. The Samiri's whole case rested on private sight: *I saw what they did not see.* The passage ends by naming the One whose knowledge nothing escapes — not a falling leaf, not a grain in the darkness of the earth. The man's secret advantage was nothing at all beside it, and the love of cow-worship he had kept in his soul was never hidden for a moment.

## Living it

**Watch what you carried in with you.** The Samiri was there among the Children of Israel, acting as though he had accepted Islam with them, and holding his old attachment intact underneath. It is possible to be inside the community, going through everything the community goes through, and still be holding on privately to the thing you never gave up.

**Distrust "it felt right to me."** *Sawwalat lī nafsī* is the honest name for a great deal of what people call conviction. Ibn Kathir's gloss — his soul considered it good and it was pleasing to his self — is a warning to check whether a course of action is pleasing to Allah or merely pleasing to us.

**Disagreement in method is not disagreement in religion.** Musa and Harun differed over how to handle a community in crisis, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to rule between them, adding that those who differ by ijtihād cannot be charged with having broken the religion. Two sincere people can weigh the same duty differently.

**No good deed is wasted.** The Samiri's generosity did not save him from exile — but it is reported to have saved him from execution. If that is true of a man who built an idol, the kindness of a believer is not lost either.

passages.title: The Reminder given, and the burden of refusing it
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat come at the close of the account of Musa and Fir'awn, and they turn the spotlight around: the point of all that history was never the history. It was the Book that carries it. Ayah 99 names what has been given — a Reminder from Allah Himself; ayah 100 states what happens to the one who turns his back on it; ayah 101 shuts the door on any escape from that outcome. Story, gift, and consequence: one movement, three steps.

## "This is how We relate to you"

Ayah 99 opens with *kadhālika* — "thus", "this is how". It points backwards. Ibn Kathir reads Allah as addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly: We have told you the story of Musa and what happened with him, Fir'awn and his armies, **just as it actually happened**. And, he adds, this is how We relate to you the information of the past in general — "just as it happened, without any increase or decrease."

That phrase deserves a pause. Ibn Kathir is not only saying that the account is true; he is saying that it is exactly proportioned — nothing padded on, nothing trimmed away. What reached the Prophet ﷺ reached him from Allah, and it reached him unaltered.

## The Reminder — and where it comes from

The second half of ayah 99 is the hinge of the passage: *wa qad ātaynāka min ladunnā dhikrā* — "And indeed We have given you, **from Us**, a Reminder."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that according to the majority of commentators, *dhikr* here means the Qur'an itself. Ibn Kathir says the same and expands it: "We also gave you a remembrance from Us, the Mighty Qur'an, no falsehood comes to it from before it or behind it." It is a revelation, he says, from One Most Wise, Most Praiseworthy.

Two things in this short phrase are worth feeling properly.

**"From Us" (*min ladunnā*).** The Book's origin is stated in the ayah itself: it was given from Allah. Ibn Kathir keeps that origin in view throughout — and it is the reason he can move so directly from ayah 99 to ayah 100. Having described the Reminder, he writes, "Therefore, Allah says about it: *Whoever turns away from it*." The "it" that a person turns from is precisely this: something given from Allah.

**"A Reminder" (*dhikrā*).** Ibn Kathir headlines this whole passage with the idea that the entire Qur'an is the remembrance of Allah.

He then makes a claim about the Qur'an's standing among revealed books. No Prophet, he says, was given a Book like it or more complete than it, from the time of the earlier Prophets who were sent until they were sealed with the coming of Muhammad ﷺ; no Prophet was given a Book containing as much information as the Qur'an about what has passed and what is to come. And, he adds, the judgement that distinguishes between people is taken from it. That last sentence is the bridge into ayah 100. If this Book is the standard by which people are separated, then one's posture towards it is not a matter of taste. It is the dividing line.

## Ayah 100: "Whoever turns away from it"

*Man aʿraḍa ʿanhu* — whoever turns away from it.

Ibn Kathir explains this as one who **denies it and turns away from following its commands and instructions, while seeking guidance from other than it**. Three things travel together in his definition: rejection of the Book's truth, refusal of its directives, and the search for direction somewhere else. For such a person, Ibn Kathir says, Allah will mislead him and send him on the path to Hell.

**Who is addressed?** Not one tribe, not one generation. Ibn Kathir insists the warning "applies generally to whoever the Qur'an reaches of the Arabs, the non-Arabs, the People of the Book and others," and he grounds this in the Qur'an's own words about itself — *li-undhirakum bihi wa man balagh*, "That I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach" (6:19). The Qur'an, he says, is a final warning for everyone it reaches. He also brings the verse *"But those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17). His conclusion is a clean summary of these ayat: "Whoever follows it, then he is rightly guided, and whoever opposes it and turns away from it, then he is misguided. He will be wretched in this life, and he is promised that on the Day of Resurrection his abode will be the Hellfire."

## Turning away has degrees

Ibn Kathir's reading centres on outright denial and rejection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the same phrase and lists the different forms that turning aside from the Qur'an can take:

- not paying proper attention and respect when it is being recited;
- showing scant desire to learn to read it, or to comprehend its meaning;
- reading it incorrectly, without regard to correct pronunciation;
- reading it without full concentration;
- reading it not to win Allah's pleasure but to attain worldly rewards such as wealth and fame;
- not striving to comprehend the laws the Qur'an lays down;
- and — the extreme forms of disregard — having understood those laws, not complying with them, or acting in defiance of them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict is blunt: any neglect of the rights and claims of the Qur'an is a great sin, and the guilty person will bear it on his head on the Day of Judgement in the shape of a heavy load.

The two commentaries approach the one phrase from different angles. Ibn Kathir defines who the turner-away is — the denier who seeks guidance elsewhere. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the many ways neglect can show itself in practice, including in the life of someone who recites the Book but gives it little attention, little care, or little obedience.

## The weight

The image the passage chooses is not fire, chains, or darkness. It is **weight**.

Ayah 100 says the one who turns away *yaḥmilu yawma-l-qiyāmati wizrā* — he will bear, on the Day of Resurrection, a *wizr*, a heavy burden. Ibn Kathir gives the plain gloss: "Burden here means sin." So the burden is not something foreign attached to the person; it is his own sin that he carries.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it has been related in several traditions that the evil deeds and the sins a person has committed in his lifetime will be placed on his head, in the shape of a heavy burden, on the Day of Resurrection. (The commentary reports this without naming a collection, so the teaching is conveyed here as it gives it, with no chain or source claimed.)

Then ayah 101 closes with the word again, in a different form: *wa sā'a lahum yawma-l-qiyāmati **ḥimlā*** — "and evil indeed will it be, that **load** for them, on the Day of Resurrection." The closing phrase pronounces judgement on it: *sā'a* — how evil a load.

## Ayah 101: "abiding in it"

Between the two words for weight comes the sentence that removes the last exit: *khālidīna fīhi* — "They will abide in that."

Ibn Kathir's comment on it is a single short sentence: **"They will not be able to avoid this or escape it."** That is the horror of ayah 101. It is not only that the load is heavy; it is that there is no avoiding it and no escaping it.

## Living it

Read as a unit, these ayat make a single argument. Allah has given, from Himself, a Reminder that relates the past without any increase or decrease, and from which the judgement distinguishing between people is taken (ayah 99). To turn from it is to bear on that Day a burden which is one's own sin (ayah 100) — one that cannot be avoided or escaped (ayah 101).

And the same passage states the other side just as plainly. In Ibn Kathir's words: whoever follows it, then he is rightly guided. Concretely, from what the commentators say, the opposite of "turning away" looks like:

- **Attention when it is recited.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names inattention and lack of respect during recitation first among the forms of turning aside — so listening properly is the first form of turning towards.
- **Wanting to understand it.** Not merely reciting, but desiring to learn to read it and to comprehend its meaning, and taking care to recite it correctly and with full concentration.
- **Purity of motive.** Reciting to seek Allah's pleasure, not worldly rewards such as wealth and fame.
- **Taking guidance from it and not elsewhere.** Ibn Kathir's definition of the turner-away includes "seeking guidance from other than it" — so the believer's discipline is to let the Book be the thing that decides.
- **Acting on what you have understood.** Understanding the laws the Qur'an lays down and then not complying with them is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, among the extreme forms of disregard.

The heaviest sentence in the passage is Ibn Kathir's remark that the Qur'an is a final warning for everyone it reaches. That includes the reader of these lines. The Reminder has reached you; ayah 100 begins the moment it does.

passages.title: The Trumpet, the levelled earth, the caller
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat carry us from the first blast of the Trumpet to the moment the whole of humanity is walking, silently, towards the place of judgement. They hold together as a single scene: a sound goes out (ayah 102), the guilty are gathered and start whispering about how short their lives were (ayat 103–104), the mountains that anchored the world are blown away and the earth is flattened into one bare plain (ayat 105–107), and across that plain everyone follows one caller with all voices hushed (ayah 108). Two threads run through it. One is the Trumpet — what it is, and what it means to live knowing it will sound. The other is a question about the mountains, which ayah 105 puts into the Prophet's ﷺ mouth to answer. Both lead to the same place: a warning about how little the world was worth.

## The Sur: a horn we are told about but cannot picture

**"The Day the Trumpet will be blown"** (ayah 102). The Arabic word is *aṣ-Ṣūr*. Ibn Kathir records that it has been confirmed in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the Ṣūr and replied that it is **a horn that will be blown into**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same report through Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar: a Bedouin asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Ṣūr, and he said it is something like a horn which will be blown — meaning that when the angel blows into it, all those who have lain dead for centuries will return to life.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds the sentence that should govern how we hold this: **only Allah knows the true nature of the Ṣūr.** We affirm exactly what the Prophet ﷺ said — a horn, really blown, really sounding — without trying to reduce it to something we can imagine, and without emptying it of meaning by treating it as mere imagery. Ibn Kathir also relates a hadith on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that it is a huge horn whose circumference is as large as the heavens and the earth. He follows that report with the statement that the angel Isrāfīl will blow into it.

**The Prophet ﷺ lived with this waiting.** Ibn Kathir relates another hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"How can I be comfortable when the one with the horn is holding it in his lips and his forehead is leaning forward, waiting to be given permission (to blow it)?"* The image is of an angel who has already raised the horn to his mouth, head bowed, waiting only for the command. Nothing remains between us and that sound except permission. When the people asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what should we say?", he told them to say:

> *Ḥasbunā'llāhu wa niʿma'l-wakīl, ʿala'llāhi tawakkalnā*
> "Allah is sufficient for us and what a good protector He is. Upon Allah we place our trust."

That is the passage's first piece of practical guidance, and it is striking that the answer to overwhelming fear is not more fear but reliance. (Ibn Kathir reports these narrations without naming a collection here, so we take the teaching as he transmits it.)

## "Blue-eyed": what terror does to a face

*"And We shall gather the criminals blue-eyed"* — **zurqan**. Ibn Kathir reports that it has been said this means having blue eyes **due to the severity of their horrifying situation**. It is a physical detail of dread: the resurrection is not an abstract accounting but something that visibly marks the bodies of those who denied it.

## The whispering (ayah 103) — and why they whisper

*Yatakhāfatūna baynahum* — "they will speak in a very low voice to each other." Ibn ʿAbbās explained this as **whispering among themselves**. It is worth pausing on how small this sounds against the scale of what has just happened: the Trumpet has shattered the world, and the guilty are muttering to one another like people caught out.

What are they whispering about? Time. *"You stayed no longer than ten"* — Ibn Kathir explains: in the abode of the worldly life you only tarried there for a little while; the time was equivalent to ten days or so. Then in ayah 104 Allah answers before they finish: *"We know very well what they will say"* — that is, Ibn Kathir says, in their condition of conversing amongst themselves. Whispering is what people do to keep a conversation private. Nothing is private. The knowledge of Allah reaches into a murmur exchanged between two terrified souls on the plain of gathering.

**"The most reasonable of them"** — *amthaluhum ṭarīqatan*, rendered "the best among them in knowledge and wisdom." Ibn Kathir glosses him as **the one with perfect intelligence amongst them** — and his verdict is even shorter than theirs: *"You stayed no longer than a day!"* The clearest mind among the deniers is the one who states most sharply how brief it all was.

## Why a whole lifetime feels like a day

Ibn Kathir gives the reason with unusual beauty: on the Day of Judgement **they will sense the shortness of the worldly life within themselves**, for the worldly life, *with its repetitious time periods and successive nights, days and hours, is as if it is just one day*. For this reason, he says, on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will think the worldly life was very short. Repetition compresses. A life of the same sunrises and the same evenings, seen from the far side, collapses into a single day — which is how it feels looking back even now, in this life.

But Ibn Kathir also detects a motive underneath their words. By insisting the time was so short, **they mean to prevent the establishment of the evidence against them** because of the shortness of the time they had — as though to plead: we hardly had a chance, how could we be held to account for a mere ten days? He answers this from the Qur'an itself, quoting Allah's words: *"Did We not give you lives long enough, so that whosoever would receive admonition could receive it? And the warner came to you"* (35:37). Both the time and the messenger were given. The excuse fails.

He also brings two parallel scenes. In Sūrat ar-Rūm: *"And on the Day that the Hour will be established, the criminals will swear that they stayed not but an hour"* — up to Allah's words *"but you knew not"* (30:55–56). And in Sūrat al-Muʼminūn: *"What number of years did you stay on earth?" They will say: "We stayed a day or part of a day. Ask of those who keep account." He will say: "You stayed not but a little, if you had only known!"* (23:112–114).

Ibn Kathir's conclusion here is the heart of the passage: *you only remained in it a little while — **if you only knew, you would have preferred the eternal life over the temporal life.** Yet you conducted yourselves in an evil manner. You gave the present, temporary life precedence over the eternal and everlasting life.* The tragedy is not that they miscalculated the length of the world; it is that they knew the truth only when knowing it could no longer help.

## "They ask you about the mountains" (ayah 105)

Here the passage answers a question. Ibn Kathir explains what is being asked: **will the mountains remain on the Day of Resurrection, or will they cease to exist?** For people who measured permanence by what they could see, mountains were the very definition of what does not move. The answer is dictated to the Prophet ﷺ word for word: *"Say: My Lord will blast them and scatter them as particles of dust."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks it: **He will take them away from their places, wipe them out and remove them completely.** Not toppled, not eroded — uprooted and dispersed.

## A level plain with nothing left to hide behind (ayat 106–107)

*"Then He shall leave it a level smooth plain."* The pronoun "it" refers, Ibn Kathir clarifies, to **the earth**. Two words do the work:

- **Qāʿ** — a piece of land that is level. Ibn Kathir says the phrase means **one expanse spread out**.
- **Ṣafṣafā** — Ibn Kathir says this word is used to **place emphasis** on that levelness. It has also been said that *ṣafṣafā* means that which has no vegetation growing in it. He prefers the first meaning, while noting that the second is **included by necessity** — a plain scoured flat has nothing growing on it anyway.

Then ayah 107 seals it: *"You will see therein no crookedness nor curve."* *ʿIwaj* and *amt* cover both directions — Ibn Kathir explains that on that Day you will not see in the earth **any valley, hill, or any place, whether low or elevated**. He notes that Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah and others of the Salaf all said the same — an unusually solid agreement among the early authorities.

Feel what this does. Every landscape we know is a landscape of hiding places: a fold in the ground, a ridge, a slope out of sight. All of it is gone. One flat, featureless expanse, and every single person standing on it, visible, with nowhere to step out of view.

## One caller, and no one turns aside (ayah 108)

*"On that Day mankind will follow strictly Allah's caller, no crookedness will they show him."*

Ibn Kathir writes: on the Day they see these conditions and these frightening sights, **they will hastily respond to the caller. Wherever they are commanded to go, they will rush to it.** *Lā ʿiwaja lah* — no crookedness — is the same word ayah 107 used of the earth, now used of the crowd's movement; Ibn Kathir explains it as being **without going to the right or left of that voice**.

And then Ibn Kathir lands the point a reader should carry away: **"If they had been like this in the worldly life, it would have been more beneficial for them, but here it does not benefit them."** In this world they were called and turned aside; called by the Messenger ﷺ and looked away. On that Day the same people obey instantly and perfectly — and the obedience no longer benefits them. Obedience counts while refusing is still possible.

He supports this with two other ayat about the same reversal: *"How clearly will they see and hear, the Day when they will appear before Us!"* (19:38), and *"hastening towards the caller"* (54:8).

## The great hush

*"And all voices will be humbled for the Most Gracious."* **Khashaʿat al-aṣwāt.** Ibn ʿAbbās explained the phrase simply: **"they will be silent."** As-Suddī said the same.

And it is *lir-Raḥmān* — for **the Most Gracious**. The name chosen at the moment of maximum awe is a name of mercy; for the believer, that is not a small comfort.

**"And nothing shall you hear except Hamsa"** — *hamsan*. The early scholars offered two readings, both reported by Ibn Kathir:

- **The steps of feet.** Saʿīd bin Jubayr related that Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "the steps of feet," and ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, Qatādah, Ibn Zayd and others all said the same.
- **A hidden voice.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that *hamsa* means "a hidden voice." This was also reported from ʿIkrimah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Saʿīd bin Jubayr combined them: *hamsa* means **the secret speech and the steps of feet**. Both readings paint one picture. All the noise of the world — its arguments, its boasting, its markets — reduced to the shuffle of countless feet on bare ground and, at most, a murmur under the breath. It is the same low whispering the guilty were doing in ayah 103, now the only sound left in creation.

## What this passage asks of us

- **Judge time honestly, now.** The deniers' verdict — "a day," "ten days" — is not wrong; it is only late. Ibn Kathir's point is that if they had known, they would have preferred the eternal life to the temporal one. Our task is to reach that conclusion while it can still change how a day is spent.
- **Do not save your obedience for when it is free.** Following the caller with no swerving is exactly what is asked of us now, when there is still a cost to it — and still a benefit in it. Ibn Kathir's words are plain: had they been like that in the worldly life, it would have been more beneficial for them.
- **Answer dread with reliance.** The Prophet ﷺ, who could not be at ease knowing the horn is already at the angel's lips, taught the people around him the response: *Ḥasbunā'llāhu wa niʿma'l-wakīl, ʿala'llāhi tawakkalnā.*
- **Live as though there is nothing to hide behind** — because on a plain with no valley and no hill, before the One who knows what is said in a whisper, there will not be.
